en: *Fahua Yishu*, Scroll One. Chapter One: The Introduction. Prior to entering the text, three points are first clarified:
first, the differences among the various versions; second, the distinctions in the sequence of chapters.
Third, the classification of the extent of the scriptures.
Regarding the differences in their categories, there are briefly seven examples:
first, taking a single assembly’s discourse as one section, such as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and other similar sūtras;
Second, many assemblies are combined into a single work, such as the *Avataṃsaka* and its like;
third, the initial portion of a scripture is treated as a single work, such as the six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
fourth, two complete portions are combined to form a single work, such as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Fifth, those that condense the original text into a single work, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya Sūtra* (*Xiaopin jing*) and others;
sixth, those that take the extensive version as a single work, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (*Dapin jing*) and its like;
seventh, those that treat a single chapter as a single work, following the precedent of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
Now, among the seven versions, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the complete original;
according to the Sanskrit text, it should be a concise version consisting of six thousand verses.
Second, regarding the distinctions in the sequence of the chapters (*śāstra-paṭala*), there are five further points of exposition:

first, the order of their arising; second, clarifying the extent of the meanings contained therein; third, the sequential arrangement of the chapters; fourth, clarifying the presence or absence of specific chapters; and fifth, the separate explanation of the introductory chapter (*nidāna-paṭala*).
Regarding the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), there are generally two gateways for the sequence of great mantras (*vidyā*):
first, the sequence of roots and conditions, which refers to teaching according to the specific capacity of the recipient;
second, the sequence of meaning and principle, which arises from the successive development of meanings.
Although the Buddha’s discourses possess both approaches, they mostly follow the sequence of faculties and conditions;
whereas the treatises composed by his disciples also possess both approaches, they mostly follow the sequence of principles and meanings.

Regarding the sequence of the mutual generation of the twenty-eight aspects: Now, when a person of ultimate realization preaches the Dharma, there must necessarily be a source and basis. Therefore, the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) is elucidated first. Once the introduction is concluded, the main body of the teaching (*saddharma*) should be opened;

for the purpose of revealing that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the ultimate truth, the prior opening of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) serves as a skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (*Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*) is elucidated next.

Those of superior faculties attain realization immediately upon hearing the preceding discourse on the Dharma; those of middling faculties, however, are unable to grasp the Dharma apart from its words. Therefore, they must wait for an analogy with an open mind. For this reason, the "Parable Chapter" is explained next, so that they may receive the preceding discourse on the Dharma and partake of the subsequent analogies.

Furthermore, because they attained understanding in common, there is the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding," which confirms their realization as being true; and because the parables are restated and elaborated for their sake, there is the "Chapter on the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs."

Having understood [the teaching] previously and now having it confirmed subsequently, they may expect their future fruition and are worthy of receiving a prediction of enlightenment; thus, there is the "Chapter on the Prediction.

Since those of superior and middling faculties have already attained realization from the beginning, while those of inferior faculties have not yet understood, he speaks of the origins of past karmic connections and the parable of the resting city in the present; thus, there is the "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter.

Those of inferior capacity, upon hearing the teachings of the two previous weeks as well as the subsequent account of past-life causes and conditions, immediately attained understanding and became fit to receive a prediction of enlightenment; hence there is the "Chapter on the Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples."
Since those of the exoteric tradition have already understood and those of the esoteric practice have also awakened, there is the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions upon Learners and Non-learners.

When the three proclamations were completed and the three faculties had simultaneously awakened, [the Buddha] further desired that this Dharma be heard by different people across successive ages; thus, he praised both the Dharma and the person to encourage the propagation of the Great Way, resulting in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master."
To verify that the three preceding discourses are not false and further to reveal the fruit-virtues of the Dharma-body, there is the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa.

Although the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" and the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa" praise those who realize the Dharma through others, they do not equal the case where Devadatta himself attained Buddhahood; thus, this chapter is presented as a verification to exhort beings to propagate the sutra, hence there is the "Chapter on Devadatta."

The preceding three chapters praised the Dharma through beautiful women to encourage the propagation of the sutra; since Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas received their mandate to proclaim and uphold it, there is the "Chapter on Upholding" (Dhāraṇī-parivarta).

As there are many hardships and difficulties in propagating the good path during an evil age, the methods for propagating the sutra are explained to enable one to dwell securely in the four practices with physical and mental happiness; hence there is the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" (Anrakugyō-parivarta).

The four practices having been established as causes, it is appropriate that the wondrous fruit be revealed; furthermore, there is the occasion for the Bodhisattvas to emerge, providing the conditions for opening up the matter of the long life-span; thus, there is the "Chapter on the Emergence.

Since the conditions for this revelation have already been manifested, it is appropriate that the main body of the teaching on the life-span be revealed; next, the "Chapter on the Life-Span" is explained.
It is taught that hearing [this teaching on] the lifespan yields twelve kinds of benefits; now, these are extensively analyzed, hence there is the "Chapter on the Analysis of Merit.

From the beginning up to the end of the "Chapter on the Analysis of Merit," two provisional and two real [teachings] have been clarified; these are mostly harsh to the ear and contrary to the mind, yet if one can rejoice in them, their merit is immeasurable, hence there is the "Chapter on Rejoicing."

The merit of the disciples' sympathetic joy is already boundless; because the Dharma Master proclaims and upholds it so that the six sense faculties become pure, there is the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master.

Although it is proclaimed that the five kinds of Dharma Masters obtain six thousand merits, this chapter now cites the past to provide direct testimony, demonstrating that these are not in vain and clarifying the merits of the superior grade; hence there is the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging."

Since the preceding chapters have already elucidated the meaning of praising the Dharma and its practitioners, the Buddhas of the ten directions, seeing that sentient beings of the two periods of time believe in and uphold this sutra, give rise to joy in their hearts and manifest seven kinds of supernormal powers; therefore, there is the "Chapter on Supernormal Powers."
The great illumination and circulation [of this teaching] consists of two parts: first, praise; second, entrustment.
Having concluded the section on praise, we now present the entrustment; therefore, there is the "Chapter on Entrustment."

The Medicine King received the sūtra and personally experienced its benefits; he sacrificed his body, life, and wealth as an offering to repay his debt of gratitude, thereby establishing a model for those who receive the mandate to propagate the Dharma.
Now, in order to explain this original account of the benefits for the assembly at this time, there is the "Chapter on the Original Deeds of the Medicine King."

Although Bhaiṣajyarāja repaid his debt of gratitude through offerings, he had not yet been able to propagate this Dharma; therefore, [the Buddha] summoned the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara to manifest emanations throughout the six realms of existence to widely disseminate the sutra for the sake of sentient beings, which is why there is the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara."

Although sentient beings desire to uphold this sutra, they encounter many obstacles; therefore, it is necessary to universally reveal all gates of practice to rescue them through great compassion. For this reason, the "Avalokiteśvara Chapter" is explained next.
Having already clarified how the person of Avalokiteśvara rescues from calamities, the *Dhāraṇī Chapter* is next taught to explain the method of protection through divine mantras.

Because propagating the sutra for the sake of sentient beings constitutes a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to them, the *Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha* is taught immediately thereafter.

To practice the One Vehicle is precisely to practice the conduct of Samantabhadra; therefore, Samantabhadra comes from afar to exhort and inspire [the practitioner], and thus there is the "Chapter on the Exhortation of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra."
Next, secondly, regarding the section clarifying the categories of the number of meanings possessed: although there are twenty-eight chapters, they receive their names according to three principles:
first, those named by means of a single meaning;
second, those designated by means of two meanings; [and third, those named by means of multiple meanings].
Third, there are three types of titles.
Regarding those that derive their names from a single meaning, four kinds are briefly explained:

first, those named after the Dharma, such as the "Expedient Means" chapter; second, those designated by way of analogy, such as the "Parable" chapter; third, those titled after a person, such as the "Devadatta" chapter; and fourth, those designated according to an event, such as the "Emergence from the Earth" chapter.
Regarding the establishment of names based on two meanings: sometimes both the person and the dharma are mentioned together, as in the "Universal Gate Chapter on Avalokiteśvara" and others;
sometimes the subject and object are combined into a single title, as in the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stupa" and others.

Regarding the establishment of names based on three meanings, as in the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples": "five hundred" is the name for the number, "disciples" is the designation for those individuals, and "receiving the prophecy" is the title for that dharma.
Question:
Is the title of this chapter spoken by the Buddha,
was it established by the compilers of the canon, or was it composed by later generations?
Answer: There are three meanings:

first, if a chapter title is indicated within the text—such as when it says, "Hearing the merits of this 'Chapter on the Original Acts of Bhaiṣajyarāja' are immeasurable"—this is spoken by the Buddha.

Second, as for the fact that the chapter titles are placed at the beginning of the text, this is because those who compiled the Dharma-piṭaka established these titles based on their understanding of the Buddha’s intended meaning.
Third, for example, the ninety chapters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other such texts lack chapter titles; these were all established by later generations.
In the "Preface to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*" (Dapin xu), Dharma Master Rui recounts the words of Master Kumārajīva, saying:

"The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of only three chapters, namely: the 'Introduction Chapter' (*Nidāna-parivarta*), the 'Chapter on the Deeds of Māra' (*Mārakarma-parivarta*), and the 'Chapter on Non-retrogression' (*Avivartika-parivarta*)."
"Because this chapter was not spoken by the Buddha, its other two parts were omitted and only the 'Introduction Chapter' (Xùpǐn) was retained.
Thus we know it was not spoken by the Buddha, but was composed by later people.

Third, regarding the sequence of the chapters: while the "Entrustment Chapter" (Parīndanā-parivarta) generally appears at the end of most sutras, the placement of this chapter after the "Supernatural Powers Chapter" (Rddhy-abhisaṃskāra-parivarta) in this sutra follows the Sanskrit original and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-upadeśa*.
Furthermore, in this land of Qin, the newly translated *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* places the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) at the very end of the scripture.

Now it is clear that Kumārajīva was skilled in the Qin language and perfectly grasped the profound purport of the sūtra; that he placed the "Chapter on Entrustment" immediately after the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Rddhy-abhisamskāra-parivarta*) must surely have a deep significance.

The reason for this is that if the "Chapter on Entrustment" were located at the end of the sutra, then it would be only upon the conclusion of the preaching of the sutra that the emanations would be commanded to each return to their own lands.
If that is so, then even until the conclusion of the sutra’s exposition, this remains a pure land.
When Gadgadasvara arrived, for what reason was he cautioned not to conceive a notion of inferiority regarding this land?

Furthermore, since the Bodhisattvas from the lower regions have already universally prostrated before the emanations, the Great Master of the Eastern Land should not alone receive the feet of Prabhūtaratna; likewise, Avalokiteśvara’s offering of the pearl should not be divided into only two portions.
Inferring from this, we know that the "Chapter on Entrustment" does not belong at the end of the sutra.
Regarding the placement of the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" at the conclusion, there are two great ways in which the One Vehicle is manifested:
first, that which all Buddhas ride upon; [and second, that which they entrust to others].
Second, it is that which is mounted by Bodhisattvas.
Thus, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states: "It is called 'Great' because it is that which is mounted by the Buddhas, the Great Beings;
furthermore, it is called 'Great' because it is that which is mounted by the great spiritual adepts (mahāsattva), such as Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya."

From the beginning of the sutra up to the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers," the Dharma upon which all Buddhas ride has been elucidated. The emanated Buddhas have come to reveal the extent of their lifespans; now that their remote longevity has been made manifest and they have each returned to their own lands, those lands revert to their former state of defilement. This concludes the meaning of this section, and for this reason, the entrustment is given.

From the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" through the "Samantabhadra-utsāha-parivarta," the vehicle upon which the bodhisattvas ride is elucidated; once both the causal and resultant vehicles are perfected, the assembly disperses. For this reason, the "Parīndanā-parivarta" (Chapter on Entrustment) is placed before the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta."
Furthermore, since the "Entrustment" chapter already clarifies the act of entrusting, the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" and subsequent chapters constitute the reception of the mandate to propagate the sutra.
Inferring from this, they ought not to be placed at the end of the scripture.

Fourth, regarding the presence or absence of chapters: in Kumārajīva’s translation of the sutra, there were only twenty-seven chapters. As for the subsequent addition of the "Devadatta Chapter," Shi Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu* states: "The monk Faxian of Shang Dinglin Monastery obtained this one chapter in the kingdom of Khotan."

The śramaṇa Shi Fayi of Waguan Monastery translated it in the twelfth month of the eighth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty as the *Devadattaparivarta Sūtra*, but he did not include it within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

"At the end of the Liang dynasty, there was a man from the country of Ujjayinī in Western India named Paramārtha (translated as Zhendi). He also translated and produced this chapter, which was first placed after the 'Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa'."
Question:

Dharmarakṣa translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in which the "Account of Devadatta" follows the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa. For what reason did Kumārajīva not translate this section?
Answer: This matter is difficult to clarify; for now, I shall explain it by means of three points.
First, foreign traditions state: "To the west of the shifting sands, this chapter is frequently found; to the east of the shifting sands, it is often absent."
The reason for this is that those of the Hīnayāna school all claim that the various Vaipulya sūtras were composed by Devadatta; consequently, some countries have omitted them.
Because Kumārajīva was in the kingdom of Kucha at that time, he did not see this chapter and therefore did not translate it.

Second, when Kumārajīva translated the scriptures, he often adopted a concise style in accordance with the capacities and dispositions of his audience; had he translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in its entirety, it would have been ten times longer than this, and fearing it would be difficult for people to seek out and study, he abridged it to one hundred fascicles.
Just as the *Śata-śāstra* was translated [into Chinese], it would have been of no benefit to this land; therefore, only a brief version was retained, consisting of fifty verses.
Thus, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* originally comprised ten fascicles, its redundant passages were deleted and it was abridged into seven scrolls.

Third, in the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stupa," the Buddha issues a command, and in the "Chapter on Upholding," it responds to that command; the flow of the discourse is thus continuous. However, the sudden insertion of the "Devadatta" chapter breaks this continuity, making the text appear inconsistent. Fearing that many might be confused by this in future ages, I have therefore deleted it.
Fifth, the separate explanation of the Introduction Chapter (*nidāna-varga*).

"Introduction" (*xu*) means gradual progression. By way of borrowing time, relying on a location, shaking the earth, and raining down flowers, these serve as the preliminaries for the formal teaching; because they proceed gradually, it is called the "Introduction."
Furthermore, "preface" (*nidāna*) means "sequence. First the dependent origination is clarified, and subsequently the main scripture is analyzed; this is indeed the sequence of its meaning.
Moreover, "preface" refers to an auspicious sequence; at the beginning of the scripture, the events are listed so that their auspicious order may be observed.
Furthermore, it is said that "preface" (*xu*) means "to unfold" (*shu*); because one wishes to manifest the meanings of the matters in an expansive manner, it is called a preface.

As for "chapter" (*pin*), the foreign term is *varga*, which here is translated as "chapter. A chapter is termed a "distinction" (*bie*); because the twenty-eight sections clarify different meanings, they are called distinctions.
Second is the classification, because their meanings are each organized into distinct categories.
Third is the clarification of the differences in the structural sections.
Question:
Examining the traditions from India and China, whether through written records or oral transmission, those who expound the sutras and engage in discussion employ no more than two methods:
first, the classification of topical sections (*ko-chang-men*); second, direct exegesis (*zhi-jie-shi*).

For instance, while Maitreyanātha explains that *Nirvāṇa* has seven divisions, Nāgārjuna’s commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā* contains no topical headings; this likely reflects the two categories of Indian masters: those who do and those who do not employ such structural divisions.

Hexi composed the *Nirvāṇa-śū* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra), opening it into five sections; Daorong lectured on the new *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, classifying it into nine tracks. As for the compilation of commentaries on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and the composition of annotations for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they merely dissected its profound subtleties without establishing a formal structure from beginning to end; this likely reflects the two perspectives—those who do and those who do not establish such divisions—held by various masters in China.
What is the meaning of this current exposition? The answer is: Indeed, the methods of transformation are manifold and the means of guidance are not uniform.

Examining the Sage’s intent, it takes the cessation of suffering as its primary aim; synthesizing the purport of the teachings, it takes the opening of the Way as its central principle. If one attains awakening through the opening [of the teaching], then the Sage’s instruction serves to open; if one receives the Way through convergence [with the teaching], then the Sage’s instruction serves to converge. Thus, if both are understood, they together constitute nectar; if both are misunderstood, they together become poison.
If this is so, how can one merely cling to a single path to respond to those who block the nine thoroughfares?
Question:
Some people say:
Whether a sutra is large or small, it generally consists of three sections: the introduction (nidāna), the main body (dharmadeśanā), and the dissemination (parīndanā).
How is this so? Answer:

Having received the treatise that leads toward Perfect Penetration and the discourse that opens the Way to extinguish afflictions, one is fully able to discern the right and wrong of various paths; why then need one inquire further about the merits or failings of the "Three Stages"?
If one insists on adhering strictly to three chapters, one’s errors will be many.

If sentient beings attain awakening by means of the initial division, then the initial division is correct; if they receive the Way by means of the later chapters, then the later chapters are not peripheral. How can you claim that the initial and later sections are not the orthodox scriptures while only the middle section constitutes the ultimate principle? Is this not to grasp the compass and square while confining the interpretation of the Great Dharma?
Question:

The first section describes entering meditative absorption, emitting light, raining down flowers, and shaking the earth; since these serve as the gradual prelude to the formal teaching, why is it called the "main scripture" (sūtra)?
Answer:

The Treatise states: "The Dharma-treasure of Nirvana enters through many gates. The Sūtras proclaim: "Awakening is received differently, and the Buddha’s deeds are not of one kind. Sometimes one reforms the mundane by means of sound; sometimes one achieves sainthood through silence; sometimes one transcends the secular through light; and sometimes one enters the Way by means of fragrant food. Thus, the three karmas are none other than conditions for benefit, and the six sense-objects are all Buddha-deeds. This is because the former sages flowed forth through perfect transformation, whereas those of the Semblance and Final Ages are entangled in narrow texts—this latter state is certainly not acceptable.
Heqidao Lang opened this sutra into five sections. As for these five sections:
first, from "Thus have I heard" through the Introduction Chapter, it sets forth the signs that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* must inevitably be transformed;
second, from the "Expedient Means" Chapter to the "Dharma Master" Chapter, it clarifies that the essence of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the non-dual Dharma.
Third, from the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa" through the "Chapter on the Lifespan," it clarifies the fruit of the eternally abiding Dharmakāya of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
fourth, from the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" to the "Chapter on Entrustment," it clarifies the merits produced by practicing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
fifth, from the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" to the end of the sutra, it clarifies the methods for the circulation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Dharma Master Longguang divided this sutra into two sections:
from the first chapter through the thirteenth chapter, the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (Anle xing pin), is the opening of the three vehicles to reveal the One Vehicle;
next, from the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth" (Yongchu pin) onwards, the fourteen chapters constitute the opening of the near to reveal the distant.
Within each of these two sections, the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination are further divided, resulting in a total of six sections.
Master Yin categorized this sutra into four sections:
the "Introductory Chapter" constitutes the introduction.

From the "Expedient Means" chapter through the "Peaceful Practices" chapter, spanning twelve chapters, the three vehicles are opened to reveal the One; this elucidates the provisional vehicle and the true vehicle.

From the "Chapter on the Emergence" to the two and a half chapters preceding the verses spoken by Maitreya in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," the near is opened up to reveal the distant, clarifying the provisional body and the true body.
From the end of the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" until the conclusion of the sutra constitutes the section on the dissemination of the teaching (*pariṇāmanā*).

Although it is stated that everything preceding the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" belongs to the causal section (*hetu-bhāga*), the three chapters following the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" also represent the gradual progression toward the ultimate fruit; thus, one must view these two sections from both perspectives.

Why is this? Because in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa," Many Treasures (Prabhūtaratna) assists in prolonging life to seek out those who can transmit the sutra; thus, it is only then that the "Chapter on Upholding" and the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" circulate the cause, and so these are designated as the "Entrustment of the Causal Section.

Next, the emergence of the Bodhisattvas from the earth serves as the formal introduction to the method for the lifespan; since they emerge due to the aforementioned prolongation of life, the first three chapters also carry the meaning of establishing the discourse on the lifespan. Therefore, both aspects must be discussed.
Question:
Among the doctrines taught by the various masters, which one accords with the fundamental tenet? Answer:
If all [teachings] can open the Way and accord with the capacities and conditions of beings, then among these various expositions, none is not the true doctrine.
However, when one traces the texts and examines their meanings, the three sections are the most extensive; thus, they ought to be employed.
Question:
Since it was previously established that there are faults in these three sections, why are they used now? Answer:
There are two aspects to this meaning:
the general and the specific.
To discuss them generally, if one receives [the teachings] from all three and attains awakening through them, then all three constitute the correct teaching.
Now, speaking of them separately, it is appropriate to open three sections.
If one fully grasps the meaning of both the general and the specific, there is no logical flaw.
Question:
What is the significance of establishing [the treatise] in three sections?
Answer: Briefly stated, there are ten meanings:

First, when the Sages preach the Dharma, they invariably follow a systematic order; profound principles used to transform ordinary people must startle the ears and eyes. To speak haphazardly would fail to arouse a sense of reverence; therefore, a preface must be placed at the beginning of a sutra.
Since the mind has already been stilled through faith, it is appropriate to establish the school and transmit the Dharma; therefore, the "Correct Exposition" follows next.
Because sentient beings are inexhaustible and great compassion is limitless, and because one desires to pass on these instructions, the "Circulation" section concludes the work.
Second, the three periods are clarified in order to counter the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
The non-Buddhists say:
"Only the beginning is auspicious; the middle and the end are not auspicious. Because the beginning is auspicious, the middle and the end are also auspicious."
The Buddha-dharma is not like that; it is divided into three parts, and all three are auspicious.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The initial words are good, the intermediate words are good, and the final words are also good."
Third, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All Buddhas provide benefit at three times:

first, when they are bodhisattvas, they benefit beings in the past; second, when they have attained Buddhahood, they benefit beings in the present; third, after their parinirvāṇa, they benefit beings in the future."
The introduction and the main body refer to benefiting sentient beings in the present, while the circulation [of the teaching] refers to benefiting them in the future.
Fourth, the introductory discourse inspires faith, while the main discourse generates wisdom.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith and crossed by means of wisdom. These two constitute one's own practice (*sva-caryā*);
what follows, the propagation [of the teaching], is what is called transforming others (*para-caryā*).

Fifth, there are two further types of persons: those with profound merit and wisdom who encounter the Buddha and hear the Dharma, and thus clarify the sequence and correctness; and those with inferior merit and wisdom who merely encounter the physical scriptures and must therefore ensure their circulation.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in the "Sadāprarudita" chapter, states: "Those with abundant merit and wisdom hear the teaching of Prajñā directly from Dharmodgata; those with meager merit and wisdom merely encounter the Prajñā written upon golden tablets. This refers precisely to that matter.
Sixth, there are two ways in which the Tathāgata’s true Dharma is elucidated and propagated:
first, the lighting of the lamp; second, the transmission of the lamp.
Lighting the lamp refers to the introduction and the main body [of the teaching], while the transmission of the lamp refers to its circulation.
Seventh, there are generally two types of Buddhas of the three periods:
first, those who receive the entrustment from a preceding Buddha; second, those who entrust [the teaching] to a subsequent Buddha.
The Introduction and the Main Body constitute receiving the entrustment from a preceding Buddha, while the Dissemination constitutes entrusting it to a subsequent Buddha.
Eighth, there are only three parts:

first, the preliminary expedient means, which is the introductory discourse; second, the body of the sutra, which is the main discourse; and third, the function of the sutra, which clarifies the discourse on its circulation.
Ninth, there are furthermore three types of exposition:
first, exposition by gradual progression; second, the correct exposition; and third, eulogistic exposition, which is synonymous with circulation.
Tenth, as there are superior, middling, and inferior faculties among sentient beings, the Tathāgata’s teaching likewise possesses three stages.
The first chapter is called the "Introductory Exposition" (Nidāna).

From the "Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya) chapter through the halfway point of the "Distinguishing Merits" (Puṇyaparyāya) chapter—comprising fifteen and a half chapters—is called the "Main Exposition" (Prakaraṇa).
From the verse on "measuring" (*gaṇanā*) onwards, through eleven chapters and a half of the sutra, is called the *pariṇāmanā-vibhāga* (the section on dissemination).
Question:
Since the introductory section is named the "Introductory Chapter," why are the main body and the dissemination not named the "Chapter on the Main Exposition" and the "Chapter on Dissemination"?
Answer: Because the text of the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) is brief and its meaning is clear without confusion, it is simply named the "Introductory Chapter.

Because the text of the "Main Exposition" (Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra) is extensive and its meaning is broad, the general name is set aside in favor of a specific designation. The same applies to the "Circulation" (Pariṇāmanā).
Each of these three sections is divided into two chapters.
The Introduction is divided into two:
first, the Prologue of Authentication; second, the Prologue of Origination.

The "Certification of Faith" (samyak-pratyaya) causes future sentient beings to generate faith in the sutra; by manifesting various spiritual wonders, it inspires the authentic scripture to benefit those in the present. Thus, through its transformative influence, it benefits both worlds, which is why the two prefaces are explained together.
The correct exposition consists of two parts:
first, from the "Expedient Means" chapter through the end of the "Dharma Master" chapter, it clarifies the expedient means of the vehicle and the reality of the vehicle;
second, from the "Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa" chapter through the "Comparative Merit" chapter, it clarifies the expedient means of the body and the reality of the body.

The reason for establishing these two categories is that "vehicle" refers to the dharma that is mounted, while "body" refers to the person who mounts it; only when these two gates are complete is the meaning of "vehicle" fully realized.
Question:
Regarding bodily skillful means and bodily reality, what is this person? Answer:

The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fa-hua lun) explains the "Life Span" chapter by clarifying the three Buddhas, while the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* distinguishes the three Buddhas in its "Chapter on the Three Bodies. Thus, we know that the three bodies are the three Buddhas, and the Buddha is none other than the person.
Question:
Regarding the provisional vehicle and the ultimate vehicle, if the One Vehicle is taken as the ultimate and the other two as provisional, what is the meaning of "body" (śarīra)? Answer:
Among the three bodies, the Dharma-body is further regarded as the reality, while the Reward-body and Transformation-body are regarded as the provisional.
Question:

If the Dharma-body is established as the reality and the response to sentient beings' needs is established as the Reward-body, such that only one reality and one response are posited, does this principle also apply to the vehicles?
Answer:

The Mahāyāna is taken as the ultimate reality (śūnyatā) and the Hīnayāna as the provisional (upāya). Furthermore, regarding the one provisional and one ultimate, there are three meanings concerning the differences between the present and the past:
first, speaking of both together; second, concealing both together; and third, revealing both together.

Regarding what is called "teaching by pairs": when he first attained perfect enlightenment at the site of the tranquil and extinguished Way-place (śānta-mārga-kṣetra), he elucidated two meanings for the sake of the bodhisattvas. This is evidenced, for example, in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Adhimukti-parivarta*), where the parable of the elder distinguishes the true body, and the array of precious objects illustrates the true vehicle (*yāna*). This is precisely that proof.

Next, regarding "double concealment": one removes precious, noble garments and puts on tattered, soiled clothes; by means of this physical expedient, one conceals the reality of the body, hiding it from the side so that another person may be sent. This is precisely using the expedient of the vehicle to conceal the reality of the vehicle; this is what is meant by "double concealment."

Regarding the "opening of the three pairs": this clarifies that the three vehicles of the past were expedient means (*upāya*) and the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the present is the ultimate truth; it distinguishes that the bodies of the past were expedient means and the body of the present is the ultimate truth—this is what is meant by "opening the pairs."
However, the vehicle and the body have no separate substance; they are one and the same right contemplation, spoken of differently according to the occasion.

Because its functioning is sovereign, it is called a "vehicle" (yāna); because its substance can be taken as a model, it is called the "Dharma"; and because the Dharma constitutes the body, it is termed the "Dharmakāya."

Regarding the two aspects of circulation: first, from the conclusion of the verses on comparative evaluation up to the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Ṛddhividhi-parivarta) is called circulation by way of praise;
second, from the "Chapter on Entrustment" (Parīndanā-parivarta) up to the end of the "Chapter on Exhortation" (Saṃcodana-parivarta) clarifies circulation by way of entrustment.

The reason for clarifying these two points is that, as one intends to entrust the Dharma to others so that they may propagate it, it is necessary to praise the profound efficacy of the Dharma and the weighty virtue of the person; only when beings rejoice in these benefits will they accept the mandate to propagate the sutra. Therefore, the former section clarifies the praises, while the latter section distinguishes the entrustment.
Now, in explaining the text of the Preface of Certification and Faith, there are generally two intentions:
first, a general explanation;
second, a detailed explanation.
In the general explanation, there are briefly six sections:
First, the Section on the Origin.

The Buddhas of the three periods all preach the twelve divisions of the sūtras through six matters; however, they invariably wait for an attendant to pose a question before commanding him to record them.
As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha-sūtra*: "The attendant Ānanda posed four questions in total:

first, who should be taken as one's teacher; second, by what path should one practice; third, how should one dwell together with evil persons; and fourth, what words should be placed at the beginning of the Buddha’s sūtras?"
The Tathāgata replied:

"The precepts can instruct and guide, and thus may serve as a teacher; the four foundations of mindfulness destroy the perversions, and by relying on these one practices the Path; the Brahma-dharma remains silent to subdue those evil persons; and at the beginning of all sūtras, these six matters are invariably set forth."
Question: For what reason are only four matters asked, neither more nor less? Answer:

First, correct practice is clarified; next, correct understanding is clarified; and finally, the conditions for practice that eliminate obstacles are distinguished. These three gates must necessarily rely upon the sacred teachings; since these four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are already complete, they cannot be increased or decreased.

2. Regarding the section on determining the number [of categories]: The masters of the ancient translations explained only five matters; this interpretation is rejected because it contradicts the meaning and lacks textual authority.

Herein, we clarify that there are generally six matters: first, "Thus" (*evam*), referring to the Dharma heard; second, "I heard" (*śrutam mayā*), referring to the person who heard; third, "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), referring to the time when the Dharma was heard; fourth, identifying the Buddha as the Teacher; fifth, clarifying the place where the Dharma was heard; and sixth, clarifying that it was heard together with the assembly.
When these six gates are possessed, the meaning is fully perfected.
Furthermore, as the verse in Vasubandhu’s *Pradīpa-śāstra* states: "The first three clarify the disciples; the latter three testify to the Teacher's teaching. All sūtras and dharma-gates are thus."
Thus we know that these six matters originate from the authentic text.

Regarding the first three points clarifying the disciple: "Thus" refers to the disciple’s faith; the following phrase is the disciple’s self-designation as "I"; and the third phrase clarifies that there was a specific time for hearing the Dharma. Since the section beginning with "The Buddha dwelling" identifies the Teacher, it is known that the final three phrases serve as evidence of the Master’s teaching.
Third, regarding the section on the purpose of the introduction: there are three general intentions for establishing these six matters.
First, it is to generate faith; "Thus" (evam) is precisely faith itself.
The final five phrases are intended to engender faith; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By specifying the time, the place, and the persons, one causes faith to arise.
'Time' refers to 'at one time'; 'place' refers to the location where [the teaching was given]; and 'persons' refers to Ānanda, the Buddha, and the assembly of fellow listeners."
Therefore, these three matters encompass the preceding five gates; because they include the time, place, and person, what has been transmitted is trustworthy.
Second, these six matters are established to distinguish [this teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

The scriptures of the non-Buddhists all begin by marking the two characters "A-yu" (Āyuṣmat). At the head of the Tathāgata’s teachings, six matters are placed at the beginning; three of these are intended to distinguish them from heterodox doctrines, while disciples composing treatises offer reverence to the Triple Gem. Thus, in the sūtras of the Tathāgata, these six matters appear at the outset.

Fourth, regarding the gate of existence and non-existence: when the Buddha was preaching the sutras, they possessed the six essential elements but had not yet been arranged into written form. As he was about to enter nirvana, he commanded that they be established; thus, at the beginning of the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka, they were first placed at the head of the sutras.

Fifth, regarding the gate of completeness and incompleteness: other sūtras fully possess six elements, whereas the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* lacks the element of "those present" (the assembly) in its abbreviated version; this shall be explained later.

Sixth, regarding the sequence of the opening and closing sections: most sūtras begin with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). Because faith is the primary gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma, the phrase "thus" (*evam*) is placed first;
because one must establish the validity of this faith, the phrase "I have heard" (*mayā śrutam*) follows immediately after.
As stated in the *Jentaka Sūtra*: "Thus have I heard. This initial phrase identifies the person who possesses faith; only after this can one subsequently give rise to faith in the sūtra.
Question:
When the Buddha preached the sūtras, how were there six matters? Answer:

Since one preaches the Dharma only when beings possess faith, we know that when the Buddha spoke this sutra, there were necessarily an attendant, those who heard the Dharma, the time, the teacher, the dwelling place, and those who heard it together; thus, we know that these six matters truly exist.
Next, the six matters are explained individually, constituting six sections.
Regarding the term "thus" (*evam*), the *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra* states: "'Thus' is the beginning of resonance and response."

Just as names are established in accordance with the capacities [of beings], there is nothing that does not constitute a designation; sentient beings respond through what is non-erroneous, while the Tathāgata responds by conforming to their capacities.
The transmitters of the scriptures maintain that the "Name-Teaching" (myōkyō) arises from responsive resonance; therefore, they say, "Thus.

Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "When the Perfected One preaches the Dharma, he does so solely to manifest the 'Suchness' (nyo). Since only Suchness is what is 'thus,' it is called 'Thus' (ninyo)."
Master Yao said:

"In this way, transmitting what has been heard to those who have not yet heard it is truly because it is trustworthy; now, it is clear that the words being transmitted must surely reach the ultimate."
"To act in accordance with principle and not miss the opportune moment is what is meant by 'Thus' (evam).
Tanshen said: "'Thus' refers to words that are neither disparaging nor laudatory."
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"Regarding 'thus' (evam): it is called 'thus' because it is free from the five kinds of slanders.
As for the five kinds of slanders:"
First, to say that the cause and effect in this sutra definitely exist is called the slander of exaggeration (*samāropa-mithyādṛṣṭi*);
second, to say that the cause and effect in this sutra definitely do not exist is called the slander of deprecation (*apavāda-mithyādṛṣṭi*);
third, to say that the cause and effect in this sutra both exist and do not exist is called the slander of contradiction (*virodha-mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Fourth, as when one says that the cause and effect in this sutra neither exist nor do not exist, it is called the slander of delusion;
fifth, as when one says that the cause and effect in this sutra are neither non-existent nor non-non-existent, it is called the slander of frivolous conceptualization.
"Because it is free from these five kinds of slander, it is called 'Thus' (Evam). Guangzhai said:
"'Thus' refers to the title placed at the beginning before transmitting what has been heard; it designates a specific section of the canon."
"This sutra, such as it is, I have personally heard from the Buddha; thus, for me, hearing it constitutes its transmission.
Emperor Wu of Liang said:
"'Such as this' means that these words are what was spoken by the Buddha; therefore, it is called 'such as this' (evam)."
Some say: "There are three ways to understand this: first, in relation to the Buddha;
second, in relation to the principle; and third, in relation to Ānanda."
Regarding the term "conforming to the Buddha": the teachings spoken by all Buddhas of the three periods of time do not differ; therefore, they are called "Thus" (Tathā).
Because they are taught identically, they are called "Correct" (Is).
All Buddhas teach this in common; therefore, it is to be trusted.
As for the statement "conforming to principle": the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not differ between past and present, and is thus called "Suchness" (*tathatā*);
because it is taught in accordance with that Suchness, it is called "Correct" (*satya*).
Since these are words of ultimate principle—neither adding nor subtracting and thus decisively trustworthy—they are called "Thus" (evam).
To explain this in terms of Ānanda: with respect to the Buddha’s teaching, what he transmits does not differ from the original, and is therefore called "Thus" (like);
with respect to the principle, whatever he speaks is nothing other than the truth, and is therefore called "Right" (is).
Some say: "In this way, 'ru' (如) refers to the pattern being in accordance with principle, while 'shi' (是) means that two things resemble each other;
'shi' (是) means that there is nothing that is not so regarding a single thing."
Because the words are able to express the principle in a manner that corresponds to it, they are called "like" (yathā);
as for the principle, it is ultimately correct and nothing about it fails to be "is" (tathā).
Now, regarding the term "thus" (evam), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
Question: "Why is it that at the beginning of all sutras one says 'Thus' (evam)? Answer:
"The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith and crossed by means of wisdom; 'Thus' is precisely faith."
"Because of faith one says 'it is thus' (evam), whereas if one lacks faith one says 'it is not thus'; this is why the Buddhist sūtras initially state 'it is thus'.
Question: What is the difference between "thus" (ru) and "what" (shi)?
Answer:

As for the name, it is such as it truly is and not false; this is called being ultimate and appropriate, having no meaning other than its literal sense. Because one believes that the Buddha’s Dharma is such as it truly is and not false, and because it is not erroneous but correct, one’s faith is described as "thus" (evam).
Question:
Is this based on the substance of faith,
or is it due to the characteristics of faith?
Answer: This is called the characteristic of faith (*śraddhā-nimitta*), not the essence of faith itself.

Because one expresses it in speech externally, saying "this matter is thus," it indicates that there is sincerity within the inner mind; therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "‘Thus’ refers to the characteristic of faith."
Question:
Is this based on that which is able to believe,
or is it based on that which is believed?

Answer: The *Śāstra* states, "Faith is that which enables entry into the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma. This indicates that the Buddha-dharma is what is entered; therefore, we know this refers to the capacity for faith.
If one says that this matter is thus, then this matter belongs to the object of faith; thus, such a statement inherently contains both the subject and the object.
Question:
Is this a communication of faith?
Is this distinct faith? Answer:

To believe in the correctness of the Buddha-dharma and thereby disbelieve the heterodoxy of external paths constitutes the beginning of distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, and the foundation for establishing all virtues; it belongs to the category of general faith.

However, the sutras comprise both the Great and the Small Vehicles, and the teachings comprise both the provisional and the real. The faith that trusts the Great Vehicle is not the same as the faith that trusts the Small Vehicle; this is what constitutes "distinctive faith.
Question:
Is this intended to clarify Ānanda’s faith?
Question: Is this to clarify the faith of other people? Answer:
Those who possess faith immediately enter the Buddha-dharma; this is a general exhortation for all to believe and accept, not one restricted solely to Ānanda.
Question:
Who is able to believe in the One Vehicle? Answer:
There are six kinds of people who cannot give rise to faith:
first, those sentient beings who give rise to craving and are deeply attached to worldly pleasures, and thus cannot believe or accept [the teaching].
Second, those of the class who give rise to views, who judge themselves right and others wrong, and likewise do not give rise to faith.

Third, those who seek the two vehicles mistake fish eyes for pearls and cast away the night-shining gem while clutching their swords; thus, the followers of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna in foreign lands drink from separate rivers, and so they do not produce faith or acceptance toward the One Vehicle.
Fourth, they claim that the teachings of the Lotus Sūtra are still impermanent, and thus do not give rise to faith or acceptance upon hearing the discourse on eternal abiding.

Fifth, they claim that while this sūtra clarifies the nature of permanence through concealed expressions, they do not give rise to faith or acceptance when hearing the explicit teaching of permanence.

Sixth, this sutra clarifies that those who cling to permanence establish the view of eternalism; hearing the teaching of the path of quiescence—which is neither permanent nor impermanent—they do not give rise to faith. Thus, the "Chapter on Seeing the Stupa" states: "To grasp empty space with one's hand is not difficult; to believe, accept, copy, and uphold [this teaching] is truly not easy. These words are proven true!
Now, if one is free from the aforementioned faults and the mind has nothing else to rely upon, one will then be able to believe and accept [the teaching].

Regarding the phrase "I have heard": this single expression refers to the fruit of the faith that is produced; the five matters below refer to the causes that produce such faith. Because Ānanda witnessed three instances of public censure yet possessed eight meritorious qualities, and because he personally attended the Tathāgata for over twenty years, transmitting the Buddha’s words, people would certainly believe him.
Therefore, this is the cause for the arising of faith.
Question:

Ānanda was born in the middle of the night on the very night the Buddha attained the Way; he began attending the Buddha at the age of twenty-five. Thus we know that what was taught during the first twenty-five years was not heard by Ānanda, while what was taught during the subsequent twenty-five years he heard in its entirety.
In the subsequent twenty-five years, there are generally three categories:
first, those that were heard, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others;
second, those that were not heard, such as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and others.
Third, there are cases where one hears what was not heard. For example, in the single scripture of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, there are four assemblies:
Ānanda heard [the teachings] in the two assemblies at the Āmra grove, but he did not hear them in the two gatherings at Vaiśālī.
For what reason do all the sutras of this dispensation begin with "Thus have I heard"?
Answer: I shall now cite two sutras and explain this by means of their fundamental and manifested aspects.
First, regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, explained according to its fundamental meaning: Ānanda, the learned one (*bahuśruta*), was naturally able to comprehend both the permanent and the impermanent;
since he understood them naturally, he also naturally attained hearing [the Dharma].
2. According to the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), if one explains based on the manifested traces, it is only through the Buddha’s repeated instruction that [the teaching] can be heard.
Question:
By what virtue and by what samādhi was Ānanda able to uphold the Buddha’s sutras?
Answer: Shi Dao’an stated: “The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* says, ‘It was transmitted by Ānanda, who had attained the Buddha-mind Samādhi.
The *Vajrapuṣpa Sūtra* says, ‘It was transmitted by Ānanda, who had attained the Dharma-nature Awakening Samādhi.’”
Question: Since it was actually heard by the ear, for what reason is it called "heard by me"? Answer:
There are seven reasons why one says "I have heard":
First, the Buddha commanded that it be said "I have heard"; now, in accordance with the Buddha's instruction, it is called "I have heard.
Second, at the time of compiling the Dharma-piṭaka, Kāśyapa asked Ānanda:
"Where did the Buddha first preach the Dharma?
Ānanda answered the assembly by stating, "Thus have I heard.
Thirdly, he says "I heard" to provide testimony that the Dharma was transmitted by a person; thus, by specifying the time, place, and person of the teaching, he inspires faith.
Fourth, Ānanda gave rise to the three types of wisdom upon hearing what the Buddha taught; because he exercised mastery [in this regard], he said, "I heard.

Fifth, when Ānanda listened to the Buddha's teaching, he was like a vessel that is not overturned—possessing no distracted mind; like a vessel that does not leak—possessing no forgetful mind; and like a vessel that does not stink—possessing no perverted mind. The first is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the second is the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*), and the third is the power of wisdom (*prajñā*). Because he possesses these three kinds of mastery and is thus entitled to be called "I," he said, "I heard."
Sixth, the ear is particular while the self is universal; because the universal is established and the particular is set aside, it is said "I heard.
Seventh, the self is the root while the ear is the branch; because the root is established and the branch is set aside, it is called "I heard."
Question:
What is meant by "hearing"? Is it heard by a person?
Is it heard by means of the sense organs (*indriya*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), or objects (*viṣaya*)? Answer:
It is heard through causes and conditions; since hearing occurs through causes and conditions, there is nothing that is heard. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
"Phenomena produced by causes and conditions are, in their very nature, quiescent extinction. Therefore, one hears while not hearing, and does not hear while hearing.
Because hearing is as if not hearing, one explains the true mark without destroying conventional designations;
because not hearing is as if hearing, one establishes all phenomena without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, because one hears while appearing not to hear, it is "hearing the non-hearing";
because one does not hear while appearing to hear, it is "non-hearing hearing.
Is "non-hearing hearing" truly hearing?
Is it not the case that hearing and non-hearing are both non-hearing?

Therefore, that which is neither hearing nor non-hearing is called the Middle Way, while hearing yet not hearing is termed a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). Thus, the *Śāstra* states: "It is also a provisional designation, and it is also the meaning of the Middle Way."

However, the Middle and the Provisional are themselves dependent origination; therefore, the Middle is called the "Provisional-Middle" and the Provisional is called the "Middle-Provisional. Since the Middle-Provisional is not the Provisional and the Middle-Provisional is not the Middle, they are neither Middle nor Provisional. Thus, the characteristics of verbal expression are quiescent. This does not mean that one must transform prior phenomena to then call them quiescent; rather, the hearing of dependent origination is fundamentally quiescent from the very beginning.
Therefore, this sutra says: "All dharmas, from their very origin, are eternally characterized by quiescence.
Question:
What benefit is gained by hearing this?
Answer: This sutra correctly elucidates the causal conditions for the Great Matter, namely, the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision refer to the four wisdoms:
The Tathāgata’s wisdom, the Buddha’s wisdom, spontaneous wisdom, and teacherless wisdom:

by knowing that there is nothing heard in what is heard, the Tathāgata’s wisdom arises; by hearing that which is not heard, the Buddha’s wisdom arises; the simultaneous and effortless manifestation of these two is called spontaneous wisdom; and because these three are not obtained from a teacher, they are called teacherless wisdom.

Once hearing has given rise to the four kinds of wisdom, all that is performed must be understood with precise awareness of causes and conditions as they give rise to these four wisdoms, thereby entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
"At one time" means that there was a specific occasion for the preaching of the sutra; therefore, it is trustworthy.
Now, I shall briefly clarify four meanings.

First, the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma over fifty years spanned a vast period of time; here, in contrast to that long duration, this sutra is clarified as being spoken on a single occasion, and thus it is called "at one time."
Second, "one" refers to a single section of a sutra;
that is, when a single section of a sutra is being taught, it is called "at one time.

Third, it refers to the moment when the mental activities of sentient beings are unified—that is, when the capacity for the One Vehicle is awakened and the teaching of the One Vehicle is expounded, it is therefore called "at one time."
Question:
Since all sūtras state that they were spoken "at one time," can it be said that the One Vehicle was taught simultaneously? Answer:

This sutra states, "All that is done is for the sake of a single matter"; thus we know that all teachings are spoken to open the way to the One Vehicle, and are all designated as being given at one time.
Fourth, because the capacity of the disciples and the teaching coincide without discrepancy, it is called "at one time.
Question:
Is this a provisional time?
Is this the ultimate reality? Answer: The *Samyag-darśana-śāstra* states:

"The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and sometimes speak of non-self; yet within the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is neither self nor non-self. Furthermore, one should also say: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of the provisional (*prajñapti*), and sometimes speak of the non-provisional; yet within the true mark of all phenomena, it is neither provisional nor non-provisional."
Question:
How are the provisional and the non-provisional explained? Answer:
The transformation of internal disciples into those bound by precepts clarifies that this is not a provisional time;
the universal transformation of both monastics and laypeople to distinguish provisional names is as explained at length in the *Śāstra*.
"Buddha" refers, fourthly, to the designation of the Master.
There are five general reasons for designating him as "Buddha":
first, Ānanda’s response to Kāśyapa’s question.
Kāśyapa asked: "In what place did the Buddha first preach the Dharma?
For this reason, he specifies "the Buddha."
Second, if one did not specify that it is the Buddha who speaks and directly clarified these five matters, then one would not know whether this sutra was spoken by a Māra or by the Buddha;
nor whether it was taught by those within the Buddhist path or by outsiders.
Now, wishing to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, or the internal and the external, I have designated "Buddha" [as the primary authority].
Third, there are five types of persons who speak the Buddha-dharma:
first, the Buddha himself;...
2. Disciples' discourse;
3. Devas' discourse; 4. Rishis' discourse;
Fifth, regarding the teaching by an emanation:
now, in order to clarify that this sutra was spoken by the Buddha and not by any other person, the Buddha is designated.
Fourth, so that sentient beings of future generations, upon hearing it was spoken by the Buddha, may give rise to profound respect and faith, the Buddha is designated.
Fifth, because one wishes to establish it as a sūtra, the Buddha’s name must be cited.

Whatever is spoken by the Buddha must be prefaced with the Buddha’s name; even the words of his disciples must likewise be prefaced with the Buddha’s name. As in the *Vimalakīrti* and *Śrīmālā* sūtras, all are prefaced to the Buddha; were they not so prefaced, they would not constitute sūtras.
The Buddha has three meanings:
first, he is self-awakened, distinguishing him from ordinary worldlings;
second, he awakens others, distinguishing him from those of the two vehicles.
Third, the perfection of awakening distinguishes [the Buddha] from those bodhisattvas.
According to the three types of Buddhas as determined by traditional exegesis, none of them possess the true meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*):

First, if it is said that this sutra describes the Buddha as still being impermanent, then he is merely awakened to impermanence but has not yet realized the reality of all phenomena; therefore, he is not called "Awakened."

Second, if one says that this sutra clarifies permanence through concealed characteristics, then since it is described as "concealed," it is still a state of non-awakening and cannot be called Buddhahood.

Third, if one says that this sutra establishes that the Buddha is definitively and eternally abiding, then this is the view of eternalism and is still termed ignorance; therefore, it is not called awakening.

Now, as for what is called "awakening" (bodhi): it is the awakening to the fact that all phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent, and furthermore, that they do not exist within or without the four propositions; because one thoroughly comprehends the reality of phenomena, it is called awakening.
Question:
Where in this sutra does this passage appear? Answer: [The answer follows].
The "Chapter on the Lifespan" states: "The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are: there is no birth and death, nor any passing away or emerging.

Furthermore, there is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa; it is neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor otherwise. These refer precisely to the six "no's" and four "neither's."

In foreign lands, the Buddha is called the "Celestial Drum. When enemies are about to arrive, the celestial drum sounds; when enemies are about to depart, the celestial drum likewise sounds. When the celestial drum sounds, the hearts of the devas are filled with courage; when the celestial drum sounds, the asuras are struck with fear. When the afflictions of sentient beings are about to arise, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for them; when the afflictions of sentient beings are about to subside, the Buddha likewise preaches the Dharma for them. When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, the hearts of his disciples are filled with courage; when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, all the māras are struck with fear. Although the celestial drum performs these four functions, it does so without a mind; though the Tathāgata speaks, he likewise does so without a mind. For this reason, the Buddha is designated as the Celestial Drum.
Furthermore, although the Tathāgata has awakened, there is in fact nothing realized; this is analogous to the celestial drum which, though it resounds, is in fact without mind.
As for "abiding," we now take that which is capable of abiding as "abiding"; therefore, the meaning of abiding belongs to the Buddha.
There are two kinds of abiding:
first, the abiding of the body;
second, the abiding of the mind.
There are also four ways in which the body dwells:
first, dwelling in transformed lands, wherein each of the Buddhas of the ten directions has their own realm;
second, dwelling apart from the secular world, wherein the Buddhas of the three periods of time mostly reside in monasteries.

Third, he remained by not relinquishing his life-constituent; for the Buddha had not yet answered the King Māra’s request for an immeasurable lifespan, whereas had he answered that request, he would have retained only eighty years and relinquished all the rest.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "Regarding 'renouncing the fifth portion of one's lifespan': of a hundred-year lifespan, twenty years constitute one portion; thus, there are five portions.
When the Buddha responded to the request of Māra, he renounced twenty years and retained only eighty; hence it is said that he renounced the fifth portion of his lifespan."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that being near to *nirvāṇa* should refer to abiding through the relinquishment of the lifespan.
Fourth is the abiding of majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*), which means that walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are all termed "abiding."
Second, regarding dwelling in terms of internal virtues, there are also four kinds:
first, the celestial dwelling (*devasthāna*), which refers to dwelling in generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth;
second, the Brahma dwelling (*brahmasthāna*), which refers to dwelling in the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Third is the noble dwelling, which refers to abiding in the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Fourth is the buddha-dwelling, which refers to abiding in the manifold virtues of the resultant stage, such as the ten powers.
The Tathāgata is endowed with these eight abidings, both internal and external; this is precisely abiding in non-abiding, abiding in that which has no place to abide.
It is, for example, like Mañjuśrī’s coming without coming, coming where there is no place to come.
This is also as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* during the Lion’s Roar, when it was taught while dwelling in the Śāla grove.
Regarding "the city of Rājagṛha," this is the fifth [point], clarifying the place of residence.
Since these teachings must have their source, they are worthy of belief.
The claims of those heterodox outsiders—some saying it was bestowed from mid-air, others saying it was brought by a red bird—are all devoid of foundation.
Regarding the place of residence, there are two types: first, the general location;
second, the specific location.
The form of the Perfected One has no fixed direction; how could it have a permanent location?
It is only for the sake of establishing faith and understanding that one must describe it with such circumlocution.
Furthermore, because one wishes to transform both the bustling and the tranquil realms, both mountain and city are mentioned.
The kingdom is named Magadha, which in this language means "Non-Harming" (*Ahiṃsā*). Although people commit crimes, there is no execution or capital punishment; therefore, it is called "Non-Harming.
The city is named Rājagṛha. In small kingdoms, the kingdom itself serves as the city, just as the kingdom of Vaiśālī is also called the city of Vaiśālī.
This is a great kingdom; it is distinguished from other countries by its capital city.
To provide the foreign language term in full, it should be called Rājagṛha-mahā-gara.
"Rājagṛha" is translated here as "King's House" (Wángshè).
"Mahā" means "great," and "gira" means "city.
Among the sixteen great kingdoms and six major cities, this city is the largest; therefore, it is called the Great City of Rājagṛha.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Ajātaśatru, because the population had diminished, abandoned his original great city and constructed a smaller one; yet among all cities, this one was still considered large—how much more so was the original city of Rājagṛha?"

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "That city was three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, containing eight hundred million households; those belonging to Rājagṛha consisted of eighty thousand villages."
Question: Since all six great cities have palaces of various kings, why is this city alone called Rājagṛha (the King’s Abode)?
Answer:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* offers three interpretations:

first, it is said that in the past, a king of Magadha had a son with one head, two faces, and four arms. People of the time regarded this as an ill omen, so they tore apart his body and head and cast them away in the wilderness.
A rākṣasī named Li Jian joined her own body and head together to nourish him with milk.
Later, he grew into a great man whose strength enabled him to annex various kingdoms; he took eighteen thousand kings and placed them within these five mountains, ruling Jambudvīpa with great power.
This explanation clarifies that many kings resided in this city, and for that reason it is named Rājagṛha (the King’s Abode).
The other two interpretations are as stated in the *Śāstra*.
Furthermore, some say:

"There was once a king who lost the correct path; the people of a thousand kingdoms collectively deposed him and established these five mountains as his domain. Later, reflecting on how to amend his past errors, he returned to govern the kingdom together with them. Therefore, this city is named Rājagṛha (the King’s Abode)."

The Tripitaka Master Paramārtha, citing the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*, states: "Whenever a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, it has been handed down that he resided upon these five mountains; therefore, this city alone is named Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence)."
Furthermore, the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* explains:

"In the past, the Four Heavenly Kings together churned the ocean of milk and obtained the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*). Before they had divided it, they built a palace upon these five mountains to guard it."
Only after seven days was it finally divided; therefore, it is called "Rājagṛha" (King’s Abode).
Thus, what was previously referred to as the abode built by the human king is here [referred to as] the abode built by the celestial king.

According to the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), it is said: "King Pañcāla captured one thousand kings and placed them within the Five Mountains. This city was named after its many kings; since no other city possesses such a multitude of circumstances, this city alone is called Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).
The five mountains encircle it like a city wall, and within them a palace is erected; because these two things are mentioned together, it is named Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence).
Question:
If it is named Rājagṛha by mentioning these two things together, there should not then be two separate locations for the mountain and the city.
Answer:

The name "Rājagṛha" (King’s House) is spoken by combining two things; however, because the king built a separate city within the five mountains, there are thus two locations: the mountains and the city.
"Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain" is translated here as Vulture Peak Mountain.
Among these five mountain peaks, each has its own characteristic form; since this particular mountain resembles the head of a vulture, it is named after the vulture.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka saw that the summit of the mountain resembled a vulture; he therefore had men carve out two wings, two feet, and a tail, so that it appeared exactly like a vulture.
Lu Deng’s *Dili ji* states: "The distance between the city and the mountain is fifteen li in total.
Question:
Since the Buddha’s great compassion is universal, for what reason did he dwell predominantly in Rājagṛha to preach the Dharma?
Answer: The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Lotus Sūtra Commentary) presents two meanings:
first, that it intends to manifest the teaching through its causes and locations.
Among all cities, this city is the greatest; among all mountains, this mountain is the most excellent. This represents the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as being superior among all sūtras.
Second, it is because it manifests the accomplishment of sovereign merit.

This statement specifically cites the city of Rājagṛha as a metaphor; just as a king possesses sovereign power over the world, this sutra is revealed to be the king of all sutras, for it subsumes all vehicles within the One Vehicle and causes all vehicles to return to the One Vehicle.
The *Śāstra* explains six meanings:
first, it is because of repaying the kindness of the Dharma-body.
Since the Tathāgata originally attained enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha, he dwells there extensively in order to repay this kindness.
Second, because that place has vast lands and a large population, the scope for transforming beings is extensive; therefore, he dwells there frequently.

Third, because that place abounds in intelligent and highly wise people—such as those in the lineage of Śāriputra and Kāśyapa, or the likes of Dīrghanakha and the six heretical teachers—and he wishes to subdue them, he dwells there frequently.

Fourth, that country has two dragon kings who are brothers; they send down rain at the proper times so that the land never suffers from years of famine. Since those who have left the household life can thus easily provide for their physical needs, it is also easy for them to cultivate their spirits, and therefore many reside there.

Fifth, there are many monasteries in this place; on level ground there are bamboo groves, and within the five mountains of the monastery complex there are five vihāras. Since these are scarce in other countries, [the monks] dwell here in great numbers.

Sixth, this place abounds in numinous flowers and auspicious grasses, and is tranquil, serene, and pure; it is truly a dwelling where the various sages roam and a lair for the divine immortals, and thus many reside here.
"Accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus," and so forth: sixth, next follows the listing of the assembly of those who heard [the teaching].
Now, regarding this chapter, it shall be briefly analyzed by way of six gates;
first, the gate of the purpose for coming.
Second, the gate of determining the number of the assembly;
third, the gate of the provisional and the real;
fourth, the gate of existence and non-existence.
Fifth, the gate of sequential order;
sixth, the gate of possession and non-possession.
Regarding the gate of the purpose for coming, there are briefly ten meanings:
First, it is to establish Ānanda’s status as a listener; because Ānanda heard [the teachings] together with superior persons, the transmission of the sūtra is trustworthy.

Second, it is to manifest the Buddha’s virtues; when the Buddha is surrounded by a superior assembly, his virtues become even more venerable, and since such a person is revered, his Dharma will necessarily be received.

Third, it is for the purpose of elucidating the true sutras: just as because of Śāriputra’s three requests, the provisional vehicle and the ultimate vehicle were revealed; and because of Maitreya’s three requests, the provisional body and the ultimate body were revealed.

Fourth, they assist the Buddha in propagating his transformation; just as the Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra in three cycles, the noble disciples also spoke in three cycles to introduce their own realization and understanding, and Maitreya’s realization and praise of this matter were likewise so.
Fifth, it is because they wish to make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise the Buddha, as explained in the subsequent text.
Sixth, it is because they wish to make a vow to propagate the sutra, as explained in the "Chapter on Upholding" and the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers."
Seventh, they wish to guide sentient beings to the presence of the Buddha.
Eighth, they wish to hear the Buddha preach the Dharma in order to seek profound awakening.
Ninth, they come for the purpose of verifying the sutras, like the gathering of the emanation-bodies of the Buddhas.

Tenth, they come for the purpose of establishing gates of teaching; as in the cases of Samantabhadra and Avalokiteśvara, they perform buddha-work by means of bodhisattvas, and it is for this reason that they come.

Second, regarding the section on determining the number of the assembly: from beginning to end, this sutra comprises two assemblies; the first assembly consists of twenty-three groups, and the latter assembly consists of six groups, totaling twenty-nine groups.

Regarding the "twenty-three assemblies," there are two types of *saṃgha* assemblies, and the same applies to the *bhikṣuṇī* assemblies; furthermore, there are the Bodhisattva assemblies and the five assemblies of the noble ones (*ārya*).
There are eighteen ordinary assemblies: among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten assemblies, namely:
the sons of the three luminaries, the Four Great Kings, Śakra, Īśvara, and Maheśvara.
The two assemblies of the Form Realm—
Śikhin and Mahābrahmā Prabhāsvara— combine with these to form twelve assemblies.
Next, there are six assemblies of miscellaneous types, which are easy to understand from the text.
