Regarding "accomplishing all unwholesome roots": the preceding section specifically clarified one latent tendency (*anuśaya*) and two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), which refers to householders—that is, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). As stated in the "Parable Chapter," these are like venomous insects.

Now, to explain in summary the two unwholesome roots along with the various fetters and impurities: these refer to the heterodox practitioners who have left the household life, namely the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), which are the evil spirits mentioned in the "Parable Chapter."

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, the Buddhas distinguish and teach three within the single Buddha-vehicle," the preceding section clarified that because the five turbidities have increased so intensely, beings are incapable of receiving the one vehicle; thus, this section now clarifies that the three vehicles are taught as skillful means.
"If my disciples claim for themselves... refers to the third section, the gate that demonstrates gain and loss.

Above, it was clarified that the ultimate principle is one; next, it was clarified that there are three provisional means within the five turbidities. Since the presence or absence of the provisional and the real is clearly credible, those who do not believe this are indeed evil people; therefore, the gate of gain and loss is explained next.

However, the teachings capable of transforming beings do not go beyond the real and the provisional; and those who receive these teachings likewise possess nothing other than attainment or failure. Thus, the entirety of the work of conversion is encompassed within this single matter.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of loss; second, the explanation of gain.
Each of these—loss and gain—concerns two types of people, making four people in total.

Regarding the two types of those who have lost the middle way: the first are those who have not yet attained the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) but claim they have, and thus do not believe in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; the second are those who have already attained the fruits of the Small Vehicle but, because those fruits are not ultimate, falsely claim them to be ultimate, and consequently do not seek the Great [Vehicle]. This too is called "losing" it.
The former refers to the errors of ordinary beings, while the latter refers to the errors of sages; these two categories collectively encompass all instances of error without exception.

Regarding the phrase, "If my disciples claim for themselves to be Arhats and so forth," the preceding section clarified that the One Vehicle is the ultimate reality and the Three Vehicles are skillful means. Now, by failing to grasp these two points, it is shown that they cling to the Lesser Vehicle as real while remaining deluded regarding the Three Vehicles as provisional.

This clarifies that those who have not attained the ultimate fruit of the Hīnayāna claim to have attained it; this describes the errors among the followers of the Hīnayāna, namely the five thousand disciples.

Regarding the statement, "Not hearing and not knowing that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach and transform only bodhisattvas," this passage clarifies that such ignorance concerns the fact that all paths return to the Single Vehicle; it is precisely a delusion regarding the reality of the Single Vehicle.
This describes the errors within the Mahāyāna.
"Not hearing" refers to not hearing the teachings;
"not knowing" refers to not understanding the principles.
The five thousand people above did not hear the extensive exposition of the true reality of the One Vehicle; therefore, it is said that they "did not hear and did not know.
Regarding the passage beginning with "These are not disciples of the Buddha," the first two lines restate their subjective misconceptions, while this current text judges their success or failure.

The five thousand followers had not yet attained the ultimate realization of the Hīnayāna, yet they claimed to have attained it; because they clung to and adhered to the Hīnayāna, they were not subsumed within the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, because they neither heard nor knew [the Mahāyāna], and were instead taught only as bodhisattvas, these people were deluded regarding the Great Vehicle and thus were not subsumed within the Mahāyāna. Therefore, they were not disciples of the Buddha. By clarifying that they were not disciples of the Buddha, it is shown that they were not ordinary practitioners (pṛthagjana) within the Buddhist fold; the following clarifies that they were not among the seven types of noble persons (āryapudgala).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra," and so on, marks the second section, which clarifies the failure of the sages.
This also consists of three points:

the first point clarifies that those who have already attained arhatship preserve their own attainment as ultimate and adhere to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, failing to recognize the provisional nature [of those teachings].
"Those who do not advance in their quest" marks the second section, which clarifies the failure to recognize the reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"You should know that these types of people" marks the third sentence, which judges their success or failure.

When an Arhat views the Mahāyāna, they are in truth not yet ultimate, yet they claim to have reached the ultimate; because they claim to have reached the ultimate, they do not advance to seek the Buddha-way—know that such a person is likewise one of overweening pride (adhimāna).
Question:
Now, regarding the clarification of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), how does it differ from the overweening pride mentioned previously? Answer:
The preceding has already been explained.
Now, to further clarify the distinctions: the first type of person possesses two kinds of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
First, to claim to have attained a minor ultimate realization when one has not yet attained it is the overweening pride of the Hīnayāna.
Second, there are those who cling to these deluded sentiments and do not further seek the Mahāyāna; this is called the "arrogance regarding the Mahāyāna.

Later, when people have attained the fruits of the Hīnayāna, they regard these minor fruits—compared to the Mahāyāna—as ultimate, though they are not. Such individuals possess only the arrogance regarding the Mahāyāna, but lack the arrogance regarding the Hīnayāna.
Question:
How is it known that there are two persons? Answer:
The subsequent passage clarifies that the person differs from the former one; therefore, we know the two persons are distinct.

Furthermore, since the preceding passage judges this to be a failure of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), stating they are neither a disciple of the Buddha (*śrāvaka*) nor an Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, we know this is the failure of an ordinary person.
The subsequent passage judges this as a failure, stating directly that it is merely a case of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

Since he is already an Arhat, he cannot be anything other than a disciple of the Buddha nor anything other than an Arhat; however, because he considers himself to have reached the ultimate goal and no longer aspires to Buddhahood, he is given the name of one possessing overweening pride.
Question:
What kind of person is this? Answer:
Generally speaking, all those who claim for themselves to have attained the ultimate state of an Arhat are, in reality, the Śrāvakas of the three capacities;

this refers specifically to them. Thus, Śāriputra said, "At that time, my mind thought I had attained Nirvāṇa," and even Kāśyapa, who possesses the middle capacity, likewise held this attachment, as manifested in the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" and the "Chapter on the City of Illusion."
Question:

An ordinary person who has not yet attained arhatship considers themselves to have reached the ultimate goal, while a noble one who has truly attained arhatship also considers themselves to have reached the ultimate goal; what is the difference between these two?

Answer: Before these two had heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they considered themselves to be roughly equal [to the sages]. However, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the five thousand ordinary persons did not give rise to faith and acceptance, whereas the sages did. Therefore, the text says: "If one has truly attained arhatship and yet does not believe this Dharma, such a thing is impossible."
"From 'Why is this so? onwards is the second section: citing what is attained to explain what is lost, which clarifies attainment.
There are also two types of persons:
first, it clarifies that Arhats while the Buddha was in the world were those who had attained [the fruit]."
Next, it is clarified that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, arhats are those who have attained [this state].
Regarding those who attained it while the Buddha was still in the world as an arhat, there are generally two meanings:
first, to exclude ordinary people;...
Second, "striking the noble.

To say that this excludes ordinary persons clarifies that if one has truly attained arhatship, they would necessarily believe and accept the One Vehicle upon hearing it; thus, we know that if the foremost person does not believe in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he is not an arhat.
Therefore, this citation serves to refute the initial error.

As for the statement "striking the noble ones," it clarifies that one who has truly attained arhatship must necessarily have faith in this Dharma; if one does not believe it, then one is not an arhat.
This very passage is used to address those who have actually attained the second fruit—Arhats—urging them to relinquish this minor fruit and advance toward the Great Way.

Regarding the phrase "except for the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present," the second point clarifies that Arhats attain [the fruit] after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; whereas previously it was shown that Arhats attained it by hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, here it refers to Arhats attaining it without having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This passage is presented to resolve a doubt.
The doubter asks:
"Is it possible that there are Arhats who neither hear nor know anything, yet still perform the work of teaching and transforming Bodhisattvas?"
Furthermore, are there Arhats who do not believe in the provisional and the ultimate?
These two doubts arise from the preceding two passages.
Therefore, the commentary explains:

While the Buddha was in the world, Arhats who heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* would necessarily have believed it; however, after his parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is manifest before them, these Arhats do not believe in the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Therefore, the *Dharmapundarika-sūtra-śāstra* states: "This is also to resolve their doubts."
A doubt arises:
"If one hears the Dharma from the Buddha and conceives a mind of slander, why does the Buddha not become an unfit person to preach the Dharma?
To sever this doubt, it is explained that except for after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present before one, it is only because of such circumstances that slander arises.
Why is this so? It is because the Arhat Śikṣānanda did not believe in the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is difficult to hear and difficult to understand; thus, it is rare for an Arhat to become a Buddha.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that arhats attain Buddhahood; this meaning is most profound. That arhats attain Buddhahood can only be understood by a Buddha; commentators may properly discuss other matters."
Even Nāgārjuna said he did not understand; thus we know that only a Buddha can understand.
Such a person is difficult to find because they do not encounter the dual conditions of a worthy teacher and the Dharma.

These arhats do not believe in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). As stated in the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "As the Buddha has taught, all arhats shall eventually attain nirvāṇa; yet this profound sphere of the Buddha's practice cannot be known by ordinary people of inferior and foolish intellect. Therefore, it is most difficult for an arhat to become a buddha; only a buddha knows this, which is why it is called "difficult to attain."
Regarding the phrase, "If one encounters another Buddha, one will then attain definitive understanding within this Dharma," this passage is also introduced to resolve a doubt.
The doubter asks:
"Since this arhat did not encounter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* nor anyone who could explain its meaning, when shall he come to believe in the One Vehicle?"
Therefore, the commentary states:
"This arhat is born in a pure land outside the triple world; there he encounters another Buddha and, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, finally attains definitive realization."
"Resolute understanding" refers to knowing the three truths and the one truth, as well as existence and non-existence, and the provisional and the real.
Question:

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if an arhat does not encounter a person who can explain the meaning [of the teachings], but hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* directly, will they still attain faith and understanding?
Answer: This matter is difficult to clarify.
Even if one were to encounter the sutras, should one not meet a person capable of explaining their meaning, one would still be unable to understand them with perfect clarity.
Therefore, the text says: "If one encounters another Buddha, only then will one reach a definitive understanding.
From the passage beginning with "Śāriputra" onwards is the fourth section, the Gate of Encouraging Faith, Acceptance, and Upholding.
The reason this text has come forth is due to three general meanings: first,
to resolve doubts.
A doubt arises:
"If the Three Vehicles were taught first and the One Vehicle is taught later, this would constitute false speech; how can it be trusted?
To resolve this doubt, he exhorts [the audience] to have faith.

Second, having previously demonstrated the reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the expedient means (*upāya*) of the Three Vehicles, as well as revealing their respective merits and faults, we now clarify the exhortation to believe; that is, to cause [beings] to abandon what is faulty and follow what is meritorious, thereby accepting, believing, and upholding [the teaching].

Third, you are close to being born in the higher realms; if you encounter other Buddhas, you will immediately attain definitive understanding and realization. You shall never again remain forever as Arhats, but must instead hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and thereafter become Buddhas. Since you, the great assembly, have now encountered a Buddha and heard this sūtra once more, you must quickly believe and accept it.
Question:
Since the exhortation to believe was already clarified above, how does it differ from the present one? Answer:

The preceding section clarified the exhortation to faith; the present section, having concluded its clarification of the provisional and ultimate aspects of the Dharma and the true and false nature of persons, now exhorts beings to believe, understand, and uphold it—thus it differs from what preceded.

Fahua Yishu, Scroll Three. On the final day of the month of Guxian in the year of Yongren Jiawu, at the request of the Master of the Zhongguan School, this third scroll of the *Fahua Yishu* was carved.

It is my sincere hope that the nun Zheng Chan-teng Shi-niang’s sublime spirit shall, by means of this precious chariot, proceed directly to the Pure Land, so that the four debts of gratitude and the three benefits may extend infinitely.
Recorded with reverence by the monk Sùqìng, who has long cultivated the karmic conditions for this work;
compiled by Hú Jízàng. *Fahua yishu*, Scroll Four.
2. The Second Part of the "Chapter on Expedient Means.
Following the section beginning with "Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor [doubts]," the second part consists of the verse summary (gāthā).
It comprises one hundred and fourteen lines and is divided into two sections:
The first four lines praise the introductory narrative (*nidāna*);
the subsequent one hundred and ten lines praise the formal exposition (*uddeśa*).

Regarding the three parts of the introduction, the present [text] briefly omits the verses on the granting of permission to speak and the exhortation to listen; instead, it praises the second section, which censures the impure assembly, and the third section, which extols the pure assembly.
However, these two verses generally have two meanings:
first, they intend to demonstrate that the Buddha’s cessation [of teaching] and Śāriputra’s request for instruction were not in vain by means of the verse on the impure assembly;
second, they clarify that Śāriputra’s request was not erroneous by means of the subsequent verse on the pure assembly.
Second, the verses concerning the impure assembly admonish future sentient beings not to cling to the Hīnayāna and thereby obstruct the Great Dharma;
the subsequent verses concerning the pure assembly are intended to exhort all sentient beings to practice the Mahāyāna.
The first line subsumes the four assemblies into three faults; the two assemblies of those who have left the household life share the fault of having overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

This is because these two assemblies of renunciants focus their minds exclusively on the fruits of the Path and frequently attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); thus, when they attain the four *dhyānas*, they claim to have attained the four fruits, which constitutes overweening pride.
Some say: that which is the increase among forms of pride, the pinnacle of pride, is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride).

Now, it is said that "superior" (*adhika*) refers to a superior dharma; to claim to have attained a superior dharma when one has not yet attained it, and to exalt oneself based on this, is called *adhimāna*.
Question:
How does this differ from false pride (mithyāmāna)? Answer:
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said:
"To rely upon false teachings and give rise to pride without having attained any of the noble dharmas at all is called 'false pride' (mithyāmāna).
To consider oneself to have attained the ultimate when one has only acquired a small measure of the Dharma, such as the four dhyānas and so forth, is called 'exaggerated pride' (adhimāna)."
Question: For what reason is it called "possessing a womb"? Answer:

The *Commentary on the Sūtra* states: "Only those who advance in virtue without a [discursive] mind can subsequently realize the principle; to harbor thoughts regarding the 'exalted path' is what constitutes arrogance."
"To have something harbored" means that the mind harbors something; this constitutes having something attained.

Regarding "the upāsaka’s pride," such a person likewise has not attained what they claim to have attained; however, because he is a man of integrity whose resolve does not waver, he is said to possess pride.
The *Commentary on the Sūtra* states: "Though one knows there is no self, to take that very absence of self as a self is also pride.
This means that because one thinks, "I am able to understand non-self," it is called the pride of self (*asmimāna*).
Regarding the phrase "the laywoman does not believe": although all four assemblies generally lack faith in the Mahāyāna, within that lack of faith three further distinctions are made.
As for the two monastic assemblies, they do not believe because they possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

As for the layman (*upāsaka*), being a man who considers himself capable, decisive, and resolute in maintaining his will, he thinks, "I have long since believed in the principles of the Arhat as the ultimate; how could I now allow my resolve to change? Therefore, this is called the pride of self-conceit (*asmimāna*).
Since the latter is simply "woman," it carries no further meaning beyond being a direct designation for "lack of faith.
The *Commentary on the Sutra* states: "Though one believes the words that 'it does not exist,' yet to take 'non-existence' itself as faith is what is called 'lack of faith.'"
Master Zhaolun said:

"To say that something is 'not existent' clarifies that it is not *an* existent; it does not mean that it is [the state of] non-existence. Yet, the woman persisted in taking "non-existence" as [a substantive reality], and for this reason she was called "Lack of Faith."
The section beginning with "In this way" clarifies the number of the assembly.
Regarding the phrase "not seeing one's own faults": now, one who has faults yet is able to recognize them is called a wise person.
Now, to have the fault of conceited speech (*māna*) while remaining unaware of it is called being a fool.

Regarding the phrase "having deficiencies in the precepts" (*śīla-vaikalya*): the preceding section clarified that one lacks the ultimate realization of the *Hīnayāna* yet claims to possess such realization; now, this single sentence clarifies that one lacks the ultimate practice of the *Hīnayāna* yet claims to possess ultimate practice.

Furthermore, one who has not yet attained the ultimate fruit of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) claims to have already attained it, and likewise does not accept the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna); because one cannot prevent these two evils, it is said that there is a deficiency or breach in one's precepts.
Because this precept has been broken, it is called "deficient"; because the faculty of faith leaks out, it is termed a "leak.
Furthermore, the precepts are like a dam that prevents and obstructs the waters of affliction; once the precepts are deficient and leaking, afflictions will flow forth.
Regarding the phrase "guarding and cherishing one's flaws," this is introduced to resolve a doubt.
The doubt is as follows:

Since he possesses neither practice nor understanding, and moreover does not perceive his own faults, why does the Buddha, out of his great compassion, not point them out to him so that he may leave the assembly?
Therefore, the commentary states:
"Those who do not recognize their own faults and who cherish their own flaws cannot be transformed.
A flaw is a defect within jade; by analogy, this refers to the ground of the mind lacking understanding while claiming to possess it."
A flaw in jade is a blemish; this is a metaphor for when one has no actual conduct in body or speech yet claims to possess such conduct.
Furthermore, past transgressions with deep and heavy roots constitute a defect, while present instances of overweening pride (adhimāna) are like a blemish.
Furthermore, to cling inwardly to the small and refuse to let it go is a flaw; to hear the teaching of the Great outwardly and not accept it is a defect.
To conceal one's shortcomings is "protection"; to begrudge what is not [one's own] is "parsimony."
Regarding the phrase "the dregs and chaff among the assembly," this passage is introduced to resolve a doubt.
What have these five thousand people gained by entering into the Buddha-dharma?
Therefore, the commentary explains:
Five thousand people have lost the true flavor of the Middle Way and obtained only the dregs of annihilationism and eternalism.

The names of the Three Vehicles are like the husks outside the rice, while the principle of the One Vehicle is like the rice within the husks. Because they have only obtained the names of the Three Vehicles and do not understand their meaning, they are called "husks."
Furthermore, the pure assembly being fit for use is likened to rice for brewing wine, whereas the offenders being unfit for use is compared to dregs and husks.

Regarding the phrase "they departed due to the Buddha’s majestic virtue," the *Commentary on the Sutra* states: "When the wind rises, dust and sand fly of their own accord; when the sun rises, black and white distinguish themselves naturally. This is what is meant by 'sending them away' without actually having to dismiss them."
Regarding the phrase "this person has meager merit," the preceding prose section clarified the presence of the roots of transgression, whereas the present verse reveals their lack of merit.
While the previous verse explained that they depart because they cling to the Lesser Vehicle, this verse distinguishes that they are incapable of receiving the Mahāyāna.
"The assembly here has no branches or leaves" is the second [section], which praises the pure assembly.
From "Śāriputra, listen well" onwards is the second [section], which praises the preceding formal exposition.
Above, there are four gates:
first, the gate of the single vehicle’s reality;
second, the gate of the three vehicles’ skillful means.
Third, the section on gain and loss;
fourth, the section on exhortation to faith.
Now, these verses also employ four sections to explain the Dharma by shifting the momentum of the discourse:
First, the verse on the gate of the reality of the One Vehicle;
second, the verse on the gate of the expedient means of the Three Vehicles;
third, the section clarifying the gate of praise.
Fourth, the section on exhorting faith.
The reason for these four sections is as follows:
first, to clarify the reality of the One Vehicle; second, to clarify the expedient means of the Three Vehicles.
These two clarify the beginning and end of a single transformation.
Third is the praise, which, having been completed, exhorts beings to believe and accept it.
Regarding the first, the gate of the reality of the One Vehicle, there are three parts:
First, the section on Śākyamuni’s own discourse;
second, the section on citing scriptural evidence;
third, the section on concordant agreement.
Now, these three verses constitute three sections.
In the preceding prose section, the gate of Śākyamuni’s own discourse has three parts:
first, the gate of praise;...
2. The Gate of Non-falsity;
3. The Gate of Revealing the Intent of the Teaching.
Now, this verse shifts its momentum to praise [the subject] by likewise opening three gates:
I. The Section on Revealing the Intent of the Teaching;
II. The Section on Resolving Doubts;
III. The Section on Encouraging Faith.
First, the explicit clarification of the general purport of the teaching, showing that it is for the purpose of returning to the One Vehicle.
Second, the clarification of the doubts of the assembly: if it is indeed for the purpose of returning to the One Vehicle, why was the One not taught first, rather than the Three?
To resolve this doubt and clarify the reason why there are three [teachings] preceding and one following, the next section provides an analysis titled "The Gate for Resolving Doubts.
Since the intent of the teaching has been made manifest and the sequence of before and after has been clarified, the third section offers an exhortation to faith.
The first section also has two parts:
first, clarifying the intent behind the teaching of the past, which means that the underlying purport of what was taught according to suitability in the preceding prose is difficult to understand;
second, clarifying the intent of the present teaching, which means that [the Buddha] appeared in the world for the sake of the single great cause and condition, as stated in the preceding prose.
Regarding the first gate, there are two parts:
first, clarifying the intent behind the former teaching of the Hīnayāna;
second, clarifying the intent behind the former teaching of the Mahāyāna.
The first section has two parts:

first, clarifying the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) previously expounded, which corresponds to the meaning of the preceding prose stating that the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*) of what was taught according to suitability is difficult to understand;
second, versifying the intended meaning expressed by those previous teachings, which corresponds to the preceding statement that only the Buddhas are able to know it.
The first section further consists of two parts:
first, an account of the ancient teachings on humans and devas;
second, an account of the ancient teachings on the two vehicles.
The beginning consists of three sections:
the first verse praises the Buddha’s expedient wisdom and its efficacy in skillful exposition;
the second verse praises the Buddha’s wisdom that inwardly illuminates the dispositions of sentient beings.
From "The Buddha, having fully known this" onwards, the third section consists of four verses that correctly clarify the Buddha’s teaching.
As for why the previous teachings contained only these three gates: the first praises the Buddha’s skillful wisdom, referring to him as a skilled physician;
the second concerns his knowledge of the faculties and natures, referring to his diagnosis of the illness.
The subsequent teaching explains the administration of medicine.
The first verse states, "The Dharma attained by all Buddhas," which refers to ultimate wisdom (real wisdom).
"Immeasurable power of skillful means" refers to provisional wisdom (expedient wisdom).
Next, having internally possessed these two [qualities], one is externally able to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Regarding the second verse: the first three lines indicate knowledge of present dispositions and desires (*śakti*), while the final line clarifies the illumination of past karmic causes. Since present dispositions arise from past karma, the latter is explained immediately following the former.
The following four verses are divided into two parts:
the first verse generally clarifies that the teaching proceeds in accordance with conditions and that the teaching accords with those conditions;
the subsequent three verses specifically clarify the various gates of the teaching.
The preceding section provides a general overview, while the subsequent section offers specific details for the sake of clarifying the meaning.
Within the detailed exposition of the teaching, the first one and a half lines clarify the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-buddhavacana*), which refers to the Dharma as the teaching;
the next one and a half lines clarify *nirvāṇa*, the Dharma as the fruit.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the ninefold division of the Dharma is taught to enable the attainment of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*; this constitutes the gradual sequence.
Furthermore, while these nine divisions apply to all four vehicles (*catur-yāna*), the resultant dharmas clarify only the teachings of the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*).
Although there have been many explanations in the past, they do not go beyond these two.
Furthermore, the ninefold division refers to the teachings for humans and devas; the subsequent explanation of *nirvāṇa* refers to the teachings for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
However, regarding the differences between the sūtras and śāstras, there are generally four propositions:
First, both the Great and Small Vehicles are equally extensive; the Mahāyāna is complete with all twelve [links], while the Hīnayāna possesses them according to its respective capacity.

The reason only twelve are clarified is that twelve is the perfection of this numerical category, and furthermore, because they serve to cure sentient beings of the disease of the twelve links of dependent origination.

Second, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are equally concise in their common elucidation of the ninefold division of the teachings (*navāṅga*). As for why only nine divisions are elucidated: it is because this number is a complete cycle, and furthermore, the ninefold division is taught for the sake of sentient beings within the nine realms of existence.
Because the Hīnayāna is shallow in its treatment of the Dharma, three [categories] are excluded:
since the Hīnayāna teachings are limited and narrow, they lack the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings);

furthermore, the bestowing of prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*) is not the tenet of the Hīnayāna, and because followers of the Hīnayāna lack the principle of fulfilling the Buddha’s work, the category of "bestowing prophecies" is excluded.
The teachings of the Hīnayāna are shallow; because there were people capable of questioning them, they excluded the "unasked spontaneous discourse" (*anupṛṣṭa-svayambhāṣita*).

Furthermore, because Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) can act as uninvited friends to sentient beings, they possess the unasked spontaneous discourse; whereas those of the Hīnayāna cannot save others and must wait for an invitation before speaking, they lack the unasked spontaneous discourse.
The Mahāyāna, because it is adapted to those with sharp faculties, omits three [categories]:

since Mahāyāna practitioners possess sharp faculties, they understand through direct exposition; there is no need for causes and conditions or parables, nor do they rely on formal debate. Therefore, these three categories are omitted.

The third phrase is narrow in detail but broad in scope; as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is called the Vaipulya-sūtra, while the Śrāvaka-piṭaka consists of the eleven divisions of scripture.

This passage clarifies that the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna are designated as "Vaipulya" (Extensive) because they elucidate the principles of Vaipulya; since the name is derived from the principles they expound, all twelve divisions are termed Vaipulya.
The twelve divisions of the Hīnayāna do not elucidate the principles of Vaipulya; therefore, while their eleven divisions retain their original names, the designation "Vaipulya" is omitted.

The fourth phrase concerns the "great and broad" versus the "small and concise," which reveals that the Mahāyāna is the "full letter" (pūrṇākṣara) and thus possesses all twelve divisions of the canon;

whereas the Hīnayāna is the "half-letter" (ardhākṣara) and thus possesses only nine divisions. This is precisely what is taught in the present text, and it constitutes the very core of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The twelve divisions [of the canon] all take verbal teaching as their essence; therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clearly distinguishes between knowing the Dharma and knowing its meaning. To "know the Dharma" means to know the teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures; thus, it is known that these constitute the teaching.
Next, as for opening [the twelvefold division] into two: although there are twelve divisions, they do not go beyond prose (*gadya*) and verse (*śloka*).
It is also possible to open it into three: Sūtra, Geya, and Gāthā.

These three are designated by name according to their formal teaching; thus, the teaching itself constitutes the essence of these three divisions. The remaining nine divisions receive their names from specific subject matters, yet they likewise do not depart from these three.

Regarding *sūtra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarify that direct verbal discourse is *sūtra*; this refers to the *sūtra* of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, from the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) to "so it was practiced" (*iti kṛtvā dhārayati*), refers to the sūtras of general characteristics.

Among the Three Piṭakas, the Sūtra Piṭaka is vertically long and horizontally narrow; because it is vertically long, it encompasses the twelve divisions of scripture, and because it is horizontally narrow, it constitutes only one of the three piṭakas.

Among the twelve divisions [of the scriptures], the Sūtra is broad horizontally but short vertically. It is "short vertically" because it does not encompass the other eleven divisions; it is "broad horizontally" because it encompasses the Three Piṭakas.
The Gāthā is the second division, referring to verses that are not in metrical symmetry.
Question:
In various sutras and śāstras, when listing the twelve divisions of the teachings, the second is called geya; why, then, do you now explain gāthā? Answer:

To clarify that the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is not fixed, he deviates from the conventional norm; whereas previously he taught the ninefold canon (navāṅga) to clarify the Hīnayāna, now he clarifies that these same nine divisions actually penetrate the Mahāyāna. Thus, wishing to manifest the meaning of non-fixity, he speaks in this seemingly disordered manner.
Furthermore, these nine divisions are now combined into five pairs:
first, the prose (*sūtra*) and the verse (*gāthā*) form one pair.

The Buddhas sometimes speak directly to sentient beings in *sūtra*, and sometimes command that they be spoken in verse from the outset, hence the name *gāthā*. Because the term "or" (*vā*) is used to mark both categories, it is known that *sūtra* does not necessarily precede, nor does *gāthā* necessarily follow.
The *itivṛttaka* (past events) and the *jātaka* (birth stories): these two constitute the pair of "other" and "self.
The *itivṛttaka* recounts the past lives of others, such as the "Chapter on the Past Events of Bhaiṣajyarāja" and others; that which recounts one's own past lives is called the *jātaka*.
The "Unprecedented" (*adbhuta*) and the "Causes and Conditions" (*nidāna*): these clarify the two categories of wholesome and unwholesome matters.

"Unprecedented" refers to wholesome matters, such as the blue ox walking with the almsbowl, the white dog listening to the sutra, the great earthquake, and the physical dimensions of the various devas.
"Causes and Conditions" refers to matters concerning the origin and conclusion of the commission of offenses; thus, it is called the *Nidāna-sūtra*.
The *avadāna* (譬喻) and *geya* (祇夜) constitute a pair of dharma and simile.

In full, they should be called *laukika-geya* (路伽祇夜) and *gāthā-geya* (伽陀祇夜); the former preserves the specific while abbreviating the general, whereas the latter preserves the general while abbreviating the specific.

Upadeśa is termed "discourse on the meaning" (lun yi), which refers to the means of discourse; the aforementioned eight sections and four pairs are termed the "objects of discourse. Thus, the means of discourse and the objects of discourse constitute one pair.
Question:
Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are called Vaipulya; what is the difference between them? Answer:
"Great" refers to the complete Vaipulya, while "small" refers to the partial Vaipulya.

Furthermore, the principle of the Mahāyāna is called "vaipulya" (vast) because it is correct, and it is called "vaipulya" (extensive) because its meaning is rich; since the text elucidates this vast and extensive principle, it is termed a Vaipulya Sūtra.
In the terminology of the Hīnayāna, "zheng" (correct) is called "fang" (directional), while "wen" (textual expression) frequently uses "guang" (broad).
The line and a half beginning with "Those of dull faculties delight in the lesser Dharma" clarifies the dharmas of the fruits of the Hīnayāna.

Furthermore, while the preceding section clarified the ninefold division as referring to the teachings for humans and devas, the present section clarifies the teachings for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Although the paths of humans and devas differ, they do not transcend the ninefold division; and although the two vehicles differ, they both equally seek *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, within the teachings for humans and devas, the capacities of humans and devas were first expanded upon, followed by the explanation of the ninefold teaching; here, likewise, the capacities of the two vehicles are first described, followed by the explanation of the teachings for the two vehicles.
Question:
Since it has already been said that they delight in the lesser Dharma, why does it further state that they are greedily attached to birth and death? Answer:
At present, their faculties and inclinations delight in the Lesser Dharma, while in the distant past they were attached to birth and death.
Furthermore, regarding their faculties and inclinations that delight in the Lesser Dharma, it is based on their dispositions that they remain attached to birth and death.

Furthermore, to delight in inferior dharmas is to crave birth and death; since inferior nirvāṇa is itself the birth and death of the Mahāyāna, this teaching on nirvāṇa is explained as the second [part], clarifying the Hīnayāna teachings.

From the passage "I established these skillful means" onwards, the preceding section clarified the two types of past teachings; this current section clarifies the underlying intent of those two types of teachings.

Previously, by following the immediate context, the intent behind preaching the Hīnayāna teachings was explained: the purpose of the past teaching on the *nirvāṇa*-dharma was to cause [beings] to enter the Buddha-wisdom.

Regarding "definitively expounding the Mahāyāna": formerly, the words referred to the Small Vehicle while the intention was directed toward the Great; because the teaching did not accord with the intention, it was not called definitive.
Now, both words and intention are fully revealed, and thus it is called definitive.

Furthermore, sutras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* teach the bodhisattvas explicitly while transforming the followers of the two vehicles implicitly; thus, they are "definitive" for bodhisattvas but not yet definitive for those of the two vehicles.
Now, because it teaches the bodhisattvas explicitly and teaches the followers of the two vehicles explicitly, it is called "definitive."
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna is the definitive teaching; as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "lion’s roar" refers to definitive discourse, meaning that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Now, it is likewise definitively taught that all sentient beings possess the One Vehicle.
Because there is no remainder in principle and because the nature consists solely of the Buddha-nature, the Buddha-nature is called the "definitive teaching"; the One Vehicle is likewise so.
The section beginning with "These ninefold teachings of mine" is second, clarifying the intent behind preaching the ninefold teachings.
The first half clarifies the teaching of the Dharma according to the needs of the occasion, while the second half clarifies the underlying intent of that teaching.

The purpose of expounding the ninefold division of scriptures is to enable beings to awaken to and enter the Mahāyāna, and to provide them with an understanding of the Mahāyāna; this is the fundamental intent. Therefore, it is said that "entering the Mahāyāna is the foundation."

From the passage beginning "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure" onwards, the preceding section clarified the intent behind the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) given in the past; now, this second section clarifies the intent behind the teaching of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) given in the past.
If one discusses the five vehicles, the preceding section explained four vehicles, while this section distinguishes the fifth: the teaching of the Mahāyāna.
If one establishes the sequence according to the three teachings:
first, the human and celestial realms constitute the lower teaching;
next, the two vehicles constitute the middle teaching.

Now, the Mahāyāna constitutes the supreme teaching; the text is precisely composed with this intention. In every passage, it first clarifies the capacity of the recipient (the *mārga*) and subsequently distinguishes the teaching (*śāsana*); this is evident upon examining the text.

Some say: Previously it was clarified that the Hīnayāna taught in the past was a provisional means (*upāya*); now it is clarified that even the Mahāyāna within the three vehicles (*triyāna*) taught in the past was also a provisional means. This is because he intends to harmonize the three vehicles so they return to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); thus, having previously clarified the Hīnayāna, he now distinguishes the Mahāyāna.

Now, I say this is not so. Previously, the Hīnayāna was elucidated, and the text distinguished the Hīnayāna as being a provisional means (*upāya*). If the former Mahāyāna were also a provisional means, then one should have first listed the Mahāyāna and subsequently explained that the Mahāyāna is a provisional means.

The text, however, is not like that; it directly clarifies that the Mahāyāna of the past was not stated to be a provisional means (upāya). Therefore, we know that the Hīnayāna of the past was the provisional means, whereas the Mahāyāna of the past was not a provisional means.
Furthermore, the teaching of the Mahāyāna for bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās exclusively is merely a skillful means (*upāya*).

However, since the text states, "The profound and wondrous path practiced by immeasurable Buddhas, O Son of the Buddha," it follows that these are not merely persons of provisional designation who practice exclusively; thus, one knows this to be the true Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "First, for the sake of the śrāvakas, the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) characterized by arising and ceasing were taught; subsequently, for those who have already practiced and possess the great resolve capable of receiving the profound and subtle Dharma, the twelve links of dependent origination as neither-arising-nor-ceasing were taught. If this were the case, both the Great and Small Vehicles would equally be provisional (*upāya*). However, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* clarifies that the prior teaching of the Small Vehicle is provisional while the subsequent teaching of the Great Vehicle is the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*); the present text is likewise so.
Question:
One should only clarify that the former "Small Vehicle" was a provisional means; why, then, does the present text clarify that the former "Great Vehicle" was also [provisional]? Answer:

This text provides a dual introduction to the Tathāgata’s two treasuries—the Great and the Small—encompassing all teachings of both the Great and Small Vehicles from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* up until the time before Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
The reason for providing these two introductory prefaces is as follows: the preface to the Small Vehicle teaching intends to clarify the turning away from the small toward the great;
it shows that bodhisattvas of dull faculties, who had not previously attained awakening, are now finally able to comprehend and understand.

The preface to the Great Vehicle teaching praises those bodhisattvas who proceed directly, whose great capacity was already matured from the time of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* until their arrival at Vulture Peak, and who, possessing sharp faculties, attained awakening early on. This is merely a matter of praising by number the bodhisattvas who were pioneers and lamenting the belated awakening of the śrāvakas.
This is not unrelated to the great skillful means of the past.
Question:
How is this known to be so?
Answer: This is proven by two passages.

First, the "Chapter on the Emergence" states: "As soon as these sentient beings see my body and hear what I say, they immediately enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This clarifies that bodhisattvas who proceed directly awaken to the Buddha-wisdom early on.

The subsequent passage states, "Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, I shall now also cause such persons as these to hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom. This clarifies that there are bodhisattvas who turn from the small toward the great, attaining awakening only late in their careers.

Second, this sutra text clarifies that for śrāvakas who practice the Mahāyāna late, hear the Mahāyāna late, receive their prediction of enlightenment late, and feel joy late, it is a teaching of ultimate truth;
likewise, for bodhisattvas who practice the Mahāyāna early, hear the Mahāyāna early, receive their prediction of enlightenment early, and feel joy early, it is also a teaching of ultimate truth.

If the Bodhisattva Mingwen had heard the Mahāyāna early on and received his prediction of enlightenment early on, and if these were merely expedient means, then since the *Avataṃsaka* and other such sutras would all be expedient means, this would constitute a most grievous slander of the Dharma.
Question:

If the Mahāyāna teachings of the past, which clarify that bodhisattvas receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, are indeed the authentic teaching, and if śrāvakas must first refine their minds through sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* before they can subsequently awaken to and enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then one would know that the *Prajñāpāramitā* serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; how, then, could it be considered the authentic teaching?

Answer: The *Prajñāpāramitā* reveals the teachings for Bodhisattvas while secretly transforming those of the Two Vehicles. Because practitioners of the Two Vehicles rely on the Bodhisattvas’ authentic teachings to cultivate and soften their minds, they are able to enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. This is precisely a case of the later followers attaining realization by relying on the prior masters; how then can it be said that the teachings of those prior masters were merely expedient means?
Question:
Is this Mahāyāna also considered a skillful means? Answer:

The Way has never been large or small; it is only because one responds to conditions that are large or small that names and marks are provisionally established within the realm where there are no names or marks. Therefore, both the "Large" and the "Small" are expedient means. Not only are the Large and Small both expedient means, but the One, the Three, and the Ten are likewise all expedient means.

However, here the Great and Small Vehicles are contrasted: because the Small Vehicle has not yet reached full realization, it is termed a "skillful means," whereas the Great Vehicle, having already reached full realization, is called "ultimate reality.
This passage is divided into two parts:

first, praising the bodhisattvas for their merit and sharp faculties through seven points concerning their early attainment, which implicitly reveals that the śrāvakas, possessing meager merit and dull faculties, have seven points concerning their late attainment.
Second, the conclusion summarizes the intent of the previous discourse on the Mahāyāna:

"There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure. This first praises the Bodhisattvas for possessing, from an early stage in their present existence, the virtue of being capable of hearing [the teaching], thereby revealing that the Śrāvakas possess the capacity for hearing it only late in their development.
It is called "pure" because it is free from the mind of attainment held by ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
"Supple" means possessing a mind of non-attainment that accords with all Buddhas and does not oppose the Mahāyāna, like moistened cowhide which is easily bent and folded.
Regarding "sharp faculties" (*tīkṣṇendriya*): faith is their beginning and wisdom is their end; thus, the first and last of the five faculties are briefly cited.
Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, faith is that which enables entry into the ocean of the Dharma, while knowledge is that which enables crossing over; therefore, these two are mentioned.

From the phrase "at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas" onwards, the second section praises the Bodhisattvas for having cultivated the great causes early on; since they have encountered many Buddhas and their practice has been accumulated, this demonstrates that the Śrāvakas are late in cultivating the causes for the Mahāyāna.

From "For these sons of the Buddhas" onwards is the third section: praising the early teaching of the Mahāyāna to bodhisattvas, which implicitly reveals the later teaching of the Mahāyāna to śrāvakas.
As for the statement, "He preached this Mahāyāna sūtra," this Mahāyāna sūtra is precisely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
In the past, for the sake of the bodhisattvas who proceed directly, he had already finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Therefore, the "Chapter on the Emergence" states: "When these sentient beings first see my body and hear what I have taught, they immediately enter the Buddha-wisdom. This Buddha-wisdom is precisely the impartial great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; it was merely given the names of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Prajñāpāramitā* in the past.

Now, for the sake of those who turn from the Small Vehicle to enter the Great Vehicle, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is preached; thus we know that the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s manifestation of the Way is identical. Therefore it is said: "Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha speaks of various names, establishing different terms according to the capacities of sentient beings."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* further states: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is an alternative name for the *Prajñāpāramitā*"; this is clear evidence.

Regarding the passage, "I bestow upon such a person the prediction that they shall attain the Buddha-way in a future life," this is the fourth point: praising the early conferring of predictions upon bodhisattvas, which thereby reveals that the śrāvakas receive their predictions late.

"Recalling the Buddha with a profound mind": Fifth, by praising the bodhisattva for early cultivation of correct understanding and thus early receipt of the prediction of Buddhahood (vyākaraṇa), it is revealed that the followers of the two vehicles receive their prediction late because they cultivate correct understanding late.
"To recollect the Buddha with a profound mind" means to realize that the Tathāgata possesses a body that is neither born nor extinguished.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "All phenomena are unborn and all phenomena are unextinguished; if one can understand them in this way, the Buddhas will always be manifest before one."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "What is called 'recollection of the Buddha'?

It means that because there is no recollection, this is the recollection of the Buddha. This refers to the state where both internal and external are simultaneously merged in darkness, and both object and contemplation are equally quiescent; this is true recollection of the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "because of practicing pure precepts": sixth, it praises the Bodhisattva for attaining the prediction of Buddhahood early because they have practiced correct conduct early. Because they do not grasp at nor violate the precepts of ordinary beings or the Two Vehicles—which are characterized by the apprehension of objects—they are called "pure precepts. However, practice and understanding possess no separate essences; thus, within the single meaning of right contemplation, freedom from delusion constitutes understanding, while freedom from transgressions constitutes practice.

From "These [beings] shall hear and attain Buddhahood" onwards is the seventh section: praising the bodhisattvas for their early attainment of joy, thereby censuring the śrāvakas who only attained joy after receiving their prediction.
The bliss of the third dhyāna in the world is called "bliss pervading the body," yet it is still but a minor joy.

Now, having received the Buddha’s prediction, one immediately attains the bliss of a Buddha; therefore, it is called "Great Joy. Realizing that the fundamental nature of this body and mind is quiescent extinction is what is meant by "pervading the body."
"‘The Buddha knew their mental activities’" and below, the second section concludes the intent behind the previous teaching of the Great Vehicle.
Because the Buddha, upon his initial attainment of enlightenment, knew that the bodhisattvas possessed the merit and sharp faculties [necessary for it], he taught the Mahāyāna to them early on.

From "Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas" onwards is the second section, which clarifies the intent of the present teaching; it corresponds to the verse above stating that [the Buddha] appears in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition.
The prose section has three intended meanings:

first, to clarify that he appears in the world for the sake of a great matter; second, to show that he does so solely to instruct bodhisattvas; and third, to clarify that in the buddha-fields of the ten directions there is only one [vehicle] and no second, thereby explaining and establishing the preceding two points.
Now, the text shifts its momentum to present this in verse, which is also divided into three distinct sections:

first, it clarifies that [the teaching] is intended solely for one person; second, it clarifies that the principle is one and not two; and third, it distinguishes the general purport of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
The reason why it was previously explained that the teaching alone addresses a single person was to contrast with the former two teachings, each of which responded to two distinct conditions;
now it is explained that these two conditions together receive a single teaching.

In the past, because the great faculties of the śrāvakas were not yet mature, the Lesser Vehicle was taught for them; because the great faculties of the bodhisattvas were already mature, the Greater Vehicle was taught for them. Thus, the two teachings each respond to their respective conditions.

Now, at this assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the great capacities of both the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas have matured together; therefore, through these two conditions, they hear a single teaching and all alike attain Buddhahood. For this reason, it was previously explained that the teaching was intended for only one person.
Regarding "without doubt": previously, when the Three Vehicles were taught, it was held that Śrāvakas had no path of further progress while Bodhisattvas had a path of regression;

now, it is clarified that there is only One Vehicle and not three, whereby Śrāvakas possess a path of further progress while Bodhisattvas have no path of regression—hence, it is said to be "without doubt."
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions": second, this clarifies that the principle is one and not two.

This is because the principle consists solely of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and not two vehicles; therefore, both śrāvakas and bodhisattvas who hear even a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* all attain Buddhahood. The present passage explains and establishes the meaning of the preceding section.
Regarding the phrase "except for the Buddha’s skillful means," a doubter asks:
"If there is only one [vehicle] and not two, why did he previously speak of the two vehicles?
Therefore, it is explained as follows:
Based on the ultimate principle, there are no two; it is only for the sake of expedient means that one speaks of two.

Regarding the phrase "merely by way of provisional names," those who harbor doubts may, upon hearing that the two are spoken of only as expedient means, still claim that there exists a subtle essence of dharma-body for the two vehicles.
Therefore, the commentary states:
"Ultimately, there is no essence to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they are spoken of merely as provisional designations.
Regarding the phrase "guiding all sentient beings," a doubter asks:
Since there is no substantial essence, what is the use of speaking these empty names?
Therefore, the commentary explains:

it is because one desires to guide and instruct sentient beings so as to lead them out of the burning house; by means of these empty names, they obtain real benefit, and thus it is called "skillful means" (upāya-kauśalya).
As the sutra says: "When I first attained Buddhahood, I saved all beings with empty fists.
From the phrase "Because of expounding the Buddha’s wisdom" onwards is the third section, clarifying the general purpose of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.

According to principle, there is greatness and no smallness; the Buddhas are persons who realize this principle. Because, according to principle, there is greatness, they appear in the world solely for the sake of great matters; because, according to principle, there is no smallness, they do not appear in the world for the sake of small matters. Therefore, following the preceding principle, the latter clarifies the general significance of their appearance in the world.
The textual exposition is divided into two parts:
first, it clarifies that the Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of great matters and not for minor ones; second, it provides scriptural citations to explain and establish this point.
The initial text further consists of two parts:
first, the opening of the two chapter-headings; second, the explanation of these two chapter-headings.

The former verse indicates the chapter-heading that [the Buddha] appears in the world solely for the sake of the Great Matter; the subsequent half-line clarifies the chapter-heading that he does not appear for the sake of minor matters.
The first half of the preceding verse indicates that the Buddha appears in the world for the sake of a single great matter; the second half cites the true and the false to establish this point.
Since there is only one reality and the other two are not true, the Buddhas appear in the world solely for the sake of this one matter.
Question:
Above it was stated that there are neither two nor three; why, then, is it now said that "two" is not the truth? Answer:

The previous clarification that there are no two [vehicles] means there are no pratyekabuddhas; the absence of the three [knowledges] means there are no śrāvakas. Thus, in this current text, the duality is not ultimate; rather, the preceding section clarified that both are non-existent, while the present section clarifies that they are said to exist as skillful means, yet are not truly existent.

The passage beginning with “Ultimately not by means of the Hīnayāna” constitutes the half-line heading for the chapter on “Appearing in the World Not for the Sake of Minor Matters. Furthermore, the line “Only this one thing is real” explains the preceding heading on “Appearing in the World for the Sake of Great Matters. The statement that “the other two are not true” establishes the heading on “Appearing in the World Not for the Sake of Minor Matters,” because since the other two are not true, he ultimately does not deliver sentient beings by means of the Hīnayāna.
From "The Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna" onwards is the second section, which explains the two chapter-headings.

The first line explains the chapter-heading that the Buddha appears in the world for a great matter; because the Buddha himself abides in the Mahāyāna, he uses the Dharma he has attained to deliver sentient beings.
Question:
Since concentration and wisdom are themselves the Mahāyāna, why speak of "adornments of the Mahāyāna"? Answer:
"Stillness and illumination" distinguish the specific while encompassing the general; this is also using the Dharma to adorn the person.
As for the term "power," it is called power because it is capable of delivering sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding the clarification of concentration and wisdom alone: the absence of any lingering affliction is concentration, and the perfection of every virtue is wisdom.

Furthermore, the total stilling of all conditioned phenomena constitutes the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, while the unimpeded illumination of all objects constitutes the fruit of *bodhi*. These two are explained here because they collectively encompass the fruits of the Vehicle of Fruition (*phala-yāna*).

Below the phrase "Self-realization of the unsurpassed path," the second section explains the introductory heading of the previous chapter: "Why one does not appear in the world for the sake of minor matters.
If one abides in the dharma of the equality of the Great Vehicle yet delivers beings by means of the Small [Vehicle], there are two faults:
first, it contradicts the equality of the Great Vehicle; second, it falls into the error of stinginess and greed.

Because one is greedily attached to great wealth and does not share it with others, it is called "avarice. This is both contrary to the principle of equality and inconsistent with the mind of the Buddhas; therefore, it is said that "this matter is improper."
"Those who have faith and take refuge in the Buddha," and so forth: this is the second section, which establishes that [the teaching] is for the great and not for the small.
There are three types of evidence for its supramundane nature:
first, evidence from others; second, evidence from oneself; and third, evidence from the past.

Regarding the citation of external testimony: this refers to those who, with faith, take refuge in the Buddha and know that the Tathāgata’s words are not deceptive; yet, because they themselves abide in the True Dharma while presenting a counterfeit vehicle to others, it is called deception.
To use this to entice others is called deception.
Because the Buddha abides in the True Vehicle and returns it to sentient beings, he does not deceive.

Regarding the phrase "nor has he any intent of greed or envy": external speech that appears deceptive arises precisely from internal greed and envy; because one is personally greedy for the True Vehicle and envious of sentient beings, one bestows counterfeit teachings and thereby deceives. Since the Buddha is free from greed and envy, he does not deceive.

Regarding the phrase "severing all evils within all dharmas": it is not merely that he is free from greed and envy; he has completely severed all evils within all dharmas. Because internal evil contact gives rise to fear, and because the Buddha is devoid of all evils, he alone among the ten directions is without fear.
"By means of these marks, my body is adorned," and so forth, is the second section, which cites oneself as proof.
It consists of four statements:
first, because I possess this body endowed with the primary and secondary marks, it is known that within I am free from greed and envy, and without I am free from deception.
2. Since I still illuminate the world with the light of my body, I know that the body benefits sentient beings; therefore, I am free from greed and envy within, and do not deceive others without.
3. Because my wisdom is revered and looked up to by immeasurable multitudes, I am certainly not a person characterized by greed, envy, or deception.

Fourth, it clarifies that when one explains the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*) to others to settle all phenomena, one knows that one abides in the Mahāyāna oneself and causes others to abide in the Mahāyāna as well.

Furthermore, while the preceding verse clarified that the Buddha has no evil, this verse distinguishes that the Buddha possesses goodness; together they explain how the Buddha, having attained Buddhahood, abides in the Mahāyāna himself and bestows the Mahāyāna upon sentient beings.
"Śāriputra, you should know," and so forth, marks the third section: citing past vows as proof.
The first verse cites the Buddha’s past vow; the second verse clarifies that the past vow has been fulfilled.

When first resolving to attain enlightenment, one already vowed that all beings should fully achieve Buddhahood; how much more so now that one has attained Buddhahood oneself—how could one abide in greatness for oneself while leaving others in smallness?
Question:

When the Tathāgata first resolved his mind on enlightenment, he vowed that all beings would attain Buddhahood; yet now, not everyone has become a Buddha. How, then, can it be said that his vow is fulfilled? Answer:

At the single assembly on Vulture Peak, those of the Lesser Vehicle were turned toward the Great Vehicle and Bodhisattvas entered together into the One Vehicle. From that time forward, he caused the *pratyekabuddhas* (those who go directly) to receive the prediction of Buddhahood; thus, throughout his single lifetime of appearing in the world, these two types of beings alone were universally enabled to become Buddhas, whereby his vow for that lifetime was fulfilled. This is as proven by the passage from the "Emergence" chapter cited above.
Regarding "correct intention": prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Buddha’s vow was not yet fulfilled because he could only preach the Buddha-vehicle for the sake of bodhisattvas alone;
now, by enabling all sentient beings of the five vehicles and six realms to attain Buddhahood, the Buddha’s vow is fulfilled.
Furthermore, to preach the One Vehicle for others is precisely to fulfill the Buddha’s intention; it is also called "fulfillment.
The section beginning with "If I encounter sentient beings" constitutes the second part, the Gate of Resolving Doubts.
The intent behind this passage is both proximate and remote.

As for the remote meaning: all the preceding chapters have clarified that the various teachings expounded serve to manifest the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and cause all sentient beings to universally attain Buddhahood. If this is so, why does the Tathāgata not preach the One Vehicle to all people?

Second, as for "proximity": this arises from the original fundamental vows made in the past. Since you formerly vowed to cause all beings to attain Buddhahood, now that those original vows have been fulfilled, why did you not speak of the One immediately when you first appeared in the world, but instead spoke of the Three? It is only now that you speak of the One.
This chapter is presented to explain this meaning.
It consists of four parts:
first, it clarifies that one must not universally preach the One Vehicle to all beings.
2. Explaining why it is not permissible to speak of [the Buddha] as one;
3. Clarifying that because it is not permissible to speak of one, he skillfully speaks of three;
4. Clarifying that although he speaks of three, it is ultimately for the purpose of revealing the one.

Regarding the phrase, "If I were to encounter sentient beings, I would teach them all the Buddha-way," the first half of this line restates the underlying concern of the objection, assuming that upon encountering sentient beings, one would indeed preach only the One [Vehicle].
The second half clarifies that [teaching] what is harmful and without benefit has three faults:
first, the error of mismatch between a small capacity and a great teaching;
second, the fault of dull faculties becoming confused by the teaching and deluded regarding the principle.
Third, they do not believe in the fault of slander.
From the passage "I know these sentient beings" onwards is the second section, which explains the reason why [the Buddha] cannot speak of them as being of one kind.
There are two meanings for the statement that "one cannot be spoken of":
first, knowing that sentient beings possess no roots of goodness;
second, knowing that sentient beings possess various roots of evil.
Thus, two meanings are employed to explain the three faults, beginning with "lack of wisdom" and "confusion.

Regarding "absence of the roots of goodness": these sentient beings have never practiced the non-apprehension of phenomena as the root of bodhi; therefore, they lack faith and understanding—this is the first [fault].
"Being firmly attached to the five desires," and so forth: second, it clarifies that sentient beings possess evil roots.
This section consists of two parts:
first, it clarifies the presence of the evil of craving; [the rest follows].
Next, the existence of views and attachments is explained.
The reason for specifically clarifying attachment and views is that these two collectively encompass all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, householders generally give rise to attachment, while renunciants and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) generally give rise to various views.
Furthermore, because the various Māras delight in birth and death, they give rise to craving; because non-Buddhists are attached to various views, they give rise to views.
Moreover, craving is an affliction of long-standing practice, whereas views are delusions newly arisen.

Although all sentient beings equally possess both craving and views pertaining to the three realms, it is craving that predominantly manifests; it is only when they encounter false teachers that views arise.

Furthermore, the affliction of craving is termed a "single failure," yet non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), while possessing this delusion of craving, further give rise to views therein. This constitutes a "failure arising within a failure. For these reasons, craving and views are clarified here.
This section clarifies craving by dividing it into two chapters:
first, an analysis of the causes of craving;
second, an elucidation of the fruits of craving.
"Being firmly attached to the five desires" refers to the arising of craving and the emergence of the objects of that craving.
"Because of delusion and craving, affliction arises" means that the reason one craves the five desires is that craving is produced by delusion.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "Because of deception, greed arises"; and as the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says, "From ignorance and craving for existence, my illness arises."

Regarding "affliction" (*daurmanasya*): this clarifies that affliction arises in the present from the cause of craving; that is to say, by means of the conditions of craving, one afflicts body and mind, either by afflicting oneself or by afflicting others.
Therefore, delusion (*moha*) is the cause of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and affliction (*upāyāsa*) is the fruit of craving.

From the passage "by means of the causes and conditions of various desires" onwards, the preceding section clarified the arising of affliction, which refers to retribution in the present life; from this point forward, it clarifies the arising of the two subsequent types of retribution.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, an analysis of the general retribution;
second, an explanation of the specific retribution.
The first half of the verse clarifies birth resulting from immediate retribution (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*), while the second half clarifies subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma*).
Since it speaks of the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), these three types of retribution are continuous.
From the line "Receiving the subtle form of the womb" onwards is the second section, which specifically clarifies the reception of retribution, namely human retribution.
The reason for specifically clarifying the retribution of human beings is that the Buddha was born among humans and primarily transformed human beings.

Human retribution is fully comprised of the eight sufferings; the first half briefly clarifies the suffering of birth, as the suffering of birth is the beginning of the eight sufferings, while the second half comprehensively clarifies all the various sufferings.
Regarding the phrase "constantly increasing life after life": if one discusses this in detail, it refers to growth occurring throughout the various stages within the womb as successive lifetimes.
Furthermore, taking a full term as one lifetime, this constant progression occurs birth after birth; thus, the meaning of "increasing" is that from this present life one proceeds to future lives.
Question:
When sentient beings enter the womb, why is there a difference between male and female? Answer:

If the paternal seed is predominant and the maternal seed is deficient, a male is formed; if the maternal seed is predominant and the paternal seed is deficient, a female is formed; if the seeds of the father and mother are equal, one becomes a eunuch or a person with dual sexual organs.
"Entering the dense forest of wrong views," and so forth, is the second section, which clarifies the arising of views.
This section also has two parts:
first, clarifying the causes of these views; [the rest follows].
Next, the seeing of the result is explained.
Regarding the phrase "entering the dense forest of wrong views": herein there are one view, two views, and so forth, up to sixty-two views.

As for the term "one view," it is a collective designation for all the various views of the non-Buddhists as a single wrong view. Because these wrong views are numerous, like a thick forest, they are called a "dense forest" (*gahana*).
The phrase "existence, non-existence, and so forth" clarifies two views. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Those with a predominance of craving cling to existence and thus give rise to the view of existence; those with a predominance of [wrong] views cling to non-existence and thus give rise to the view of non-existence."
Furthermore, it says: "Those with an abundance of the four views are attached to existence; those with an abundance of wrong views are attached to non-existence.
Regarding the phrase "relying on these various views, they are fully possessed of the sixty-two [views]," this clarifies the sixty-two views.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, "For example, the view of self subsumes the sixty-two views," indicating that the view of self is the root of the sixty-two views.

The same *Mahāprañāpāramitā Sūtra* further states that "identity and difference are the root," while this sūtra takes existence and non-existence as the root; these three [positions] are not mutually contradictory.

Because of the conception of a self, various views arise; thus, the self is their root. Because there is a self, one conceives of the self as being identical to or different from the aggregates (skandhas); therefore, identity and difference are the root.
If the self were identical to the aggregates, then with the cessation of the aggregates, the self would cease; thus, the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi) arises.
If the self were distinct from the aggregates, then even with the cessation of the aggregates, the self would persist; thus, the view of eternalism (śāśvatadṛṣṭi) arises.
The extremes of annihilationism and eternalism constitute existence and non-existence; therefore, existence and non-existence are taken as the foundation.
Existence and non-existence are called "extreme views" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and serve as the basis for the sixty-two views; the self (*ātman*) is the root of these extreme views.

Regarding the "sixty-two views," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the "Buddhamātṛ-parivarta" (Chapter on the Mother of the Buddha), expands upon the fourteen difficult questions (*caturdaśa-avyākṛta*) to constitute sixty-two.
The fourteen difficult questions are as follows:

four concerning whether the self (*ātman*) and the world are eternal, non-eternal, both, or neither; four concerning whether the self and the world are finite, infinite, both, or neither; four concerning whether [the self] exists after death, does not exist after death, both, or neither; these together make twelve, to which are added the two positions that the body and the self are identical and that the body and the self are distinct, totaling fourteen.

Regarding "permanence" and "impermanence," these are established internally with reference to the five aggregates (*skandhas*); since each aggregate possesses four permutations of permanence and impermanence, there are twenty.
"The finite" and "the infinite" are likewise established with reference to the five aggregates, thus also resulting in twenty.

"The Tathāgata exists after death" and "the Tathāgata does not exist after death" likewise result in twenty. Combined, these total sixty; when added to the two fundamental positions of "identity" and "difference," they total sixty-two.

Another explanation is as follows: form is the self; there is a self apart from form; the self dwells within form; and form dwells within the self.
