Thus, for each aggregate (skandha), there are four views, resulting in twenty for the five aggregates. When categorized according to the three periods of time, these become sixty. With the views of annihilationism and eternalism as the basis, they total sixty-two.
Sixteen views consist in identifying with the aggregates (*skandha*), while forty-six views consist in being detached from the aggregates.

According to another interpretation: regarding each of the five aggregates, one calculates two types—existence and non-existence—thus forming ten views. These extend across the three periods of time to become thirty. Thus, there are thirty views regarding the five aggregates of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and thirty regarding the five aggregates of noble ones (*ārya*), totaling sixty. Since *nirvāṇa* is not subsumed within the three periods of time, one merely calculates its existence or non-existence; these combined form the sixty-two views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Question:
Are the sixty-two views subsumed within the five views? Answer:

The view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root of the sixty-two views; while false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) negate existence, the sixty-two views posit it, and thus false views are not subsumed [within them].

Regarding the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), one regards the sixty-two views as supreme; regarding the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one regards the sixty-two views as the path. Thus, these four views are not subsumed within the sixty-two, yet the sixty-two views themselves belong to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the phrase "deeply attached to false dharmas": previously it was explained that views arise from craving; now it is shown that craving arises further from views.
"False dharmas" refers to the various views.
Because they are deeply attached to this view, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*).
Furthermore, when the Buddha first appeared in the world, he could not immediately uproot this view; thus, he taught the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is why it is said to be "deeply attached."
Furthermore, since one regards this view as excellent, one generates yet another view upon that very view; this is called the "view of attachment to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
As for "prideful self-exaltation," it refers to relying on these various views to elevate oneself.
This reveals that when the Buddha first appeared in the world, the various non-Buddhists did not accept the path of the One Vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "a deceitful and crooked mind that is not true": previously, from the underlying proclivities (*anuśaya*) arose the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); now, from the active outbursts arise the entanglements and impurities (*paryavasthāna-mala*). Deceit (*śāṭhya*) is one of the six impurities.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "Deceit arises from views. This is because one who gives rise to views must necessarily be of sharp faculties; only such a person is capable of being deceitful and crooked, whereas those of dull faculties cannot.
The preceding section clarified that those with pride do not receive the Buddha’s transformation; this section now clarifies how he transforms his disciples through guile.
“Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of ten million billion” refers, secondly, to the manifestation of the fruits attained.

Because craving is the root of rebirth, it draws one downward into the six realms of existence; because views deviate from correct principle, they obstruct one from the Three Honored Ones above. Thus, these two passages clarify the different fruits of craving and views.

Regarding the phrase "such people are difficult to deliver": this refers generally to those sentient beings of craving and false views who cannot easily be delivered by means of the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Question:
To which category of sentient beings of craving and false views does this refer?
Answer: When the Buddha first appeared in the world, there were sentient beings with such attachments and views; therefore, he could not preach the One Vehicle.
From the words "Therefore, Śāriputra" onwards is the third section, clarifying that because the One Vehicle cannot be preached, he expediently taught the Three Vehicles.
"Explaining the path that leads to the exhaustion of suffering" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
"Showing [them] nirvāṇa" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*); these briefly enumerate the supramundane causes and effects.
Question:

It was stated above that sentient beings who give rise to false views will not hear the name of the Buddha nor the True Dharma for thousands of millions of kalpas; how is it that you can now say you may preach Nirvana to them?
Answer:

Those who abide in this wrong view cannot hear it; however, these sentient beings with wrong views have previously practiced the Hīnayāna and possess the nature of small faculties. Having given rise to wrong views midway, as their small-capacity potential was about to manifest and their wrong views were on the verge of collapsing, they were therefore able to be taught the Hīnayāna doctrine.
"Although I speak of nirvana," and so forth: fourth, this clarifies that although three [vehicles] are taught, they ultimately serve to reveal the One.
The first phrase opens the gate of expedient means; therefore, it is said that it is not the true extinction.
Regarding the passage beginning with "All dharmas from the very beginning," some say:

There are three kinds of *nirvāṇa*. The initial teaching takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) resulting from the extinction of ashes as *śānti* (quiescence); the *Prajñāpāramitā* teaching takes the equality of the Four Noble Truths as *śānti*; and this sutra clarifies that the *nirvāṇa* which is like a jewel-treasure, transcending the mundane, is *śānti*.

Now is the time for critical examination; since it has not yet been possible to clearly explain the cessation of the "Jewel Place," we shall temporarily employ the cessation described in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to refute their notion of a nihilistic, non-active unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Some say: "The dharmas of the ten thousand virtues are quiescent from the outset; because they lack the characteristics of the three vehicles, they are called 'quiescent.
Now, we clarify that neither of these two [explanations] constitutes a correct interpretation."
The current text correctly distinguishes between the two *Nirvāṇas*, the Great and the Small.
The extinction (*nirodha*) of the Lesser Vehicle is not true extinction; only the extinction of Great *Nirvāṇa* is true extinction.

The reason for this is that the Lesser Vehicle is first afflicted by the two maladies of cause and effect; therefore, its extinction—which results in the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is merely the severance of the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If a phenomenon existed previously but does not exist now, then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be at fault. Here, in contrast to the non-ultimate cessation of the Hīnayāna, it is clarified that the two afflictions of cause and effect are primordially quiescent; this is precisely the cessation of Great Nirvāṇa.
Question:
Now you clarify the One Vehicle; why then do you distinguish between the two different types of Nirvana, the Great and the Small? Answer:
It is precisely because the present fruit differs from the former fruit that the present cause must differ from the former cause.

Furthermore, the minor extinction of the past was not true extinction, whereas the great extinction of the present is true extinction; only then can one be exhorted to abandon the minor extinction in order to seek the great extinction. This is truly the grand principle of the One Vehicle.
Question:
How many kinds of differences are there between the two types of nirvāṇa, the Great and the Small? Answer:
From beginning to end, this sutra contains three distinctions.

First, the cessation [of suffering] in the Hīnayāna is narrow, as it only eliminates the four abodes of ignorance and the death-and-rebirth of segmented existence; the Mahāyāna, however, completely eliminates the five abodes and the two types of death. This is manifested at the end of the "Parable Chapter," where it says: "To merely leave behind delusion is called liberation, yet in reality, one has not attained all-encompassing liberation."
Second, in the Hīnayāna, afflictions and the body-and-mind wisdom exist beforehand and are subsequently extinguished; therefore, they are not originally quiescent.
In the Mahāyāna, it is clarified that the nature of both afflictions and body-and-mind wisdom is inherently quiescent, and thus there is no further need for extinction.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "If a phenomenon existed previously but no longer exists later, then all Buddhas would be guilty of transgression. Since the two vehicles existed previously but do not exist now, they would be persons guilty of such transgression; thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* provides the proof, stating: "If one were to claim that śrāvakas have no [practice of] giving, this is called breaking the precepts and holding false views. This is the evidence.
Third, those of the Two Vehicles perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness; they perceive only cessation and do not perceive non-cessation.
The Mahāyāna clearly perceives both emptiness and non-emptiness, which constitutes the complete perception of both cessation and non-cessation.
Therefore, the "Parable Chapter" states, "All are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s own extinction," which refers to the meaning of extinction.
It further states, "He bestows upon them all the meditative concentrations and wisdom of the Buddhas," which refers to the meaning of non-extinction.
Therefore, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states: "It is precisely because Great Nirvāṇa constitutes the One Vehicle.
Question:
Since sūtras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* have already clarified that [all phenomena] are originally quiescent and extinguished, why is it that the śrāvakas do not attain awakening?
Answer:

Although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that [all phenomena] are originally quiescent and extinguished, it has not yet opened up the teaching that the extinction of the Śrāvakas is not the true extinction; therefore, the Śrāvakas are unable to awaken to it.
Now, to clarify that "extinguishing the small" does not mean mere extinction is to open the gate of expedient means;
that its "primordial state of quiescent extinction" is to reveal the true meaning. Therefore, it is only through this that the Śrāvakas attain awakening.
From the passage "I possess the power of skillful means" onwards is the third section, the Gate of Encouraging Faith.
The first verse reiterates the Dharma that is to be believed, while the second verse explicitly clarifies the encouragement to believe.
The first half of the first verse uses Śākyamuni to clarify the provisional (upāya), while the second half relies on all Buddhas to manifest the One.
The first half of the second verse admonishes one to eliminate doubt, while the second half exhorts faith in the Buddha’s words.
From "Incalculable kalpas past" onwards is the second section, the Gate of Quoting Verses as Proof.
The verses concerning the Buddhas of the three periods are divided into three parts.
In the preceding prose, each Buddha was treated according to three gates; here, the same structure applies.
First, the principal teacher;
second, the teaching gate;
third, the assembly of disciples.
Now, this verse returns to these three points.

As for the first half-verse, which mentions many kalpas and many Buddhas, it is because a single kalpa and a single Buddha would not suffice as proof; therefore, by citing many kalpas and many Buddhas, the faith of sentient beings is engendered.
The second half clarifies that while the transformative rituals of the various Buddhas differ, they equally teach the path of the One Vehicle.
From the line "Thus, these World-Honored Ones" onwards is the second section, which versifies the aforementioned teaching.
In the preceding prose section, the teaching was presented briefly with only a single cycle;
now, in this verse section, it is expanded into two cycles:
first, elucidating the intent of the teaching by way of the Dharma-gate, and second, elucidating the intent of the teaching by way of the gate of supernatural powers.
Each of the two gates has three parts. In the first gate:
one line clarifies the teaching itself; half a line clarifies the intent of the teaching; and half a line clarifies the conditions for its benefit.

From "Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords" onwards is the second section, consisting of one and a half lines, which clarifies the intent of the teaching from the perspective of the gate of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
This is further divided into three parts:
the first line distinguishes the discernment of capacities; the next phrase manifests the supernormal power; and the final phrase clarifies the purpose of manifesting that power.
Regarding the phrase "further using different skillful means," some say:

the preceding section clarified the skillful means of the three vehicles; now, because the vehicle of humans and devas differs from the aforementioned three vehicles, it is called "different skillful means."

Some say: "The preceding section clarified the provisional means (*upāya*) of the Hīnayāna; the present section clarifies the Mahāyāna as distinct from that prior Hīnayāna, hence it is called 'distinctive provisional means' (*viśeṣopāya*).

Now, I say this is not so. In the preceding text, it was explained that preaching the Dharma constitutes the provisional means; in the present text, it is not preaching the Dharma but rather supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). Since supernormal power differs from the aforementioned preaching of the Dharma, it is termed "distinctive provisional means."

By means of preaching the Dharma and manifesting supernatural powers, the teachings and activities of all past Buddhas are briefly summarized and exhausted; it is directly clarified that whether through preaching the Dharma or manifesting supernatural powers, both serve to reveal the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Question:
What is meant by "manifesting supernormal powers"? Answer:

Just as in the past he extinguished the fire and subdued the dragon to leave the non-Buddhists' minds intoxicated with pride, so now he emits light and manifests auspicious omens to prompt the inner attendants to offer their invitation; such is the nature of these events.

Therefore, the "Introductory Chapter" states: "The present signs are like the original auspicious omens; these are the skillful means of all Buddhas. This refers precisely to the meaning of the current passage, wherein the Buddha now emits radiance to assist in the revelation of the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Question:
What is the difference between the previously explained skillful means of teaching the Dharma and the skillful means of supernatural powers (ṛddhi)? Answer:

In the present text, the manifestation of supernatural powers is called "expedient means" because it serves as the gradual basis for the commencement of the formal teaching; whereas in the preceding section, the dharma-gate of preaching was called "expedient means" because it involves teaching the three vehicles through the absence of the three.
"Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha*) refers to the singular, true Way; as its principle is supreme and unsurpassed, it is called "first," and it possesses profound grounds for being termed "truth.
The section beginning with "If there are classes of sentient beings" constitutes the third part, which praises the assembly that receives the teachings as set forth in the prose (*gadya*).
The text is divided into three parts:
first, clarifying the benefits gained from practicing during the lifetime of a Buddha in the past;
second, clarifying the benefits gained from practicing after the parinirvāṇa of a past Buddha.
Third, this section clarifies the benefits gained from practice throughout both lifetimes.

The gates of the teaching do not exceed two types: preaching the Dharma and manifesting supernatural powers; likewise, the practice does not exceed three distinct phases. This intention is intended to encompass exhaustively all matters concerning those who transform others and those who are transformed in the past.

In the preceding prose section, it was first explained that by hearing the Dharma one ultimately attains the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvajñatā); now, in this verse, it is explained that through prior cultivation one ultimately achieves Buddhahood.
This initial stage refers to the practice of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
Because the six perfections are the foundation for attaining Buddhahood, they are explained first.
"Cultivating various merits" refers to the practices of the four vehicles.
From the passage "After the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa" onwards, the second section clarifies how one attains Buddhahood through practice after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
This is divided into five parts:
first, it clarifies that by giving rise to a mind of longing and veneration upon seeing the Buddha enter nirvāṇa, one attains Buddhahood.
2. Explaining the making of offerings to the śarīra;
3. Explaining the construction of stūpas;
4. Explaining the creation of images.
Fifth, it is explained that one attains Buddhahood through the offerings of the three karmas.

These five stages thus form a sequential order: first, upon seeing the Buddha’s nirvana, a mind of longing and devotion arises; after his nirvana, one makes offerings to the śarīra (relics); following these offerings, the next stage explains the construction of stupas; because one wishes to represent the image of the Honored One for future generations, one must create images; once the images are completed, one proceeds to distinguish the offerings of the three karmas.
The phrase "if a person has a wholesome and gentle mind" refers to a mind of longing and devotion.
Furthermore, it denotes a mind of faith that accords with all Buddhas and does not contradict the gates of the teaching; therefore, it is called "wholesome and gentle."
From "After the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa" onwards is the second section, clarifying the offering of relics.
From "Erecting ten thousand koṭis of various stūpas" onwards is the third section, clarifying the construction of stūpas.
In foreign lands it is called a *stūpa*, or *thūpa*, or *khuddapā*; here [in China] it is translated as a "square mound" (*fangfen*) and is also termed a "tomb.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "There are four matters by which one obtains Brahma-merit:

first, erecting a stūpa where none exists; second, bringing the noble Saṃgha into harmony; third, repairing a ruined temple; and fourth, requesting the Buddha, when he has first attained the Way, to turn the wheel of Dharma."
Regarding "Brahma-merit": the merit of all sentient beings from the four continents up to the six heavens of the desire realm does not equal the merit of a single Brahma-heaven being.
A "temple" (miao) refers to its appearance.
When making offerings at a temple or stupa, one regards it as if a deity were actually present; thus, it possesses a manifest form.
The *muguān* (Santalum album) resembles white sandalwood in form and possesses a slight fragrance; this was personally observed by [the author] in Chang’an.
Regarding the passage "If a person, for the sake of the Buddha... and so forth, the fourth section clarifies the creation of images.
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* prohibits the use of glue;
one interpretation states that animal-hide glue is prohibited while wood-glue may be used.
Another interpretation states:
The distinction between permission and prohibition reflects a different underlying intent.
The section beginning with "If a person [makes offerings] at stupas and temples" constitutes the fifth part, clarifying the worship through the three karmas.
The section beginning with "Regarding all past Buddhas" constitutes the third part, collectively clarifying how cultivation in both lifetimes leads to Buddhahood.
"Those who hear this Dharma" refers to those who hear that all who have been taught the aforementioned Dharma shall attain Buddhahood.
Question:
How do those who merely lower their heads or raise their hands become Buddhas?
Answer:

Formerly, Zhu Daosheng composed the "Treatise on How Goodness Does Not Receive Retribution" (*Shan bushou bao lun*), clarifying that even a single hair’s worth of goodness leads to the attainment of Buddhahood and does not result in the retribution of birth and death; now we see that the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) also contains this same intent.
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* say:

A single moment of wholesome [mind] has two causes—habitual (*vāsanā*) and retributive (*vipāka*). The retributive cause brings about rebirth among humans or devas, while the habitual cause draws forth the arising of the nature [of Buddhahood] to become a Buddha.
Now, it is clear that this meaning is altogether difficult to understand.

The Sūtra states: "Wholesome deeds with attainment are neither unmoving nor emerging. Since the wholesome roots of ordinary beings, which serve as the causes for their practice, involve attainment, how can they attain Buddhahood?
Thus, by these words, one may turn the critique back upon Master Sheng.

Now, I shall clarify the principle that wholesome causes involve both receiving retribution and not receiving retribution: wholesome deeds with attainment receive retribution associated with attainment, while wholesome deeds without attainment receive retribution associated with non-attainment; this is what is meant by the principle of receiving retribution.

Wholesome deeds performed with a sense of attainment do not receive the retribution of non-attainment, and wholesome deeds performed without attainment do not receive the retribution of attainment; this is the meaning of "not receiving retribution.

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Wholesome deeds performed with attainment neither move nor emerge, whereas wholesome deeds performed without attainment can both move and emerge"—this is the scriptural proof.
Question:
Since the roots of goodness of humans and devas involve grasping at something attained, how can this sutra state that they all attain Buddhahood?
Answer: The roots of goodness of humans and devas are merely distant conditions for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it says they "attain Buddhahood."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that one should focus on what is near rather than grasp at what is distant; thus, those who have nothing to attain are well able to move and emerge, whereas those who have something to attain cannot move or emerge.
This sutra speaks of both the near and the distant; therefore, it states in all cases that they "attain Buddhahood.
Question:
How can the roots of goodness of humans and devas lead to attaining Buddhahood in the distant future?
Answer: There are two kinds of roots of goodness for humans and devas:
first, the causal condition of practice; second, the causal condition of retribution.

The retributive cause results in birth in the bodies of humans or devas; because of the habituating cause, one encounters Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and, upon hearing the teaching of the Mahāyāna, gives rise to a single thought of faith in non-apprehension. This faith in non-apprehension is the seed of the Buddha-way, which relies upon the prior state of apprehending something to give rise to the subsequent state of non-apprehension.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "That which has something to be attained is the initial gateway to non-attainment. Thus, it is said to be a remote condition (*dūrapratyaya*).
Question:
How does this [explanation of] the two causes—habitual and retributive—differ from the interpretation of the masters of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*?

Answer: That [previous passage] clarified that a single moment of wholesome [mind] possesses two causes; here, we clarify that for wholesome states involving attainment (*upalambha*), the principle of successive arising between preceding and succeeding moments is itself the *abhyāsa-hetu* (habitual cause), while the principle of eliciting retribution is the *vipāka-hetu* (retributive cause). Both this habitual and retributive [causality] lead to non-Buddhahood.

Therefore, when the *Dharmapada-śāstra* explains the passage stating that "children who heap sand to make stūpas for the Buddha have all already attained Buddhahood," it means that one attains Buddhahood only by first generating the bodhicitta; it does not mean that the roots of goodness of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) or the roots of goodness of those fixed in the Śrāvaka vehicle attain Buddhahood.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Even if one diligently applies oneself with vigor to the practice of the path to bodhi, if one lacks buddha-nature from the outset, one will ultimately never attain buddhahood."
Question:
Since these are roots of goodness involving apprehension, how can they give rise to non-apprehension? Answer:

If that which is apprehended were of a determinate nature, it could not give rise to non-apprehension; it is precisely because all phenomena lack a determinate nature that, upon encountering Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one realizes that this apprehended object is fundamentally non-existent, and thus non-apprehension arises.
Question:
Does non-acquisition also have the two causes of habituation and retribution? Answer:
There are also two causes:

practicing non-attainment gives rise to non-attainment, which is the cause of practice; and the practice of non-attainment brings about the retribution of non-attainment, which is called the cause of retribution.

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "They have attained the non-arising dharma-patience (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) as a karmic reward, and they have attained the six pāramitās as a karmic reward.
Question:
For what reason does it say that "they have all already realized the Buddha-way"?
Answer: The Buddha perceives the roots of goodness cultivated by sentient beings in the past and has already attained Buddhahood.
Question:

Now, regarding the intent of the Buddha’s teaching elucidated here concerning the past, how does it differ from the intent of the teaching elucidated in the preceding verse, which clarifies Śākyamuni’s own establishment of his school and its distinctions? Answer:

The former correctly clarifies that sentient beings of the two vehicles all attain Buddhahood; the present passage comprehensively clarifies that sentient beings of the five vehicles all attain Buddhahood.

This refutes the former view that by practicing the causes of the five vehicles, one separately attains the fruits of the five vehicles; therefore, it is now clarified that since the causes do not produce disparate effects and the fruits do not yield distinct retributions, all shall equally attain Buddhahood.
The reason why the attainment of Buddhahood by the Two Vehicles is explained first, followed by the attainment of Buddhahood by the Five Vehicles, is based on two principles:
first, since the emergence of this teaching was primarily for the sake of the Two Vehicles, with its influence extending secondarily to humans and devas, it is explained first.

Second, regarding the refutation of the two vehicles' adherence to their own tenets by citing the vehicle of humans and devas: the Buddha said, "With my Buddha-eye, I see that even the slightest roots of goodness of humans and devas in a single thought-moment have already all attained Buddhahood. Therefore, one knows that there is no such thing as the extinction of the body and the cessation of wisdom—becoming identical to great emptiness and dwelling eternally in the ultimate state—as the two vehicles claim, for they do not attain Buddhahood.
"Regarding 'the Buddhas of future ages' below," this is the second section, which versifies the aforementioned Buddhas of future ages.
This passage consists of two parts:
first, a brief versification of the three preceding matters; second, an extensive explanation of the intended meaning of the teachings of the Buddhas of the future.
Each of the two sections contains three parts.

In the first section, the first one and a half lines of verse identify the teacher; the next one line and a half explain the intent of the teaching; and the final half line describes the benefits gained by those who receive the teaching.
From "The original vows of all Buddhas" onwards is the second section, which extensively recites the purport of the future teaching; it also opens three gates:
first, one line distinguishes the original vow as the oneness of the vow;
next, one line distinguishes the preaching of the Dharma as the oneness of the teaching.
The next two lines clarify that what is realized by all Buddhas is one.
The first two verses are as they appear in the text.
"The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among Two-legged Beings" (the third line) raises the point that the realization itself is one.

In the preceding section on the gate of past Buddhas, it was explained in general that both the attainment and non-attainment of all virtues lead to the realization of Buddhahood; the present passage, however, demonstrates specifically that it is only through the fundamental virtue of non-attainment that one becomes a Buddha, thereby clarifying and establishing the meaning of the former.

The Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings may take precepts and meditative concentration as his two legs; or he may take skillful means and ultimate truth as his two legs; or he may take merit and wisdom as his two legs; or he may take understanding and practice as his two legs—all of these being the two legs of internal virtue.
In outward form, among those with two feet, celestial beings and humans are foremost; the Buddha is the most honored among these two-footed celestial beings and humans.
"Knowing that dharmas are eternally without nature" means knowing that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

As for the term "permanent," it does not mean that there is no nature because one has destroyed the nature; rather, since nature is fundamentally and eternally non-existent, it is called "eternally non-existent nature.
Regarding the phrase "the Buddha-seed arises from conditions," there are three types of seeds:
first, taking the teaching of the One Vehicle as the seed. Thus, the "Parable Chapter" states, "because they sever the Buddha-seed," which refers to destroying the teaching.
Second, because the bodhicitta serves as the seed, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Planting the seed of the Buddha in the field of sentient beings causes the sprout of perfect enlightenment to grow."
Third, [the seed] is the Tathāgatagarbha and Buddha-nature.
Now, the first verse specifically takes the bodhicitta as the seed.
Above, the absence of nature was clarified; now, the causes and conditions are being distinguished.
As for the "seed of the Buddha," it is the bodhicitta of non-apprehension that serves as the seed of the Buddha.
This bodhicitta arises through conditions; its arising is its manifestation.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, the One Vehicle is taught": since the bodhicitta arises through provisional conditions, the Buddha teaches the One Vehicle to cause [beings] to generate the bodhicitta; thus, the teaching of the One Vehicle is the very condition for generating the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, clarifying that there is only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and no Two Vehicles means that the bodhicitta possesses only progress and no path of retreat.

Regarding the phrase "this dharma abides in its dharma-position": previously it was clarified that the bodhicitta serves as the seed; now it is clarified that the inherently existing buddha-nature constitutes the seed of the Buddha.

If there were no Buddha-nature, then even if one were to preach the teaching of the One Vehicle and resolve to attain Bodhicitta, one would ultimately never become a Buddha; therefore, it is necessary to clarify the Buddha-nature.
There are three phrases in total:

the first half-verse correctly describes Buddha-nature. That "the Dharma abides in its own station" (dharmasthiti) is an alternative name for Buddha-nature, and it is also a specific designation for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding": because sentient beings in the world inherently possess Buddha-nature, this Buddha-nature is eternally abiding.

Thus, the *Juryō-hon* (Chapter on the Lifespan) states: "The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are; there is neither birth-and-death, nor even that which is neither real nor unreal. This refers to the eternal abiding of the Tathāgatagarbha and the Dharmakāya.
"Having known it at the site of enlightenment" refers to the second phrase, which clarifies the awakening to Buddha-nature;
it means that one first perceives Buddha-nature when sitting at the site of enlightenment.
"The Teacher’s skillful exposition" refers to the third phrase, which clarifies the teaching of Buddha-nature.

However, the Buddha-nature transcends the four propositions and surpasses the hundred negations; it is truly ineffable. It is only within the realm of namelessness and signlessness that it is provisionally described through names and signs for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).

This differs from the skillful means (*upāya*) of the three vehicles mentioned above, and it also differs from the skillful means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*); therefore, this sutra contains many kinds of skillful means.
"Worshipped by gods and humans" and below constitutes the third section: the verse on the present Buddhas.
There are two cycles in total.
One line and a half of verse summarize the three matters mentioned above;
one line of verse praises the principal teacher of transformation; one phrase praises those being transformed; and one phrase praises the gateway of the teaching.
From "Knowing the supreme tranquility" onwards, the second section consists of three verses that extensively praise the three aforementioned matters:

the first line clarifies the three types of Dharma wheels. "Knowing the supreme tranquility" refers to the fundamental Dharma wheel; "by the power of skillful means" refers to the derivative Dharma wheel, which arises from the root to the branches; and "in reality it is the Buddha-vehicle" refers to the Dharma wheel that gathers the branches back to the root.
"Knowing the various conducts of sentient beings" refers to the second pair of verses, which extensively clarifies the secondary wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
"Now I am also like this," and so forth, refers to the third pair of lines of verse, which clarifies Śākyamuni’s conformity with the gate of sameness.
The two verses are divided into two parts:

the first verse follows the Buddhas in clarifying the Dharma-wheel that subsumes the branches back into the root; the second verse follows the Buddhas in clarifying the Dharma-wheel that arises from the root to manifest the branches.

"Gathering the branches back to the root" means gathering the function back to the essence; "arising from the root to produce the branches" means arising from the essence to manifest the function. Although these two [phrases] are brief, they encompass the entirety of the teachings and phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings": ordinary worldlings are mired in existence, dwelling within the burning house of the triple world;
those of the two vehicles are attached to emptiness and have not yet escaped the evil paths of five hundred yojanas. Neither of these states is secure.

Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Those of shallow wisdom perceive all phenomena as either existent or non-existent, and so forth; such persons are unable to see cessation or the dharma of peace."
Now, by expounding the Middle Way of the One Vehicle, one causes [beings] to leave behind the two views of existence and non-existence held by ordinary people and those of the Two Vehicles;

therefore, it is called "peaceful and secure. By means of "various dharma-gates," one provides the method for attaining this security, leading them into the Buddha-way and establishing them in the state of peace and security.
In the first half of the second verse, the capacity [of the audience] is understood; in the third line, the teaching is proclaimed; and in the fourth line, the benefit is realized.
From the words "Śāriputra, you should know" onwards, the section on the true gate of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) concluded above is finished.
This is the second major section, which provides verses on the expedient gateways of the Three Vehicles.
In the preceding prose section, the three [teachings] were briefly and generally explained as being expediently taught by all Buddhas appearing in the world of the five turbidities;

here, the text provides a detailed exposition, clarifying that during Śākyamuni’s single period of teaching while appearing in the world of the five turbidities, there are four gates for those he transforms.

First, dwelling in the stage of the Dharma-body, he perceives that sentient beings in the five turbidities have suffering and no joy; thus, he gives rise to great compassion. Second, with this compassion fully suffusing his mind, he manifests traces from his fundamental essence;

at the time of his initial attainment of the Way, he wished to preach the One Vehicle to uproot the extreme suffering of beings and grant them ultimate bliss. However, although the Sage was able to bestow it upon beings, the beings themselves were unable to receive it; for this reason, he ceased this singular transformation.
Third, because they were unable to receive a single transformation, the One Buddha Vehicle was expediently taught as three to temper and soften their minds.
Fourth, it clarifies the convergence of the three and their return to the one.
These four gates all give rise to the five turbidities; therefore, they explain the topical headings of the preceding chapter on the five turbidities.

Because one first perceives the five turbidities, the mind of great compassion arises. Since beings possess the five turbidities and are incapable of receiving the One Vehicle, the expedient means of teaching the Three Vehicles is employed because of those turbidities. Once the obstacles of the five turbidities have been eliminated, the One Vehicle is subsequently taught. Thus, all four chapters arise from the five turbidities.
Question:
For what reason are only four chapters explained? Answer:

Śākyamuni appeared in an age of the five turbidities; from beginning to end throughout his entire career, there were only these four gates. It is like a parent who, seeing their child suffering from illness, first feels deep compassion;
secondly, they wish to bestow upon the child a wondrous medicine to cure the illness instantly, but the child’s illness is so grave that they cannot take the medicine;
thirdly, since they cannot be given the wondrous medicine, the parent provisionally uses a coarse medicine to treat the child’s severe ailment.
Fourth, once the grave illness has been removed, one is then capable of receiving the sublime medicine, and the illness is thereby cured.

The father removes his son’s physical illness through these four gates alone; they may not be increased or decreased. The Buddha treats the mental illnesses of sentient beings through these same four gates alone; they may not be increased or decreased. Therefore, throughout his single period of appearing in the world, he clarifies only these four gates.
It is not only Śākyamuni’s single appearance in the world that is complete with these four gates; all Buddhas likewise do not transcend these four gates.
Furthermore, these four gates serve as the basis for the subsequent four parables of the burning house:
the first gate serves as the basis for the subsequent parable of the elder seeing the fire.
The second section provides the analogy of failing to save the children after they have emerged;
the third section provides the analogy of successfully saving the children by means of the three carts after they have emerged;
and the fourth section provides the analogy of equally bestowing the great carts upon them after they have emerged.
However, the preceding and succeeding passages of the text correspond to one another; there are only these four [analogies], and no further divergent interpretations should be produced.
If one claims there are ten versions of the analogies or six versions of the analogies, neither accords with the text.
Since those in the末代 (final age) do not perceive the Buddha’s intent, they should rely solely on the Buddha as their teacher and must not engage in forced interpretations.
Question:
Since there were six analogies previously, why are there now only four?

Answer: In the preceding prose section, the explanation of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) consisted of only one chapter; now, in this verse section, the teaching shifts its momentum and is presented through four gates.

Within this present chapter, there are four explanations in terms of the Dharma, while the subsequent chapter contains six explanations by way of parables; these, too, are teachings delivered by shifting the momentum of the exposition.

If one were to say that what is taught later is identical to what was taught before—that the three cycles of the sūtra share the same intent as a single cycle—this would be a major error on the part of the sūtra-preachers.
This shall be explained in detail in the "Parable Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta). Question:
How many kinds of bodies do these four gates possess?
Answer: He is endowed with the three bodies (*trikāya*).
First, it clarifies that by abiding in the ground of the *dharmakāya*, he perceives that sentient beings possess suffering and lack joy, thereby giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Next, at the time of his initial attainment of enlightenment, he taught the *Avataṃsaka* doctrine for the sake of all bodhisattvas; this is the body of Vairocana.
In the third section, he taught the doctrine of the Three Vehicles for the sake of all śrāvakas; this is the body of Śākyamuni.
The first refers to the body as seen by the Buddha; the second is the body as seen by the Bodhisattvas; and the last is the body as seen by those of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, the first is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), the second is the Reward-body (sambhogakāya), and the last is the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).

The fourth section concerns hearing the teaching on the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) that brings about the realization of its beginning and end; since it possesses the three bodies (trikāya), the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Lotus Sūtra Commentary) clearly elucidates these three bodies in its explanation of the "Life Span" chapter (*Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).
Question:
How many types of teachings are contained within these four gates? Answer:
These four gates fully encompass the three teachings.

The Tathāgata, abiding in the stage of the Dharma-body, perceives that sentient beings in the five turbidities, from their initial birth to the end of their lives, possess the capacities and conditions to hear the three types of teaching gates. Subsequently, manifesting his original essence through traces for the sake of sentient beings, he expounds these three types of teaching:
at the time of his initial attainment of enlightenment, he preached the Fundamental Wheel of Dharma for the sake of all Bodhisattvas;
The second section clarifies the Dharma-wheel of the branches arising from the root, because those incapable of receiving the fundamental Dharma-wheel [are guided] from the root toward the branches;
the third section clarifies the Dharma-wheel of subsuming the branches back to the root, because it brings the three together and returns them to the one.
Question:
Since there are three kinds of Dharma wheels, can one also clarify the three bodies? Answer:
This is likewise the case.
First, manifesting the body of Vairocana for the sake of the bodhisattvas constitutes the fundamental body (*mūlakāya*).

Second, it is clarified that the followers of the two vehicles are incapable of beholding this body; therefore, the fundamental is concealed and the provisional is manifested, giving rise to the branch and derivative bodies. Thus, the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" states: "He cast off his precious and noble robes and donned tattered, filthy garments."

Third, since establishing the one and abolishing the three is also a matter of ceasing outward traces to return to the fundamental, it should be said that one sheds tattered, defiled garments to once again don precious, noble robes.
Thus, as there are three levels of teaching, so too are there three aspects of the person.
Each of these four gates contains three sections, which together constitute the twelve chapters of the sutra.
Regarding the first gate, there are three parts:
first, clarifying the capacity for seeing;
Second, clarifying what is seen;
third, giving rise to compassion.
"I observe with the Buddha-eye" clarifies the capacity for seeing.
The five eyes have two approaches:
first, the five eyes discussed in relation to the *saṃbhogakāya* (response body).
Because the Buddha took on a physical body through his parents, he possesses the flesh eye; subsequently, beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained the [remaining] four eyes.

Because there is far-reaching vision, there is the divine eye; because it illuminates the faculties and natures of the three vehicles, there is the dharma-eye; because it illuminates the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there is the wisdom-eye; and because it illuminates the realm of the Buddha, there is the Buddha-eye.
Next, regarding the five eyes as they pertain to the *dharmakāya*: there are five eyes because they illuminate five kinds of objects.

Illuminating objects within obstructions is called the flesh eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); illuminating objects beyond obstructions is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); the remaining three are as described above.
Question:

If the five eyes are discussed in terms of the five sensory objects, then that which now illuminates the six realms of existence ought to be the divine eye (divyacakṣus). Why, then, is it called the Buddha-eye (buddhacakṣus)? Answer:
The five eyes have two gates:
first, those within the stage of causes are called the four eyes, while those in the stage of fruition are called the Buddha-eye.

This means that humans possess the flesh eye, devas possess the divine eye, śrāvakas possess the wisdom eye, bodhisattvas possess the dharma eye, and Buddhas possess the Buddha-eye; therefore, when the four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye, they are all collectively termed the Buddha-eye.
Now, because this concerns the relative relationship between cause and effect, it is said that the Buddha-eye sees sentient beings; this is not what is termed the "heavenly eye.

Within the Buddha-eye, five functions are discussed in terms of their respective objects; therefore, when one among the five eyes sees sentient beings of the six realms, that belongs to the heavenly eye.
Furthermore, the Buddha-eye knows nothing that is not known and sees nothing that is not seen; it also perceives the sentient beings of the six realms.
Question:
How many types of names are there for the five eyes?
Answer:

The two eyes—flesh and wisdom—are named according to their essential nature. Because it takes flesh as its eye, it is called the "flesh eye" (māṃsa-cakṣus); because it takes wisdom as its eye, it is called the "wisdom eye" (prajñā-cakṣus).

The Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) derives its name from its object; because it perceives phenomena, it is called the "Dharma-eye. As for the names "Heavenly Eye" (*divyacakṣus*) and "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*), their designations are not fixed. This is because the Heavenly Eye receives its name in three ways:
first, by designation based on the person [who possesses it], and second, by designation derived from its specific meaning.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called the Pure Heavens (*śuddhadeva*); being born among humans, they obtain through karmic retribution the faculty of the eye that penetrates and sees the great trichiliocosm. Because their name is established based on those Pure Heavens, it is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).
Second, it is named according to its destination (*gati*).

From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), all together constitute the celestial realm (*devagati*); because one born within those heavens obtains the faculty of the eye as a karmic retribution (*vipākaja*) that can illuminate and perceive from afar, it is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).
Third, it is named after its cause.

As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) within the three abodes are termed "divine abodes" (*deva-vihāra*). By relying on these divine abodes, one cultivates and attains the pure eye; because it is named after its cause, it is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*).
The name "Buddha-eye" (buddhacakṣus) is derived from two perspectives:
first, it is named after the person; "Buddha" refers to the person, and because that person possesses this eye, it is called the Buddha-eye.
Second, "Buddha" means "awakened," and because this awakening is able to illuminate, it is termed the Buddha-eye.
Question:
What constitutes the essence of the five eyes? Answer:
If one relies on the Dharma-body, it takes wisdom as its essence; because this wisdom has five functions, it is called the "five eyes.
If one considers the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya), since "divine" and "fleshly" are names for types of matter, they take material phenomena (rūpadharma) as their essence;
the remaining three take wisdom as their essence.
If one speaks of the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), according to the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā) doctrine, it likewise takes wisdom (*jñāna*) as its essence.
Question:
How are the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) subsumed within the ten eyes (*daśa-cakṣus*) of the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra?
Answer: Regarding the "ten eyes," the first is the flesh eye, which sees all forms;
the second is the celestial eye, which sees the death and rebirth of all sentient beings as they pass from this life to another.
Third is the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which perceives the differences in the faculties and natures of all sentient beings;
fourth is the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), which perceives the true characteristics of all phenomena—that is, it perceives the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena;
fifth is the buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*), which perceives the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha.
Sixth is the eye of wisdom, which discriminates and understands all modes of phenomena;
seventh is the eye of clarity, which means seeing the light of all Buddhas;
eighth is the eye that transcends birth and death, which sees the dharma of nirvana.
Ninth is the unimpeded eye, which perceives all phenomena without obstruction;
tenth is the universal eye, which refers to the dharma-gate of seeing the equality of the dharma-realm.

The first of these is the aforementioned fleshly eye, which also incorporates the divine eye, for it perceives both the coarse and the subtle, as well as the distant and the near, due to its divine nature.
The second, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), is the aforementioned divine eye;

the third, the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*); the fifth, the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*); the sixth, the knowledge eye (*jñānacakṣus*); the seventh, the luminous eye (*vidyācakṣus*); the eighth, the eye that transcends birth and death (*saṃsāraniryāṇacakṣus*); and the ninth, the unimpeded eye (*anāvaraṇacakṣus*)—these six kinds are the aforementioned Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
The fourth, the Dharma-eye, is the aforementioned wisdom eye, because it perceives the ultimate truth (*satya*).
The tenth, the Universal Eye, is the aforementioned Buddha-eye, because it universally perceives the equal and true Dharma-realm.
Regarding the phrase "seeing the sentient beings of the six realms," the second point clarifies that which is seen.
Regarding what is seen internally, there are two parts:
first, a general explanation of seeing the six realms;
second, a specific explanation of seeing existence and non-existence.
Question:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that “the five eyes do not see sentient beings”; why, then, is it said here that they do see? Answer:

The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has attained the true divine eye and perceives all Buddha-lands without dualistic characteristics. To perceive without dualistic characteristics means that one sees them vividly while there is nothing seen; though there is nothing seen, there is nothing not seen. Thus, seeing and non-seeing are non-dual.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that seeing is to see nothing; this sutra clarifies that not seeing is seeing. Therefore, they do not contradict one another.
Question:
Since one sees the six realms, how does this differ from the perception of those within the six realms?

Answer: The Buddha perceives the non-six as six, yet knows that the six have no basis for being six; he perceives the six realms as the manifestation of the six-six. Thus, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" states: "It is not like perceiving the three realms within the three realms. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "In accordance with sentient beings, he universally enters all worlds, yet his wisdom is eternally quiescent and differs from what is seen by the world."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of sentient beings:
first, sentient beings of inverted nature; second, sentient beings who are merely conventional designations based on causes and conditions.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* clarifies that they are "not seen" because, within the ultimate principle, there is ultimately no such thing as a sentient being with a real, intrinsic nature. This sutra clarifies that because [sentient beings] are those produced by causes and conditions, the Buddha sees them with his Buddha-eye. Therefore, the preceding passage fully contains both meanings.

“The Two-legged Honored One among gods and humans knows that dharmas are eternally without self-nature” means not seeing self-nature; “the Buddha-seed arises from conditions” refers to seeing the meaning of causes and conditions.

Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "All phenomena lack a determinate nature; the Buddha possesses immeasurable skillful means, and thus may speak of the four alternatives—real, unreal, both, and neither. One should also say that phenomena lack a determinate nature, and thus, in accordance with sentient beings, he may speak of the four alternatives—seeing, not seeing, both, and neither.

Therefore, the *Treatise* says: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and sometimes speak of non-self; within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self. One should also say: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of seeing, and sometimes speak of not seeing; within the true reality of all phenomena, there is neither seeing nor not seeing."
"Poverty-stricken and lacking in merit and wisdom," below this, is the second section, which specifically clarifies the perception of existence and non-existence.
First, it clarifies the perception of non-existence, meaning the absence of merit and wisdom.
However, although one may practice with the attainment of merit and wisdom, from the perspective of the Path, these are ultimately still a lack of merit and wisdom.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Those who have something to grasp possess neither the Path nor the fruit.
The passage beginning with "entering the perilous path of birth and death" clarifies the perception of existence.

Above, it was shown that there are two kinds of non-existence: the absence of merit and the absence of wisdom; now, it is shown that there are two kinds of existence: the existence of the fruit of suffering and the existence of the cause of suffering.

First, the vision of the fruit of suffering is clarified; this also follows from the preceding text, which explains that because the provisions of merit and wisdom are lacking, one enters the perilous path of birth and death, thereby causing the fruit of suffering for sentient beings to continue in succession.
"Deeply attached to the five desires" clarifies the observation of the cause of suffering.

Furthermore, previously one entered the perilous path of birth and death, where the cause of suffering produced the fruit of suffering; now, upon that very fruit of suffering, one further creates the cause of suffering.
There are two causes of suffering:
first, craving; second, views.
To be deeply attached to the five desires is precisely what constitutes craving.

The afflictions of the three realms are collectively termed "desire" (*kāma*) because of their nature of defiled attachment; thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Arhats have severed the desires of the three realms."

Regarding "deep attachment," it means that because one holds a view of attainment, perceiving the five desires as definitely possessing reality, one subsequently becomes attached to them; this is why it is called "deep.
As for the phrase "like a yak loving its tail," the yak loves its tail due to delusion, and sentient beings give rise to craving due to delusion.
Furthermore, because of his attachment to his tail, he was captured by humans and subsequently killed; thus, attachment to the tail was the instrument of his own destruction.

Because sentient beings crave the five desires, they undergo all manner of suffering. Therefore, the *Biography of Nāgārjuna* states: "Desire is the root of calamity and the source of all evils; the ruin of virtue and the endangerment of one's person both arise from this.
If I am able to escape [this life], I vow to leave the household life."
Regarding the phrase "shrouded by craving," the preceding section clarified that craving arises from ignorance; this section clarifies the functional power of craving.
Craving possesses two powers:
first, it brings about the suffering of birth and death.
2. Delusion regarding objects obstructs wisdom.

The preceding section clarified entering the perilous path of birth and death, meaning the experiencing of the suffering of birth and death; this section clarifies how delusion regarding objects obstructs wisdom, for when craving covers the mind, it thereby obstructs insight.
"Blind and sightless, seeing nothing" refers to being deluded regarding objective realms.
"Not seeking the Buddha of Great Power" refers to those who are deeply attached to the five desires, likened to the sick.
The Buddha of Great Power is one who possesses great power capable of severing the disease of craving in sentient beings; thus, he is called the "Excellent Physician.
The "Dharma for Severing Suffering" refers to the Great Wisdom of Equality, which is the "Excellent Medicine."

Sentient beings have their minds shrouded by craving, rendering them blind and sightless; they do not know that craving is a disease, nor do they recognize the Buddha as the skilled physician or the Dharma as the wondrous medicine.
"Deeply entering into various false views" marks the second section, which clarifies the causes of [wrong] views.
Regarding "seeking to abandon suffering through suffering": for example, various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon the suffering of the three realms to be nirvāṇa;
furthermore, the Brahmin Taṇḍi pointed to his own belly and reckoned the suffering of the desire realm to be nirvāṇa.
The non-Buddhist Ārāḍa considered the state of non-perception to be nirvāṇa; thus, he regarded the suffering of the form realm as the very abandonment of suffering.

Udraka Rāmaputra considered the state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to be nirvāṇa; thus, he sought to abandon the suffering of birth and death by means of the suffering of the formless realm.
This explains the meaning of the aforementioned wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This is a general wrong view; within the five views, it is not the view that takes what is not pleasant or pure to be pleasant and pure—that is the independent *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views).
Question:
Is it that taking birth and death to be nirvāṇa constitutes delusion regarding birth and death, or does it constitute delusion regarding nirvāṇa? Answer:
To mistake saṃsāra for nirvāṇa is like mistaking a wooden bench for a human being.
The section beginning with "For the sake of these sentient beings" constitutes the third part, which clarifies the arousal of compassion.
Distant compassion consists in pitying those who lack the two virtues of merit and wisdom, and who possess the two evils of suffering and its causes;
proximate compassion consists in grieving for those non-Buddhists who mistake what is not the Path for the Path, and the Path for what is not the Path.

From the passage "When I first sat at the site of enlightenment" onwards, the second [point] explains that because sentient beings possess the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the teaching of the One Vehicle could not be realized when he first attained enlightenment.
Since the Great Compassion of the Sage has already filled his inner being, he now clarifies his skillful means to rescue others from without.
However, although the Sage is able to save, sentient beings are unable to receive his aid.
Regarding the text, there are also three parts:
First, the explanation that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) cannot be taught;
second, the exhortation by the devas;
third, the refusal of that request.
The first section also has three parts:
the first half-line clarifies the place of contemplation;
the next half-line clarifies the time of contemplation.
The subsequent one and a half lines clarify the matter of contemplation.
"I first sat at the site of enlightenment" refers to the initial attainment of perfect awakening at the Site of Enlightenment (Śītavana) in the realm of Magadha.
Regarding the phrase "observing the tree while walking," some say: the name is used to express the underlying meaning;

"tree" (śu) signifies the desire to establish sentient beings in the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna, and "walking" (kramaṇa) signifies that the Tathāgata will certainly carry out the act of establishing them.
Some say: The Tathāgata attained enlightenment beneath this tree; because he was mindful of the tree’s kindness, he gazed upon it.

The practitioner previously sat here for the sake of attaining the Way, and now that he has realized the Way, he walks in meditation (caṅkramaṇa); thus, he wishes to perform wholesome deeds and benefit sentient beings as a way of repaying the tree’s kindness.
The commentary states that this explanation is derived from the sutras. Some say:
"This follows worldly conventions; it is the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint)."
There are two kinds of contemplation practiced by people of the world:
first, contemplation on objects; second, contemplation while walking.
Now, following worldly convention, we shall also perform these two.

The *Commentary on the Sūtra* states: "The tree takes stillness as its essence, while walking takes motion as its characteristic; this is intended to manifest the signs of contemplative reflection and to resolve the pivotal point between speech and silence."
Regarding the phrase "during the three seven-day periods," this second point clarifies the duration of his contemplation.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states, "seven days of samādhi," which is consistent with the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
That treatise asks: "Originally, he sought to benefit sentient beings by attaining the Way; for what reason did he contemplate for seven days without preaching?
It answers: "To demonstrate that he himself was experiencing the great joy of the Dharma."
He manifested his own joy in the Dharma in order to cause sentient beings to increase their love and reverence for the Tathāgata;

furthermore, he relinquished such sublime bliss out of compassion for sentient beings so as to preach the Dharma for them. Thus, he did not preach during the first seven days, but only began to preach at the start of the second seven-day period.
This sutra clarifies that the teaching was given only after three weeks had passed;
the Vinaya and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* state it was given only after six or seven weeks—that is, forty-two days—had passed;
and according to the *Dvādaśa-yojana-sūtra*, he converted the five bhikṣus only in the second year after his enlightenment, meaning he did not teach for one full year.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "He did not preach the Dharma for fifty-seven days. This may refer to fifty-seven days, or it may mean fifty times seven days, which amounts to nearly one year; this accords with the *Dvādaśa-yojana-sūtra*. Since these accounts depend on specific conditions of what was seen or heard, there is no need to reconcile them.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "For what reason were the forty-two days of the sixth and seventh weeks not mentioned?

First, because Brahmā had not yet come to request [the teaching]; second, because the roots of goodness in Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others were not yet mature; third, because he first established himself in peace before beginning to teach; and fourth, to cause sentient beings to give rise to reverence."

Now it is clear that the Tathāgata has long known what should be said and what should not be said; however, in order to demonstrate the profound and subtle nature of the Dharma, and because sentient beings have dull faculties and follow worldly conventions, he demonstrates three periods of reflection before speaking.
Seven is the ultimate limit of the number one, and three contemplations are the conventional rule of the mundane world; hence there is the expression "three times seven.
Question:
In what sense is seven days the ultimate limit of the number one?
Answer:

Internal and external phenomena undergo transformation within seven days; that which is within the womb changes after seven days, and a body sustained by solid food dies if it goes without food for seven days.
"Reflecting on such matters" and below constitutes the third section, which clarifies the objects of reflection.

Some say: during the first seven days, he reflected on the subtle and wondrous nature of the Buddha’s wisdom; during the second seven days, he reflected on the dull faculties of sentient beings; and during the third seven days, he reflected that it was impossible to transmit this wondrous wisdom to those with dull faculties.

Some say: During the first seven days, he intended to preach the One Vehicle through the Dharma, but finding no receptive capacity (*anukūla*), he ceased; during the second seven days, he intended to illustrate the One Vehicle through parables, but finding no receptive capacity, he ceased; during the third seven days, he intended to explain the One Vehicle by means of past-life causes and conditions, but finding no receptive capacity, he ceased. Thus, it was the third seven days because he could not find any recipients—whether of inferior, middling, or superior capacity—who would awaken to the One Vehicle.

Furthermore, it is said that during the first seven days, he was unable to teach the Mahāyāna through the gate of exhortation; during the second seven days, he was unable to teach the Mahāyāna through the gate of admonition; and during the third seven days, he was unable to teach it by combining both admonition and exhortation.
The explanation provided above clarifies that the expression "three times seven" is used because one follows worldly conventions.
Regarding the phrase "the wisdom I have attained," the current text directly presents the three matters contemplated therein: first, the subtle and profound nature of the Buddha’s wisdom;
second, the dull faculties of sentient beings; and third, the impossibility of bestowing such subtle wisdom upon those with dull faculties.
The Buddha’s wisdom is subtle and wondrous because it is neither ignorance nor intellect, and it transcends both contemplation and conditions; therefore, it is called subtle and wondrous.
"The faculties of sentient beings are dull" clarifies that their faculty of wisdom is dull.
Regarding the phrase "blinded by attachment to pleasure and delusion," it refers not only to dull faculties but also to two further faults:
first, attachment to pleasure, which is craving;
second, delusion, which is ignorance.
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "For example, it is like a person whose hands and feet are bound and whose eyes are covered with cloth; placed in a forest of thorns, they cannot escape.
So too, sentient beings are bound by craving and shrouded by ignorance, and thus cannot emerge from the dense forest of birth and death."
"Those of such a kind," and below, the third [section]: one cannot bestow sublime wisdom upon those of dull faculties.
"At that time, the various Brahma-kings," and below, the second [section]: the various devas entreat [the Buddha] to preach.
Regarding the text, there are also three parts:
first, one and a half lines clarify the person who makes the request;
next, one line clarifies the ritual procedure for the request.
The final phrase explicitly clarifies the request for instruction.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The ritual protocols of the various devas differ: the Śuddhāvāsa devas exhorted him to leave the household life, the Four Heavenly Kings offered the alms bowl, and Brahmā King requested him to turn the wheel of Dharma."
Question:
Since the Buddha appears in the world for the sake of sentient beings, he should naturally preach the Dharma himself; why does he wait for an invitation? Answer:
The *Śāstra* states: "Although the Buddha does not require being requested, he causes those who request him to obtain merit.
The seven-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "Requesting the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma can extinguish the sin of slandering the twelve divisions of the scriptures."
Furthermore, it is the natural law of all Buddhas to teach only after being requested.
Moreover, if one were to teach without being requested, non-Buddhists would mock and revile them.

Furthermore, as non-Buddhists mostly serve Brahmā, if Brahmā makes the request, the minds of the non-Buddhists will be subdued. Additionally, if one were to teach without being requested, one would have to answer the fourteen difficult questions; because he waits for a request before speaking, he does not answer them.
Question:
For what reason is it that the invitation by the devas is explained, while the invitation by humans is not? Answer:
Because the devas surpass humans, it is said that the devas requested [the Buddha].
Furthermore, humans were unable to request it; because the devas possess wisdom and know that the Buddha had attained enlightenment, it is said that the devas requested it.
Moreover, the Buddha attained enlightenment while dwelling alone in the forest; since there was no one there, humans did not request it.
Question:

For what reason did the sixteen princes first request [the Dharma] from the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, while the Brahma King requested it only later? Furthermore, why is it that in the present case, only the invitation by the gods is mentioned, while the invitation by the princes is not?
Answer: The *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra* states: "The previous Buddha appeared in a favorable age, and his succession of the father’s legacy was profound;
now Śākyamuni Buddha appears in an evil age, and the son’s succession of the father’s meaning is meager."
"Then I thought to myself," and so forth: third, clarifying the refusal of the request and the cessation of the transformative teaching.
This section also has three parts:
first, clarifying the provisional intention to preach the One Vehicle;
Second, it clarifies that which is unbeneficial and harmful;
third, it clarifies the cessation of transformation.
Question:
Question: What is the difference between the previous contemplation and this present contemplation? Answer:

The previous [contemplation] clarifies that it is impossible to transmit the wondrous wisdom to those of dull faculties; whereas the present contemplation considers that if one were to provisionally accept the invitation of the Brahma King and forcefully preach the One Vehicle, there would be harm rather than benefit.
Following "Sentient beings are submerged in suffering," second, it clarifies that [teaching the Dharma] would be without benefit and even harmful.
Following "I would rather not preach the Dharma," third, it clarifies the refusal of the request and the cessation of the transformative activity.

Initially, the One Vehicle was taught through the manifestation of the fundamental reality in order to benefit sentient beings; however, if the One Vehicle were taught now [without such manifestations], it would be of no benefit and even detrimental. Therefore, by relinquishing the provisional response and returning to the ultimate truth—what is called "entering nirvana"—there is nothing that is lost.

From "Reflecting upon the Buddhas of the past" onwards is the third major section, clarifying that when he first attained enlightenment, because sentient beings were unable to receive the One Vehicle, he provisionally taught three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Question:
Does the Buddha speak of the Three Vehicles of his own accord, or does he wait for an invitation before speaking? Answer:

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said: "When Brahmā first requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma, the Tathāgata replied that the Buddha-dharma is exceedingly profound while sentient beings possess dull faculties; thus, he declined the request and did not preach."

Next, Brahmā King presented the fact that sentient beings possess superior, middling, and inferior faculties, and earnestly requested the preaching of the Dharma; because the Buddha accepted this earnest request, he taught the Three Vehicles.
This section also consists of three parts:
first, clarifying the illumination of the faculties and natures of the assembly.
Second, the correct teaching of the three vehicles;
third, the attainment of benefit by following that teaching.
Thus, the analogy is established for the children who were subsequently transformed by means of the three carts.
The initial text has three parts:
first, explaining that the Three Vehicles are taught because it accords with and is identical to the Buddhas of the past;

second, explaining that the Three Vehicles are taught because one receives the exhortation of the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present; [and third, explaining that the Three Vehicles are taught because one will receive the exhortation of the Buddhas of the future].
Third, because he accepts the exhortation and accords with sentient beings in the five turbidities, he teaches the three vehicles.

Of these, the former two accord upward with all Buddhas, while the latter one accords downward with sentient beings; thus, it is due to these three causes and conditions that he teaches the three vehicles.
If one accepts the response to the Brahma King’s invitation, there are four conditions.
The first verse is divided into two parts:

the first half contemplates the Buddhas of antiquity, while the second half clarifies that Śākyamuni accords with and follows the path and dharma of those ancient Buddhas; because he could not convert sentient beings through the One Vehicle alone, he taught the Three Vehicles within the One Vehicle.
Śākyamuni is faithful and fond of antiquity; it is fitting that he should accord with and conform to this.
From the passage "At the time of reflecting thus" onwards is the second section: the encouragement by the Buddhas of the ten directions to preach the Three Vehicles.
The text consists of two parts:
first, praise; second, exhortation. The first part has three sections: [End of section]
The first half of the passage clarifies how the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest their bodies.

As for the reason they manifest their bodies: because Śākyamuni expounds the principle of "one teaching and three harmonies" in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, he frequently inspires the Buddhas to respond by manifesting their bodies.
Next is the half-verse on consolation and praise.
Regarding "consolation": concealing one's actual virtues and employing the Dharma that accords with the preferences of the poor to deliver sentient beings—this is the matter of enduring suffering.
Now, because one must conform to worldly conventions, it is necessary to offer consolation.
As for subsequent praise: if the expedient means of the Three Vehicles are established in accordance with principle and suited to the capacities of beings, they may indeed be praised.
The next line expresses words of praise, the meaning of which is as stated in the text.
From the phrase "We, too, have all attained," onwards is the second section, clarifying the self-narration of the Buddhas; this serves as an exhortation.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, it clarifies that the present Buddhas, like their predecessors of the past, employ skillful means to teach the Three Vehicles;
second, the verse clarifies that the present Buddhas, following the capacities of sentient beings below, therefore teach the Three Vehicles.
The third half-verse clarifies the intent behind the teaching.
From the passage beginning "Śāriputra, you should know," the third section clarifies Śākyamuni’s joyful acceptance of the exhortation.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
the first verse clarifies the expression of joy in response to the praise of the aforementioned Buddhas;
the subsequent verse clarifies the acceptance of their exhortation in response to the encouragement of the aforementioned Buddhas.
“Namo” means to take refuge and to seek salvation.
To take refuge means to surrender one’s life to the Buddhas of the ten directions.

When the Buddhas exhort and teach the Three Vehicles, they thereby prolong the wisdom-life of sentient beings; this is precisely to prolong the life of Śākyamuni. For this reason, Śākyamuni surrenders his life to the Buddhas.
The Buddhas exhort and teach the Three Vehicles; since they provide salvation for all sentient beings, they are likewise saving Śākyamuni, and thus are said to save me.

"Furthermore, he forms this thought: 'I have appeared in an age of turbid evil'"—this marks the third point: he teaches the Three Vehicles in accordance with sentient beings living in the five turbidities.
Regarding the phrase "I then reflected within myself," there are four reflections throughout the beginning and end of the two chapters:
two reflections concerning the non-teaching of the One Vehicle, as explained previously;
