Recorded respectfully by the monk Sùqìng, who served as the general supervisor of affairs.
*Fahua Yishu*, Fascicle Six.
Compiled by Hu Jizang.
Part Two of the Chapter on Parables.
From the passage "At that time, each of the sons addressed their father," this is the fifth section: the parable of bestowing the great chariots equally.
According to the text, there are three parts:
first, the solicitation for the vehicle;
second, the bestowal of the vehicle.
Third, the joy of obtaining the chariots.
"Seeking the chariots" refers to the awakening of the Mahāyāna potential.
"Bestowing the chariots" refers to the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"Those who obtain the vehicle with joy" refers to awakening through understanding the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
In meaning, there are only these three; one cannot find more or less than this. This is analogous to what was taught as the One Vehicle in the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter.
The "Seeking a Chariot" (*Sakṛdāgāmin*) is a major theme of this sutra; I shall now briefly explain it.

Some say: Once one has attained arhatship and subsequently goes out to observe with the mind, one uses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to perceive that there is still birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) in the future. This means that afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been exhausted and the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has not yet been attained; because there is still birth-and-death, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) has not yet been attained.
For what reason did the Buddha say that Arhats possess the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?
Because they seek the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising from the Buddha, it is said that they "seek the vehicle"; the vehicle is precisely this knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.

Now, I say this is not so. Since in the past one already saw that birth and death were not yet exhausted, one would have known that the Three Vehicles are not ultimate; one should likewise have known immediately that the One Vehicle is ultimate. Why, then, is there still a search for it?
Furthermore, within the Tripitaka teachings, it is explained that Arhats already know external matters beyond the three realms.
If the Lesser Vehicle already clarifies external matters beyond the three realms, what difference is there between it and the Great Vehicle?
What is clarified here—the parable of seeking the vehicle—is distinguished solely in relation to the present; it does not imply that the former teaching still exists.
Generally, there are two approaches to this parable of seeking the vehicle:
first, the metaphorical assumption of seeking where there is no actual seeking; second, clarifying the existence of seeking based on the presence of doubt.
Regarding the statement that there is no "rope" yet one metaphorically posits a rope, there are generally two meanings:
first, to reveal that the three vehicles are expedient means; second, to reveal that the one vehicle is the ultimate reality.

This reveals that the three vehicles are expedient means while clarifying that, in principle, there are no three; it reveals that the one vehicle is the ultimate truth while also clarifying that, in principle, there is one. Since this constitutes the primary thesis of this sutra, the parable of seeking the carts is established as a provisional illustration.

To reveal that the three vehicles are expedient means: previously, it was clarified that the elder discerned that there were no three vehicles, yet he falsely pointed outside the gate and spoke of three where none existed;
here, it is explained from the perspective of the father that the three vehicles are expedient means.
If there were actually three carts outside the gate, and you saw those three upon stepping outside, you would not have sought them.

Because you sought them, we know that there were no three carts outside the gate; this verifies that the father’s previous words were logically devoid of three, and that he spoke of three as a skillful means (*upāya*). This instance of the son seeking three serves to reveal that these "three" are merely a skillful means.
Question:
For what reason are both father and son used as metaphors to reveal that the three vehicles are expedient means? Answer:

The very purpose for which this teaching arose was precisely to refute the attachment to the three vehicles as being real; therefore, it is appropriate to clarify that the three vehicles are skillful means (*upāya*). This constitutes opening the gate of skillful means, after which one can finally reveal the true meaning. Thus, by means of the analogy of father and son, it is clarified that the three vehicles are but skillful means.

Regarding the statement that the parable of requesting a carriage illustrates that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is the reality: the following section clarifies that the equal bestowal [of carriages] signifies the existence of this One. To clarify the existence of the One, it is appropriate to distinguish the non-existence of the three; if the non-existence of the three is not manifested, the existence of the One will not be revealed. Therefore, the request for the three is used as a pretext to manifest their non-existence.

If the three actually existed, there would be no request for them. Because they requested the three, we know the three do not exist. Since the three are absent, the existence of the One is then revealed, and thus the One is finally bestowed.
This is indeed the primary intent of this sutra; there is no need for alternative interpretations.

As for the statement that "there are those who seek" based on their state of doubt: in truth, neither the gate of delusion nor the gate of enlightenment contains such seekers. In the past, because they clung to the three [vehicles], they saw the existence of carts; once they had realized the minor fruits, they no longer sought them.

Now, if they were to attain awakening and realize that there is only one and not three, they likewise would not seek the three. That we speak now of "those who seek" refers merely to their state of doubt.

The Buddha previously taught that there are three [vehicles], but now he teaches that there are clearly no three. Those who are deluded take this present absence of three to search for the previous existence of three; thus it is said they "seek" them.
Question:
Does one person seek three, or do two people seek three?

Answer: Regarding the statement that three [kinds of carts] were sought upon leaving the gate, this refers only to the two types of practitioners—the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha—who sought the three.

In the Śrāvaka vehicle, it is explained that from the initial generation of the mind until reaching the stage of the "near-attainment" (the stage preceding Buddhahood), the Bodhisattva has not yet severed the afflictions and remains a worldling (*pṛthagjana*); therefore, while still within the gate, one cannot say they have gone outside the gate to seek the carts.
Mahāyāna bodhisattvas have already transcended the three realms; they know for themselves that they have not yet reached the fruit of Buddhahood, and thus they do not seek a carriage.

Furthermore, the three carriages are metaphors for the fruits of the three vehicles: because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas reach the stage of their respective second fruits and find no further fruit there, they seek it.
There is no such thing as a bodhisattva reaching the stage of Buddhahood and finding no Buddha-fruit, and therefore there is no case of a bodhisattva seeking a carriage for the fruit of Buddhahood.
Question:
If that is so, and only two people are requesting, one should only request two; how can one request three? Answer:
Whether one person or two persons, both may obtain the three [robes]; there is no doubt about this.
Question:
If that is so, when it is said that "two persons seek [the robes]," why does the text say "all the sons seek them"?
Answer:
"Sons" is a general designation for all [disciples], not referring specifically to the three individuals outside the gate.
Therefore, the subsequent combined analogy explains it as follows:

If one sees immeasurable billions of sentient beings emerge from the suffering of the triple world and attain the bliss of nirvana, this merely clarifies that those of the two vehicles emerge from the triple world and attain the bliss of nirvana; it does not speak of bodhisattvas. Thus, we know that not all of them necessarily represent the three sons who sought [the jewels].
Question:
Is there also any bodhisattva who seeks the carriage? Answer:

If one relies on the gate itself, there is no "seeking" (suo) among the bodhisattvas; however, if we discuss it generally from within the gate in terms of their state of doubt, although it was previously said there were three types and now it is said there are not three, the bodhisattvas nonetheless possess seeking, as they use the absence [of the three] to verify the presence [of the One Vehicle].
Question:
Since you have sought three, why do you grant only one? Answer:

Since he sought [the Dharma] out of a state of doubt, and doubt is the very ford to liberation, if there is such a ford to liberation, the great capacity [of the seeker] has already been stirred. To strike the Buddha and ask for "one" is precisely to seek "one"; therefore, the Buddha subsequently bestowed "one" upon him.
"At that time, the elder bestowed gifts upon each of his sons"—this second section clarifies the bestowing of the chariots.
Regarding "that which they sought but was not given," there were three things for which they could not go seeking.
Regarding that which was not sought after, there is one point granted to facilitate understanding.
This is divided into two sections according to the text:
first, the two topical headings that mark the equal bestowal of the great vehicle.
Next, the two topical headings are explained.
To set forth these two topical headings:
first, the heading of "equal bestowal"; second, the heading of the "great vehicle."
The recipients are not limited to one; therefore, it is said that "each is granted.
Regarding "equality": in the past, the three capacities were manifested separately, and the Great Vehicle was granted to Bodhisattvas but not to the two vehicles, which was thus a partial grant.

Now, since the three ailments have been eliminated and the great capacity has been universally awakened, the Great Vehicle is given equally to all. In contrast to the previous partial granting, this present teaching clarifies the equal granting.

Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "I do not allow anyone to attain extinction alone; rather, I cause all to be extinguished by means of the Tathāgata’s own extinction. This is precisely the proof of that point.
The phrase "not allowing anyone to attain extinction alone" means not allowing bodhisattvas to attain great *nirvāṇa* by themselves.
The phrase "extinguishing all through the extinction of the Tathāgata" also means causing those of the two vehicles to realize great *nirvāṇa*.
"Great Carriages" below marks the second section, the heading for the Chapter on Great Carriages;
this refers to the presentation of the carriages bestowed.
"Those carriages were high and wide" below marks the second part, the explanation of these two headings.
First, the explanation of the chapter heading "The Great Chariot";
second, the explanation of the chapter heading "Equal Bestowal.
There are three parts to the explanation of the chapter heading "The Great Chariot":
First, the great carriage is explained;
second, the white oxen are explained;
and finally, the attendants are explained.
The first section also has two parts:
first, the explanation of "great," and second, the explanation of the "body of the chariot.
Regarding the phrase "the chariot is high and broad," this explains the meaning of "great."
It is "high" because it transcends the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); it is "vast" because it is replete with the myriad virtues.
Furthermore, its transcendence of the two deaths constitutes the meaning of the "fruit of fruits" (*phala-phala*) within Great Nirvāṇa;
its repletion with the myriad virtues constitutes the meaning of the fruit of *bodhi*. Below, these two fruits will again be combined.

Furthermore, when the two types of birth-and-death are transcended, all burdens are exhausted without exception; when one is fully endowed with all virtues, those virtues are perfected without exception.

That the burdens are exhausted without exception cannot be called "existence," and that the virtues are perfected without exception cannot be called "non-existence. Because it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is named the Middle Way; the Dharma of the Middle Way is termed the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Therefore, it is described as "vast and sublime."
In contrast to these two assemblies, this [vehicle] merely emerges from the immediate vicinity of the stage of segmented existence; therefore, it is termed "inferior.
Because it does not possess the ten thousand virtues, it is designated as "narrow.

If one explains it according to the causal vehicle (*hetu-yāna*), briefly citing its vows and practices: the vow to seek the Buddha-way above is "high," while the vow to deliver sentient beings below is "broad."
"Practicing for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi is its height; studying all paths universally is its breadth.
Regarding "adorned with various jewels," this is the second explanation of the chariot's body.
First, a general explanation; second, a detailed explanation.

Although it was previously indicated as being lofty and vast, one might fear it is not composed of various jewels; therefore, the subsequent clarification of its adornment with various jewels shows that the myriad virtues constitute the body of the resultant vehicle. If we refer to the causal vehicle, the myriad practices mutually support one another to form its functional application.
Below the section on "the surrounding railings," secondly, there follows a specific explanation of the chariot.
First comes the general heading, followed by the specific explanation; this is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning.
Regarding the separate explanation of the chariot, it is further divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the external adornments of the chariot;
second, the explanation of the internal adornments of the chariot.
Explaining the external adornments of the chariot praises the Mahāyāna virtue of transforming others;
explaining the internal adornments of the chariot clarifies internal virtues. These two encompass the infinite qualities of fruition, for they do not transcend these two.
In praising his external virtues, five categories are briefly set forth:
first, praise for his dhāraṇī;
second, praise for his four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Third, praising the four immeasurables;
fourth, praising the four great vows;
fifth, praising the four means of integration.
The first is that which can maintain, while the latter four are that which is maintained.

The railing is used as a metaphor for *dhāraṇī* (total retention): it acts as a "railing" (*lan*) by maintaining internal things so they are not lost, and as a "shield" (*shun*) by blocking external things so they do not intrude;
*dhāraṇī* is likewise, maintaining all virtues so they are not lost and blocking all evils so they do not arise.
The term "pari" (周匝) signifies the universal upholding of all virtues and the comprehensive exclusion of all faults.
Since this is the foundation of all virtues and is something not possessed by those of the Hīnayāna, it is mentioned at the beginning; this is the same as the previous praise of the Bodhisattva.
Regarding the phrase "bells suspended on all four sides," this next praises the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Since the dhāraṇī is the foundation of all virtues, it is placed first; because the four analytical knowledges are the essential means for transforming sentient beings, they are explained next.

Just as a carriage equipped with bells emits sound when it moves, so too does the Great Vehicle’s transformative activity employ the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) to produce its resonant voice.

Furthermore, this commentary takes up only the analytical knowledge of eloquent exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*); because it uses the sound of the bell to transform the four types of birth, it speaks of "four directions. Thus, within the previous praise of the Bodhisattva’s virtues, the first part clarified the attainment of *dhāraṇī*, while the subsequent part clarified the attainment of the analytical knowledge of eloquent exposition; these two current lines correspond exactly to that.

Regarding the phrase "spreading out the canopy and awning," this next section praises the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). The four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) are externally manifested because they must be internally filled by the four immeasurables;
therefore, they are praised next. The function of a canopy is necessarily to rise high above while covering what lies below;

compassion and the other immeasurables are likewise: they rise high above the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) and extend their cover downward over the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*). Although it is said that they "cover the vehicle," they actually cover the people within the vehicle.

The phrase "also adorned with rare and various precious jewels" clarifies that because [this] compassion is accomplished through all virtues, its essence is true reality; it is not like the provisional or conceptual compassion of non-Buddhists or those of the Two Vehicles.

Regarding "bound and entwined with jeweled cords": this next praises the Four Great Vows. If a carriage is not provided with cords, it will flutter and fly about; therefore, cords are installed to hold it securely from afar so that it does not move.
By means of these four great vows, one governs the four immeasurables, never abandoning the four modes of birth until the end of the future.
Furthermore, one maintains them through restraint so as to avoid the faults of craving and false views.
Regarding the phrase "hanging down flower garlands," this next praises the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Although one possesses the four great vows, it is still necessary to practice the four means of integration; like flower garlands hanging down to delight the assembly that has come, the four means of integration cause all to follow in harmony and take refuge as if in a forest.
"Layered with fine, soft rugs" refers to the second point, clarifying the adornment within the chariot, which serves as a metaphor for inner virtue.

The softness of these rugs constitutes the chariot's finery, capable of providing physical comfort; this is analogous to how the pliancy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) can bring peace to the body. Because there are eight layers of concentration, it is said they are "layered."
Furthermore, because there are hundreds of thousands of samādhis, it is said to be "layered.

As for *wǎnyán*, this refers to fine silk from foreign lands called *pánshuò xiù*; those who are wealthy and noble spread it out in multiple layers, which serves as a metaphor for the fact that the samādhis are not singular.

Regarding the phrase "placing a red pillow," some say that the two horizontal crossbars at the front and rear of a carriage are called the "carriage pillows"; based on these two pillows, four vertical bolts are erected to provide the framework for the side walls.
Faith is the foundation of all goodness, and precepts are the root of all virtues; the virtues of the Mahāyāna likewise rely upon these two dharmas, just as a carriage relies on its two wheels.
Now, you claim that these are not the wheels of the carriage.
How do we know this? It is because one only places the pillow down after the elaborate coverlet has been spread; this is therefore a pillow for lying down, not a carriage pillow.

Furthermore, the following verse states, "Upon the bright coverlet, a white cotton cloth is spread," which indicates that the cloth serves as a substitute for a pillow; thus, we know it is a pillow for supporting the head.
Question:
For what reason is a pillow placed inside the carriage? Answer:
Since this clarifies the internal virtue, it carries the meaning of ceasing transformative activity, like the image of one lying down.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Having entered the cave of profound meditative concentration of Great Nirvāṇa, because the multitudes do not see him, he is said to have entered Nirvāṇa."
Now, placing a pillow upon the richly adorned bed further represents entering parinirvāṇa within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Moreover, there were times when the Buddha entered profound samādhi for as long as eighty thousand kalpas; this was also a cessation of his transformative activity, and thus it is the image of his desire to lie down.
Question:
For what reason is it called the "Cinnabar Pillow"? Answer:
Cinnabar is the most magnificent among red hues; because it arises from profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*), its efficacy is as brilliant and radiant as the color of cinnabar itself.

Furthermore, it is explained that ancient sages combined divine elixirs to make pillows, thereby attaining long-lasting, spiritual longevity—this is analogous to entering *nirvāṇa*, which is characterized by permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity.
"Drawn by white oxen" is the second [point], explaining the oxen that draw the chariot.
Master Zhu Daosheng, employing the intent of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, explained this passage as follows:
"The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) free from defilement are called 'white oxen'; therefore it says, 'The elephant and horse gallop with the five supernormal powers.'"
Now, it is clarified that the ten thousand virtues and the great wisdom of equality differ in their significance.
The ten thousand virtues possess only the capacity for movement but lack the capacity for guidance; therefore, they represent the vehicle alone, not the ox.
The great wisdom of equality possesses both the capacity for movement and the capacity for guidance; therefore, it embodies the dual significance of both the vehicle and the ox.
The meaning of the five perfections in relation to Prajñā is likewise so.
"The great white ox-cart" refers to the Great Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-mahāprajñā*).

"The skin and color are full and pure": the perfection of the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) constitutes the fullness of the skin, while being stainless and undefiled constitutes the purity of the color.
Regarding "a beautiful physical form": that which is without [discursive] characteristics is the physical form; that which is tranquil, extinguished, and subtle is what is meant by "beautiful.
Regarding "possessing great strength and vigor": the former clarified the essence of wisdom, while the present clarifies the function of wisdom.

The profundity of its illuminating function enables it to sever great delusions; the weight of its universal bearing allows it to traverse the long path of the Way without exhaustion. Possessing these four meanings constitutes its great strength.
"His gait is level and upright" means that he wanders in the Middle Way, his conduct free from partiality or deviation.
"He is as swift as the wind" means that though he exerts no haste, he is rapid; his resonance is such that there is nothing to which it does not respond.

Furthermore, to universally know all phenomena in a single thought-moment is likewise as swift as the wind; employing the transformation of the Mahāyāna, one enters the five realms of existence as a vehicle, wandering therein with them as if in play.
The phrase "Furthermore, many attendants and servants serve and protect him" clarifies the third point: the retinue.

Since the myriad virtues of the Buddha-fruit constitute the chariot, the Buddha is the one who ascends it; those who follow the teachings and practice cultivate their service like a forest. Thus, the subsequent verse states: "That which the Buddha approves, and that which all sentient beings should praise, make offerings to, and prostrate before"—this is precisely the meaning of the retinue.

If we rely on the metaphor of the carriage, since this passage clearly elucidates the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), who has already emerged from the house, this marks the beginning of mounting the carriage;
those from the stage of one in training (śaikṣa) downward are all his attendants.
From "For what reason? onwards is the second section, which explains the chapter on equal bestowal.
This section is divided into two parts:
first, it clarifies the reasons why there are great carts; second, it clarifies the equal bestowal itself.

The preceding explanation of why he possessed chariots was intended to clarify the bestowal of those chariots; thus, the preceding explanation of why he possessed chariots serves as the introduction, while the passage beginning with "and he had this thought" clarifies the equal distribution.
First, it clarifies that they should not be treated unequally.
The section beginning with "Now this young child" below clarifies that they should be granted [gifts] equally.
First, it clarifies that because they are equally his children, they should be granted [gifts] equally.
Regarding the phrase "Loving without partiality," because his love is impartial, it is appropriate that he bestows gifts equally.

Regarding the passage beginning with "I have such great seven-jeweled chariots," the first two lines clarify the equality of his mind, while this current section distinguishes the abundance of his wealth.
Regarding the phrase "their number is immeasurable": the chariots are not two, yet those who ride them are not one; because those who ride them are not one, they are said to be immeasurable.
The section beginning with "Why is this so? uses the many to illustrate the few.
Regarding the phrase "providing for the entire nation," "nation" refers to sentient beings.

Even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were to simultaneously resolve their aspirations and be granted the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna), the Buddha-vehicle would still not be exhausted; "exhausted" means to be completely depleted.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time all study Prajñā, yet Prajñā is inexhaustible. Thus, Prajñā is the One Vehicle.
The phrase "how much more so for the sons" clarifies that those in this assembly who are capable of hearing and awakening are beyond the need for further explanation.
From the words "at that time, the sons" onwards is the third section: the parable of the joy upon obtaining the carts.
Question:
Since the great vehicle is already an analogy for the resultant vehicle (phala-yāna) and the sons represent the causes, how can they ride the resultant vehicle?
Answer:
Understanding is obtained from the Buddha; as each attains it according to their own capacity, they are said to "each ride" [a vehicle].
Furthermore, because a cause must necessarily yield its fruit, they are said to "obtain a carriage.
What was expected was small, yet what was ultimately attained is great; that the gift exceeds what was intended is called "not what was originally hoped for."
"Śāriputra," and below, is the sixth section, which clarifies the analogy of non-futility.
The reason this analogy appears here is that it arises from the preceding passage where [the Buddha] granted his promise.
The assembly was struck with doubt and said:
"At first you permitted three, yet in the end you did not grant them; this seems like empty words.
At first you did not permit even one, yet later you bestowed one; this again appears to be a false statement."
Now, wishing to harmonize these views and grant a resolution to sever that doubt, this chapter has been composed. It consists of three sections:
first, a counter-interrogation; [the second, a refutation; and the third, a conclusion].
Second, the respectful response;
third, the praise. As for the counter-argument:
it means that the Buddha’s falsehoods originally emerged from the śrāvakas.

Now, if one causes him to declare for himself that [his claim] is not false, then the fact of its being non-false becomes established; thus, the *Śāstra* says: "The Buddha cross-examined Śāriputra, causing Śāriputra himself to declare in his own words that he was inferior to the Bodhisattva, thereby verifying the distinction between the superiority and inferiority of the Great and the Small Vehicles."
The present case is likewise.

Furthermore, since Śāriputra has already attained realization, he understands that the three are one; thus, when the traces return to their source, the underlying intent accords with it. Therefore, by entrusting him with this harmonious integration, all doubts are stilled.
Regarding the statement, “Śāriputra said, ‘No’,” this is the second response in accordance with the inquiry. “No” means it is not false.
Question:
Why is it that some are permitted but not given [the gift], while others are given but not permitted? Answer:
The reason they are permitted is that, in accordance with their faculties and conditions, they are able to escape from the burning house; therefore, permission must be granted.
In principle, there are ultimately no three [vehicles], nor is this the Buddha’s original intent; how then could he grant it?
Therefore, he ultimately does not grant it.

As for granting it yet not permitting it: if he were to finally permit the Great [Vehicle] while it did not accord with their faculties and dispositions, they would have no means of leaving the house; thus, he initially did not permit it.

Regarding "in the end, he finally grants it": since the great capacity [of the disciples] has been stirred, it accords with the Buddha's fundamental intention; there is a single principle, and for this reason he grants it.
This section consists of two parts:
first, clarifying that the three previous teachings of the three vehicles were not false; second, based on the present granting of the One Vehicle, clarifying that there is no falsehood.

The Buddha merely briefly countered [the objection] by showing that the present is not false; Śāriputra, however, provides a detailed response to fully clarify that both the past and the present are not false.

Furthermore, he uses the past as an analogy for the present: if in the past there were no three [teachings] yet the three were still not false, how much less could the one [teaching] of the present and the one [reality] be false?
Regarding the two passages, each has one interpretation and one analogy.

First, to clarify the single interpretation: the elder merely caused his sons to emerge from the peril of the fire so that they might preserve their dharma-body and wisdom-life; he did not give them the carts at all, yet this was not false.
The reason for this is that having attained the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body is precisely what is meant by "worth preserving"; therefore, it is not empty.
Question:
On the basis of what meaning is it clarified that this is not empty?
Answer: It is not in vain because it yields two kinds of actual benefits.
First, one truly transcends the three realms.
Second, it is because one truly preserves one's body and life, and thus it is not in vain.
Question:
For what reason does he further say that if one preserves one's body and life, one has already obtained objects of enjoyment?
Answer: Although it was stated above that one obtains two kinds of real benefits and is therefore not deceived, one does not obtain the chariot; thus, [the claim] should be false.
To explain why this is so:
"If one were to preserve their entire life and body, it would already not be in vain, for they would have obtained cherished treasures;
how much more so when, through skillful means, one rescues them from that burning house? This is the second "how much more so" (kua).

If it were merely a case where the father directly enabled his sons to escape the fire and preserve their lives, it would still not be false; how much less so when he used skillful means to speak of three chariots to enable them to avoid the disaster—how could there be any falsehood in that?
Since it was previously based on actual benefit, it was already not false; how much more so, since the elder’s mind is sincere—how could it be false?
"World-Honored One!
If this elder... and so forth, constitutes the second [section], clarifying that it is not false at present.
There are also two stages: first, the explanation; second, the illustration.
Within the initial explanation, there are three parts:
first, the indication that [the teaching] is not in vain;...
2. From "For what reason" onwards, there is the explanation of non-falsity;
3. From "By these causes and conditions" onwards, there is the conclusion regarding non-falsity.

The general meaning clarifies that although the elder’s words promised the three [vehicles] so they might leave the house, his intention was not to grant the three, as he intended to fulfill his original purpose; because this is true, there is no falsehood.
"Let alone the elder," and so forth, is the second section, which employs an analogy.

Previously, it was explained that his original intention was not to give the small [portion]; even if he had ultimately not given the smallest portion at all, it would not have been a falsehood. How much less, then, could it be a falsehood when his original intention was to give the great [portion], yet he has now indeed given it?
From "The Buddha told Śāriputra" onwards is the third section, the praise.
One "Excellent! praises the resolution of the three past non-falsities; one "Excellent! praises its present single non-falsity.

"Thus it is with the Tathāgata as well," and so forth, constitutes the second section: the application of the parables (*upamā-saṃyojana*). This application of the six preceding parables forms six chapters.
Now, first, I shall provide a general summary of the overall intent of this application of the parables, which briefly comprises four points:
first, those [aspects] clearly manifested within the parables that are not explicitly correlated [with the dharma] shall not be correlated.
Second, that which is incomplete within the analogy is to be supplemented.
Third, while the analogy follows a single sequential path, once the analogy is joined, one further demonstrates another path, namely, the teaching by shifting the momentum.
Fourth, one correctly correlates [the meaning] based on the illustrative text.
Regarding the intent of the six illustrations herein: correlating with the first general illustration clarifies that the Buddha possesses ultimate bliss and no ultimate suffering;
correlating with the second illustration of seeing fire describes that sentient beings possess ultimate suffering and no ultimate bliss.

The third analogy, that of failing to save the children, clarifies that at the time of his initial attainment of enlightenment, he intended to uproot the extreme suffering of sentient beings and bestow upon them ultimate bliss; however, because they were not yet capable of receiving it, he suspended his transformative activity.
The fourth analogy, that of successfully saving the children, illustrates how he first uproots their heavy suffering and bestows upon them minor happiness.
The fifth analogy, that of equally granting the great chariots, illustrates how he uproots their light suffering and bestows upon them great bliss.
This combines with the sixth "analogy of non-futility" to clarify that the prior concession of minor happiness and the subsequent bestowal of great happiness are not contradictory in meaning.

Above, there were six general analogies; now, we specifically correlate them with the transformer (the Teacher), while also correlating the remaining five. Since the transformer is the foundation from which transformation arises, it is necessary to correlate him directly.
"All worlds" (*sarvaloka*) combines the aforementioned kingdoms, cities, and villages.
There are two kinds of worlds; here, we specifically take the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
The phrase "his father" corresponds to the aforementioned "venerable one.
The section beginning with "regarding all fears" corresponds to the aforementioned "immeasurable wealth.
As for the text itself, it is divided into two parts:
First, the praise of what is relinquished; second, the praise of what is attained.
That which is relinquished is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that which is attained refers to the meaning of non-emptiness.

Because the meaning of emptiness is free from all burdens, the Dharma-body is not existent; because it possesses all virtues, the Dharma-body is not non-existent. This state of being neither existent nor non-existent is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
Furthermore, being free from all burdens refers to liberation; possessing all virtues refers to the Dharmakāya and Prajñā.
Moreover, being free from all burdens refers to the fruit of fruits; possessing all virtues refers to the meaning of the fruit.

Furthermore, it is precisely because he is free from affliction that he is able to rescue those in affliction; since the intent is to clarify his ability to rescue those in affliction, the preceding section first describes his freedom from affliction.

It is precisely because he possesses virtue that he is able to save those who lack virtue; since the intent is to clarify his ability to save those who lack virtue, the preceding section first extols his possession of virtue.
Within the section on "departing from faults," the first part clarifies departing from the suffering of the fruit, which refers to the two kinds of *saṃsāra* fruits.
The passage beginning with "obscured by the darkness of ignorance" concerns departing from the suffering of the cause.
Thus, since the causes of the two types of birth-and-death have ignorance as their sole root, it is specifically mentioned here.
"Exhausted forever without remainder" refers to the simultaneous conclusion that there are no longer any afflictions regarding either cause or effect.
From "and all are fully accomplished" onwards is the second section, praising what has been attained.
This section also consists of two parts:
first, praising one's own virtues; [the second follows].
Next, there is the praise of the virtue of transforming others.
Initially, there are four pairs:

first, immeasurable knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*)—knowing all phenomena is "knowledge," and knowing them with such clarity as if seeing them with one's own eyes is "vision"; thus, knowledge and vision form one pair.
Power constitutes the internal [aspect] and fearlessness the external; these two form a pair.

Possessing great supernormal power refers to the wheel of spiritual powers (*abhijñā-cakra*), while possessing the power of wisdom refers to the wheel of turning the Dharma (*dharma-cakra*); these constitute the pair of manifesting spiritual powers and preaching the Dharma.
Regarding "Endowed with the Perfection of Skillful Means and Wisdom," this fourth section clarifies that both provisional and ultimate wisdoms are perfected.
From "Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion" onwards is the second section, praising the virtue of transforming others.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, praising the foundation of transforming others;
second, praising the traces of transforming others.
"Great kindness and great compassion" refers to the desire to universally uproot suffering and universally bestow happiness;
this is the vast mind. "Always without weariness" refers to the constant mind.
"Constantly seeking wholesome matters" refers to the first mind, which desires to bestow the foremost Dharma upon sentient beings.
Furthermore, compassion consists of uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness; thus, constantly seeking wholesome matters means extinguishing evil and giving rise to goodness.
"Arising within the triple world," and so forth, is the second section: praising the traces of transforming others.
Within the essence there are two essences, namely great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and great compassion (*karuṇā*).
Within the traces there are likewise two traces:

First, the traces of Great Compassion that uproot suffering are clarified; from the phrase "teaching and transforming so that they may attain" onwards, the traces of Great Benevolence that bestow happiness are shown.

Since it is explained herein that the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) arises within the triple world, one knows that the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is without arising or ceasing; this thus reveals the two bodies of arising and non-arising.
One should not say that this sutra does not clarify eternal abiding.
Question:
How does this accord with the aforementioned "immeasurable wealth" and so forth?
Answer: It is the combination of the four pairs, such as immeasurable knowledge and vision.
This is a general praise; "attaining liberation" refers to wisdom and abandonment, which together constitute the aforementioned field of merit.
Great kindness and great compassion correspond to the meaning of the upper residence.
Possessing great supernormal powers corresponds to the meaning of servants.
Being free from the two afflictions of cause and effect corresponds to the meaning of being advanced in years and in one's final body.
Next, regarding the secondary alignment with the other five meanings: "giving rise to the decayed and ancient fire-houses of the triple world" aligns with the place of transformation;
"in order to deliver sentient beings" aligns with the five hundred people and the thirty sons.
"Birth, old age, sickness, and death" corresponds to the meaning of transformation (*hua*).
"To teach and transform" and below correspond to the gate of teaching (*jiaomen*).
"Seeing all sentient beings" and below correspond to the second analogy of seeing the fire mentioned above.
There are three parts above:
first, seeing the fire and being struck with terror;
second, recording for oneself that one has already escaped.
Third, regarding "the son being wounded but not yet separated":
here, we merely combine the meanings of the two chapters, "Seeing the Fire" and "The Son Being Wounded but Not Yet Separated.

The reason for combining only these two meanings is that they correspond to the preceding general analogy which praises the Buddha as having bliss and no suffering; now, this combines with the analogy of "Seeing the Fire" to introduce the fact that sentient beings have suffering and no bliss. This is intended to contrast the presence or absence of [bliss/suffering] between the transformer (the Buddha) and those to be transformed (sentient beings).
Combining these two constitutes two meanings:
first, clarifying the vision of sentient beings suffering, which corresponds to the aforementioned vision of fire.
This further consists of four parts:
First, seeing sentient beings currently undergoing various sufferings;
second, seeing sentient beings being born and undergoing various sufferings;
third, seeing them undergoing various sufferings in the future.
Fourth, this summarizes the suffering of the three periods of time.
Within each of the aforementioned sufferings of the three periods, there are individually three types of suffering.
Regarding the three sufferings of the present life:

First, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—these collectively constitute the sufferings of the internal body; therefore, the sutra text groups them together as a single suffering.
Question:
To which category of suffering do sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction belong?
Answer: All are subsumed under the suffering of death. The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:

"At the time of separation through death, the feverish mind of the foolish person who is greedily attached is called *daurmanasya* (sorrow); the uttering of sounds and weeping is called *parideva* (lamentation); the contact of the five sense-faculties with their objects is called *duḥkha* (suffering); the contact of the mental faculty with its objects is called *daurmanasya*; and when suffering becomes increasingly deep, it is called *upāyāsa* (despair)."

The *Śālistamba Sūtra* states: "To feel sorrow for past events with a voice of lamentation is called *daurmanasya* (sorrow); the continuous succession of such recollection is called *śoka* (lamentation); the affliction of painful matters pressing upon the body is called *duḥkha* (suffering); and being bound by the fetters of the afflictions is called *upāyāsa* (despair)."
Furthermore, for the sake of the five desires and material gain, one undergoes various kinds of suffering.
Second, this clarifies how suffering arises from the external objects of the five desires.
Moreover, because of greedy attachment and pursuit, one undergoes manifold sufferings in the present; this is the third suffering.

The difference between this and the preceding section is as follows: the former clarifies that attachment to wealth is light, while the present passage distinguishes that the act of pursuit is grave. Although both are external objects that give rise to suffering, they are categorized as two based on the relative gravity of the craving involved.

"Receiving [retribution] in hell later," and so forth, is the second section, clarifying retribution in the present life (*upapadyavedanīya*), wherein the three miserable realms constitute the three types of suffering.
"If one is born in the heavens" refers to the third section, distinguishing the three types of suffering as retribution in future lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).

These refer to the suffering of poverty and hardship, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of encountering the hated; these three pertain to both humans and devas, which is why the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that even among devas there is poverty.
Question:
Why is this determined to be threefold retribution? Answer:
"Those who are greedily attached to the five desires will inevitably be reborn in the three miserable realms; only from those three realms can they eventually be born as humans or devas.
From the words "In this way, etc. below, the fourth section summarizes all forms of suffering.
Question:
How are these nine kinds of suffering correlated with the eight sufferings? Answer:

First, the manifestation of suffering through birth, aging, illness, and death constitutes the four types of suffering. The two types of suffering regarding the five desires and material gain belong to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. The three miserable realms belong to the suffering of encountering the hated. Poverty and hardship also belong to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Next, the sufferings of separation from the beloved and encountering the hated are explained as they appear in the text.
The subsequent summary—that all sufferings are the suffering of the five aggregates in their state of full growth—is the first point.
"Sentient beings sink within them, playing with joy" constitutes the second point, which corresponds to the previous [section on] grieving for one's children who have not yet departed.
"Immersed therein" means that sentient beings are submerged within the ocean of manifold sufferings.
"Rejoicing and sporting" refers to further giving rise to craving and attachment toward the fruits of suffering; this is precisely what constitutes the renewed creation of the causes of suffering.
The phrase "and the sons within the burning house delight in play" concludes [the previous section].
Regarding "unaware and unknowing," the former clarified craving (*tṛṣṇā*), while the present distinguishes delusion (*moha*); this refers to the union of delusion and craving.

Regarding the phrase "running hither and thither within this burning house of the triple world": from the preceding sections, we have seen sentient beings experiencing the fruits of suffering and creating the causes of suffering; now, we see that their cyclic wandering continues without ceasing.

Regarding the phrase "though encountering great suffering, one does not regard it as a calamity": previously, the joyful play [of the gods] clarified that sentient beings do not perceive suffering and do not weary of it; now, it clarifies that even when encountering suffering, sentient beings likewise do not weary of it. This thus corresponds to the previous passage: "When fire comes to press upon the body, the pain is most acute."
"Śāriputra! Having seen this, the Buddha... This concludes the third analogy of being unable to save one's children.
Above, there were two sections—exhortation and instruction—concerning the inability to transform sentient beings through the Mahāyāna.
Now, the present text combines these two sections and divides them into two parts:
first, the combined section on admonition and exhortation;
second, the general explanation of the cessation of transformation due to the lack of receptive capacity.

The reason for correlating compassion with the exhortation is as follows: correlating the first general analogy praises the Buddha as having bliss and no suffering; correlating the analogy of seeing fire introduces the fact that sentient beings have suffering and no bliss; and correlating the present third analogy clarifies how the Buddha extracts suffering from sentient beings and bestows bliss upon them. It is for this reason that the textual momentum of these three chapters flows together in succession.
"Śāriputra! The Tathāgata further reflects... and so forth; this is the second section, on ceasing the transformative activity due to the lack of receptive capacity.
The text contains two sentences:
First, it clarifies the provisional assumption made out of a desire to save; second, it clarifies that sentient beings are unable to receive [the gift].
The first section contains three points:

the first point clarifies the desire to bestow actual bliss—the power of spiritual efficacy (ṛddhi-bala) corresponds to the upper garment, and the power of wisdom (prajñā-bala) corresponds to the table.
"Abandoning the skillful means" refers to the second phrase, which clarifies the concealment of provisional expediency.
"For the sake of all sentient beings" and following refers to the third phrase, which intends to explain the ultimate reality.
"Sentient beings cannot be delivered by this," and so forth, marks the second section, clarifying that beings are unable to receive [the teaching].

The preceding section clarified that because they possess the suffering of the body, they cannot understand the Buddha’s wisdom and are scorched by the burning house of the triple world; this section clarifies that because they possess the suffering of the mind, they cannot understand the Buddha’s wisdom.
"Like that elder," and so forth, is the fourth section, which provides the analogy of rescuing the children by means of the three vehicles.
Above this are four chapters:
first, the analogy of knowing the children's long-standing preferences;... [and so on].
Second, the parable of preaching the three vehicles;
third, the parable of the sons' faithful acceptance;
fourth, clarifying the father's joy upon seeing his sons escape the calamity.
Now, let us consider this together.
Your Majesty knows that your son has three long-standing inclinations:
first, he understands the harm in not leaving the household life; [the other two follow].
Second, the desire to establish the skillful means for deliverance;
third, knowledge of the son's past inclinations.
At present, these are not combined; rather, the beginning and end of a single transformation are presented directly through the three types of Dharma wheels:
First, it clarifies the concealment of the real, meaning the concealment of the fundamental wheel of Dharma;
second, it clarifies the arising of the provisional, meaning the secondary and derivative wheels of Dharma;
third, it clarifies the intent behind employing the provisional, which is the gathering of the derivative back to the fundamental.

In this section, only the first two phrases are correlated; since the subsequent section separately correlates [the passage] regarding the bestowing of the great chariots, they are not correlated here. This directly clarifies the concealment of reality and the arising of expedient means, thereby generating the meaning of the teaching of the three vehicles that follows.
"Explaining the Three Vehicles for them" below constitutes the second section, which consolidates the formal exposition of the Three Vehicles.
This section is divided into four parts:
first, an admonition not to delight in birth and death;
Next, he exhorts them to quickly emerge from the triple world;
third, he clarifies that his protection is not in vain;
fourth, he praises the three vehicles.

These four [stages] arise sequentially one after another. To correlate them with the preceding four parables: the first correlates with the second [parable], which indicates the location of the chariots; the second correlates with the third, which exhorts [the children] to hasten their exit; the third correlates with the fourth, which guarantees that the gift will not be in vain; and the fourth correlates with the first, which praises the three types of chariots.
The reason why the teaching and the analogy differ is that the method of exposition has shifted.
From the passage "You all must quickly escape the triple world" onwards is the second section: the exhortation to escape quickly.
"From 'I now guarantee for you' onwards is the third section, which concerns the guarantee that it shall not be in vain.
Regarding the phrase "using these skillful means to entice and advance sentient beings," a skeptic might say:
"If one claims to guarantee that it shall not be in vain, yet later it is not obtained, then it becomes a falsehood."
Therefore, the commentary states:
"The mention of 'providing protection' is merely a skillful means to entice and advance sentient beings.
From the phrase "He further spoke these words" onwards is the fourth section, which praises the mastery of the Three Vehicles.

Regarding "unfettered" (*asaṃyukta*): ordinary beings are fettered by the three types of afflictions, karma, and suffering; because he enables them to attain liberation from these, he is called "unfettered.

Regarding "having no basis for seeking": when the mind has nothing to which it is attached, it is called "non-reliant" (*anāśrita*); when the four wisdoms are perfected, it is termed "without seeking" (*aniṣprārthana*).

"Regarding the passage 'If there are sentient beings who possess the nature of wisdom within,' this is the third section, which correlates the preceding parable of the three vehicles' faith and acceptance in leaving the house.
While the previous parable explained the departure from the house for all three vehicles collectively, correlating them individually now forms three distinct segments:
'possessing the nature of wisdom within' refers to the internal cause (*adhyātma-hetu*)."
The phrase "hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and receiving it with faith" clarifies the external conditions.
As for "receiving it with faith," because the causal conditions are fully complete, it is said that he hears the Dharma and receives it with faith.
“Diligent and energetic effort” refers to the clear understanding and acceptance previously mentioned, and now the discernment of practice.
“Desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek nirvana for oneself” clarifies the intention behind the practice.
There are two intentions for practicing cultivation:
first, the desire to transcend the triple world, which means knowing suffering and severing its origin; second, seeking nirvana for oneself, which means realizing cessation and cultivating the path.
The phrase "This is called the Śrāvaka-yāna" is a summary of the name for the Hīnayāna.
The expression "like those sons" provides an analogy to illustrate this point.
Here, *nirvāṇa* is specifically taken as the metaphor for the vehicle, because Śrāvakas cultivate the path precisely for the sake of seeking *nirvāṇa*.

Some say: "From the initial hearing of the Dharma and its faithful acceptance, one corresponds to the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); through diligent and earnest application, one clarifies the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*); and by desiring to quickly escape the triple world, one clarifies the true sage (*ārya*). This is called the Śrāvaka vehicle’s discernment of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)."
The passage beginning with “If there are sentient beings” next combines this with the Pratyekabuddhayāna, omitting a detailed explanation of its internal causes.

Regarding the phrase “seeking spontaneous wisdom” (svayambhū-jñāna): those of the Middle Vehicle do not primarily seek *nirvāṇa*; if they were to seek *nirvāṇa*, they would be no different from the Śrāvakas. Therefore, the text here cites the seeking of spontaneous wisdom to align it with the Deer Cart (*mṛga-ratha*), for the purpose of distinguishing them from the Śrāvakas.
Regarding "delighting in solitude and sublime tranquility," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that there are two types of pratyekabuddhas:
first, the *vargacārin* pratyekabuddha, who possesses a group of followers and associates; these are the lesser pratyekabuddhas.

Second, the rhinoceros-horn simile refers to the pratyekabuddha; that is, the "solitary awakener" (pratyekabuddha) is termed a "great pratyekabuddha. Such a person dwells alone and in stillness within the mountains, which corresponds to the present text’s description of delighting in solitary tranquility.

"Deeply understanding the causes and conditions of all phenomena" indicates the scope of what is to be known; that is to say, it distinguishes [the Bodhisattva] from the Śrāvakas, who know only the Four Noble Truths.
"If there are sentient beings," and so forth, next joins the analogy of the great carriage.
“Seeking all-knowledge” (sarvajñatā) refers to the wisdom of emptiness.
“Buddha-wisdom” is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), which refers to the wisdom of existence.

While all-knowledge may at times be common to the two vehicles—as stated in the "Chapter on the Three Wisdoms" of the *Prajñāpāramitā* where it says, "The two vehicles are called 'all-knowers,' whereas the knowledge of all modes belongs only to the Buddha"—it is for this reason that the title "Buddha" is used to designate the knowledge of all modes.

"Natural wisdom" (svayambhū-jñāna) generally clarifies that two kinds of wisdom spontaneously and effortlessly know the two objects—emptiness and existence; it is, that is to say, non-effortful wisdom (anābhoga-jñāna).
"Teacherless wisdom" (aśikṣita-jñāna) means that the aforementioned three wisdoms are not obtained from a teacher; hence they are called teacherless wisdom.
The intent of this explanation originates from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Regarding "the Tathāgata’s powers of knowledge and vision and his fearlessnesses," the preceding section directly elucidated the four wisdoms; here, we further distinguish these four wisdoms, namely the two pairs of knowledge-and-vision and power-and-fearlessness.
Although the Buddha-vehicle possesses all virtues, wisdom is its primary principle; therefore, it extensively elucidates wisdom.

From the phrase "compassionately mindful and bringing peace and happiness" onwards, the preceding section cited the gate of wisdom, which refers to one's own virtue; the current section cites the gate of merit, referring to the virtue of transforming others.
"Great compassion is designated as 'pity,' and great kindness is designated as 'concern'; these two terms mark the dual gates [of the Great Compassion Sūtra].

As for the distinction between 'peaceful happiness' and 'benefit': bestowing the fruit of happiness is peaceful happiness, while bestowing the cause of goodness is benefit; this explains the virtue of great kindness."
"Delivering all beings" explains the virtue of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Delivering from suffering and liberating from its origin (*samudaya*) corresponds to great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), which likewise possesses two meanings.
"This is called the Mahāyāna" summarizes that the essence of the Mahāyāna consists of the self-cultivation of merit and wisdom as well as the transformation of others.

Regarding the statement, "Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, they are called Mahāsattvas": previously, the greatness of the Dharma was clarified; now, the greatness of the person is being distinguished. They are called "Great Beings" (Mahāsattva) because they seek the Dharma of the great fruit; thus, the name is established based on the Dharma of the fruit.

From the passage "Just as that householder" below, this corresponds to the fourth section above, the analogy of seeing the sons escape danger; however, because the phrasing shifts and differs from the previous section, it should be divided into two distinct parts:
first, the simultaneous presentation of the two analogies;
second, the simultaneous application of the two analogies.
These two represent the conclusion of the Small [Vehicle] and the beginning of the Great [Vehicle]; because their meanings are interrelated, they are cited together.

Emerging from the three realms and attaining the state of no-more-learning constitutes the conclusion of the Small; the awakening of those with the capacity for the One Vehicle and the bestowal of the Mahāyāna constitutes the beginning of the Great.
The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata is likewise" combines the two parables:
first, it correlates the sight of the sons escaping danger;
the section beginning with "At that time, the Tathāgata" constitutes the fifth correlation, which correlates the equal bestowal of the great chariots.
There are three chapters above:
first, seeking the vehicle;
second, bestowing the vehicle.
Third, the joy of obtaining the chariot.
This does not accord with the beginning or the end [of the parable], but rather accords with the equal bestowal.
Since the above section on seeing the son escape danger represents the perception of the emergence of a great capacity, this section now clarifies the meaning of the equal bestowal.

In the parable, the bestowing of the great carts was clarified while the awakening of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) was not distinguished; here, the awakening of the spiritual capacity is clarified while the bestowing of the great carts is not distinguished—thus the texts manifest these aspects alternately.
Regarding the superior bestowal of the great carts, there are two parts:
first, the opening of the two topical sections.
Next, the two topical headings are explained.

Here, the two meanings of "bestowing equally" and "the great vehicle" are explained together; this constitutes an analogy that opens up the meaning while the Dharma-exposition unifies it. This is likely due to a shift in rhetorical momentum, serving to manifest the meaning through mutual illustration.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, the bestowal of the great vehicle in terms of the Great Nirvana; second, the bestowal of the great vehicle in terms of its manifold virtues.
Regarding the first [section], there are five sentences:
the first sentence clarifies that there is an abundance of the Dharma-treasure; from the words "these sentient beings" downward, the second sentence clarifies that they are all my children.
"Equally bestowing the Great Vehicle" and below constitutes the third phrase, which correctly clarifies equal bestowal.
"Not allowing anyone to attain extinction alone" and below constitutes the fourth phrase, clarifying that one should not be unequal.
Regarding the phrase "All are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s extinction," the fifth line correctly clarifies the equal bestowal.
The expression "all by means of" corresponds to the equal bestowal, while "the Tathāgata’s extinction" corresponds to that great vehicle.

The reason why the Great Nirvāṇa was previously cited as being equivalent to the Great Vehicle is that the Two Vehicles represent the primary teaching of the Lesser Extinction; now, the Great Extinction is employed to replace the Lesser Extinction.
Furthermore, because he previously saw the cessation of minor suffering, he granted them a minor cessation; now, the cessation of great suffering is called the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
From the phrase "These sentient beings" onwards is the second section, which cites various virtues to correspond with the Great Vehicle.
The phrase "bestowed upon all" corresponds to the "equal distribution.
"The meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of all Buddhas" corresponds to the "great vehicle" (*mahāyāna*).

The former [the equal distribution] corresponds to the great vehicle as the fruit-of-fruits (*phala-phala*); now, the meaning of the fruit itself is used to correspond to the great vehicle. "Fruit-of-fruits" means that there are no afflictions (*kleśa*) left unexhausted; "fruit" means that there are no virtues (*guṇa*) left unperfected. Since these two are both perfected, they encompass all meanings in their entirety; therefore, they are briefly cited here to correspond to the great vehicle.
Furthermore, the former refers to the cessation of great suffering, while the present refers to the bestowal of great bliss.

Regarding the phrase "all are of one characteristic and one kind": "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) refers to what is manifested as a mark, while "kind" (gotra) refers to the distinction of lineage. Here, it is clarified that because there are no external differing characteristics among the three vehicles, they are said to be "of one characteristic"; and because there are no internal differing essences among the three vehicles, they are said to be "of one kind."

The passage beginning with "Just as that householder" below combines the sixth analogy, the Analogy of Not Being in Vain. First, it restates the preceding analogy, and then it applies it to the present case.
The phrase "But they are not all able to receive" clarifies that it is not that the Buddha is unable to bestow [the teaching], but rather that sentient beings are not all able to receive it.

This is based on the fact that among the beings of the three vehicles in the past, only bodhisattvas were able to receive the Great [Vehicle], whereas those of the two vehicles could not; for this reason, the single Buddha-vehicle was differentiated and taught as three.

Regarding the passage beginning with "For this reason," there are two meanings for its inclusion here: first, it follows closely upon the text stating "cannot fully receive [it]," because since they cannot fully receive the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), the One Buddha Vehicle is explained through the differentiation of three vehicles.

Second, it is to provide a distant response to the request of Śāriputra above; he requested that his causes and conditions be explained, and now that the causes and conditions of the six similes from beginning to end have been fully expounded, this serves as the concluding response.
The verses consist of one hundred and sixty-five lines in total, which correspond to the preceding two sections:
first, they versify the "Proper Response to the Request for Explanation" mentioned above;
second, the line "For this reason, seeking throughout the ten directions" versifies the second part, the conclusion of the response to Śāriputra’s request.
The initial text also has two parts:
the preceding verse presents the analogy, and the subsequent verse applies it to the subject matter.
In the previous analogy, six points were explained, but here only five are versified.
The analogy of "not in vain" refers to Śāriputra’s realization; it is not versified here.
The remaining five analogies are versified in five sections:
first, thirty-three lines verse the general analogy;
Next, three lines of verse praise the analogy of seeing the fire;
next, five lines of verse praise the analogy of failing to rescue the children;
next, twelve and a half lines of verse praise the analogy of successfully rescuing the children.
Next, the twelve lines of verse praise the analogy of bestowing the great chariots.

While the preceding general analogy contained six meanings, the present verses do not praise the single gate nor the thirty sons; rather, they praise the converter, the place of conversion, the five hundred people, and the intent of the conversion. These four meanings constitute a shift in the momentum of the teaching and should be expanded into six sections:
first, clarifying the master of the house.
2. Describing the characteristics of the house;
3. Clarifying the people within the house;
4. Distinguishing the poisonous harms within the house.
Fifth, it clarifies that there is a fire disaster within the house;
sixth, it summarizes the faults and calamities of the house.
The "owner of the house" refers to the Buddha.
The characteristics of the house are that the three realms are impermanent, without self, and impure.
Those within the house are the sentient beings of the five destinies.
That the house contains poison and harm means that the afflictions of the three realms can destroy the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom.
"A house with a fire" refers to the various sufferings of the triple world burning sentient beings.

To summarize these calamities and afflictions: being possessed of all the aforementioned evils, the triple world constitutes a great calamity and affliction, which causes beings to feel weary of it and seek its transcendence.
Question:
Why are the single gate and the thirty sub-sections not included in the verse? Answer:

The "Thirty Sons" are those seeking deliverance; the "Single Gate" is the exit from the burning house. Now, these six points all introduce the faults and afflictions of the triple world and clarify that sentient beings are submerged within it; therefore, they are not praised [in verse].

The "Returning from One Gate" and the "Thirty Sons" are set aside to be combined with the subsequent parables of "Seeing the Fire" and "Failing to Rescue the Sons," along with their accompanying verses.

The reason for this is that the Buddha, having integrated the six parables, opens them into two major chapters: the first integrates the general parable to clarify the meaning of the faults and afflictions of the triple world (*tridhātu*), while the latter five parables together clarify the meaning of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*); these two are thus opened because they follow according to their respective categories of meaning.
The passage beginning with "For example, a householder" constitutes the first section, clarifying the master of the house; this verse summarizes the aforementioned teacher.

Since the prose exposition (*chāng-háng*) clarifies that the teacher is the primary subject, it requires extensive explanation; as the prose is already detailed, the verse therefore treats it concisely.
"There is a great house": the second part, the description of the house's characteristics, corresponds to the second section above concerning the place of transformation.
As for the phrase "there is a great house," the preceding passage clarifies that there are four types of places of transformation:
namely, kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages.
For now, let us speak in terms of one aspect of the triple world; therefore, it is said to be "one.
The triple world is the dwelling place of sentient beings, and as the Buddha is their transforming lord, there is the sense of belonging to the Buddha; therefore, it is said to "exist."
"Great house" refers to the meaning that his residence is vast and expansive.
"The house is old and dilapidated" extensively describes the characteristics of the residence.
Since the prose section is brief, the verse expands upon it.
The three realms are impermanent and decaying things, which is why they are called "ancient.
Because they are impermanent all at once, they are said to be "suddenly obscured"; obscuration arises from decay.
"The hall and buildings are high and perilous" is a general summary of the characteristics of the dwelling from above; now, it is explained specifically.
This section consists of three parts:
first, the analogy of the impermanence of the triple world.
Second, the analogy of the selflessness of the three realms;
third, the analogy of the impurity of the three realms.
Since a fire subsequently arises separately to serve as an analogy for suffering, the specific analogy for suffering itself is not explained here.
The term "hall" (*táng*) is explained as above; because sentient beings of the six realms gather together within the three realms, it is called a hall.
Regarding why what was previously termed a "pavilion" (*gé*) is now referred to as a "house" (*shè*), there are two meanings:

first, it was called a pavilion to distinguish the different ways of ascending and sinking within the three realms; second, it is now called a house to indicate that it is a dwelling place for beings.

Second, because the three realms revolve and turn, rising and falling without constancy—sometimes being born in the higher realms and sometimes in the lower realms—they do not exclusively maintain a fixed name.
The phenomena of the three realms are called "high" because they are layered and accumulated, while the retributions of the six paths are called "perilous" because they are not stable dharmas.

Furthermore, since heaven and hell face one another at their gates, that which is high must necessarily be precarious; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "It is like a flock of sheep, where those that are fattest die first."
Regarding the phrase "the pillar-base is crushed and rotten": previously, this generally clarified the impermanence of the three realms; now, it specifically clarifies impermanence.

The pillar-base supports the foundation of a single house, just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) sustains the master of a single body. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "As long as a person's life-faculty remains, the other faculties remain; if the life-faculty ceases, all other faculties are utterly extinguished. For this reason, the life-faculty was analyzed first.
"To diminish and destroy moment by moment" means to crush and decay.
Regarding "the beams and rafters leaning," this clarifies that the dharmas of the mind are impermanent, as explained previously.
Because consciousness has no fixed form and its arising and ceasing are like an illusion, it is described as "leaning."
Regarding the phrase "the foundation and steps have collapsed": the three types of karma serve as the foundation and steps for the three realms. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"By reason of the causes and conditions of sinful karma, one is born in the three evil destinies; by reason of the causes and conditions of meritorious karma, one is born among humans and devas in the desire realm; by reason of the causes and conditions of immovable karma, one is born in the form and formless realms. Thus, we know that the three karmas constitute the foundation and steps of the three realms.
The gradual exhaustion of the constituent elements (*saṃskāra*) constitutes "ruin.

Regarding the phrase "walls and partitions collapsing," the "base of the pillars" distinguishes the impermanence of that which is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*); the "beams and rafters" clarify the impermanence of mental phenomena (*caitasika-dharma*); now, the impermanence of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) is clarified.

The first two [types of impermanence] have their characteristics of impermanence obscured, and thus they are explained briefly; the characteristic of impermanence in material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) is manifest and should be elucidated in detail.

The four external great elements (*mahābhūta*) are like a wall, and the four internal great elements are like a partition; the nature and characteristics of these four elements are mutually antagonistic, like a collapsing structure.
"Qi" (圮) means destruction;
"che" (坼) means fissuring.
As for "nitutuotuo" (埿塗陀落), "nitu" (埿塗) refers to the four subtle elements (*catur-mahābhūta*).

According to the *Abhidharma* (Vibhāṣā), the four subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) always coexist; thus, the four great elements produce the four subtle elements.
According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, however, the four subtle elements constitute the four great elements, just as mud and plaster form walls.
Now it is said that the four subtle elements (*mahābhūta*) are also impermanent, and are thus called *dhra* (decay).
Furthermore, subtle impermanence is like crumbling and splitting, while gross impermanence is like peeling away and falling off.
"Peeling away" (*dhrī*) refers to collapsing and withering; "falling off" (*luta*) refers to dropping and tumbling down.

Regarding the phrase "the thatch falls in disarray," *shàn* (thatch) refers to materials used for roofing, whether tiles or straw; since this house is currently covered with straw, it is specifically called *shàn*.
Sentient beings wrap their single bodies in thin skin, just as fragile straw covers a single house.
"Chaos and falling" refers to a state of disordered collapse;
it is the appearance of slackened skin, wrinkled faces, sparse teeth, and an exhausted physical form.

Regarding "the rafters and eaves are out of alignment": the faculty of mind (*manas*) is the ridgepole (*dōng*), the faculty of body (*kāya*) is the eaves (*lǚ*), and the four faculties of the eyes and so forth are the rafters (*chuān*). That upon which the rafters depend is fixed above by being nailed to the ridgepole and below by being joined to the eaves. Thus, the two [primary] faculties are the main structure while the four faculties are dependent upon them, mirroring this architectural analogy.

"Deterioration" (cha-tuo) means that the faculties function by mutually supporting one another; when even their power of support becomes weakened due to decay and infirmity, this is termed "deterioration."
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "In youth, one is far from death and near to birth; thus, the six sense faculties are all clear.
In old age, one is far from birth and near to death; thus, the six sense faculties are all obscured."

Regarding the phrase "surrounded by winding enclosures," the preceding section clarified that the five aggregates and the six sense organs are all impermanent; this refers to the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya-vipaśyanā*).
Now, describing the appearance of the house as leaning and crooked clarifies the contemplation of non-self (*anātma-vipaśyanā*).

It is like when old age, sickness, and death are approaching, such that the four limbs and the entire body lose their autonomy; it is like a house leaning to one side and unable to stand upright, thereby manifesting the absence of a self.
Regarding the phrase "filled with various impurities," this third section clarifies the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Some say that from the passage "There was a great house" up to "and it became suddenly dilapidated," the text provides a general summary of the impermanence of the three realms (*tridhātu*).
