Regarding the śrāmaṇeras who first recite and subsequently believe and understand: one who wishes to provide a commentary must possess two qualities:
first, the ability to recite and uphold [the text].
Second, because they have attained understanding, these two [qualities] are possessed.
Regarding the statement, "Those of inferior faculties all give rise to doubt," there are four meanings:

first, while those of middle faculties among the śrāvakas who have a karmic affinity with the Buddha are all able to attain faith and understanding, other sentient beings—due to having formed heavy causal conditions with the sixteen śrāmaṇeras—cannot be saved by the Buddha; it was from such individuals that the matter of the "repeated preaching" originated.

Second, it is intended to clarify that when the Buddhas of the past preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were sentient beings who believed and those who did not; likewise, it demonstrates that among the people of the present, there are likewise those of the three capacities who either awaken or do not awaken.

Third, wishing to encourage those of inferior faculties in the present who have heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* spoken by the Buddhas of the past—those of sharp faculties being able to believe and understand it, while those of dull faculties give rise to doubt—he said: "You bhikṣus should be like those of sharp faculties; why do you instead resemble those of dull faculties?"

Fourth, [I thought]: "Both you and I were together at that assembly to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; since I attained awakening early on, yet you still do not understand it even now—how truly distressing this is!"
Regarding the statement, “The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas,” this third section clarifies the duration of the preaching.
Because the text is extensive, the time is long; hence it is said below that “he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
"Having finished preaching this sutra," and so forth, is the fourth section, clarifying that after the preaching of the sutra is complete, he enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This section also has three parts:
first, the actual clarification of entering the quiet chamber;
Below "dwelling in," second, the dwelling in meditative concentration is clarified;
below "eighty-four thousand," third, the duration of remaining in concentration is clarified.
The reason he entered meditative concentration was his desire to have the sixteen śrāmaṇeras recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* on his behalf.
However, the methods of transformation employed by the Buddhas vary; generally, there are three types of ways this sutra begins and ends.

First, after the Buddha Dīpaṃkara finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he immediately entered parinirvāṇa. This indicates that those who were to be saved through their karmic connection with the Buddha had all already been delivered.

Second, it is now clear that regarding the Buddha’s karmic connection with those he delivers, there is both completion and non-completion: those of sharp faculties have already been delivered, while those of dull faculties have not yet been delivered. It was necessary for the Buddha to arise from his meditative absorption, praise the śrāmaṇera, and exhort sentient beings to draw near to him; therefore, the Buddha has not yet entered parinirvāṇa.

Third, after Śākyamuni Buddha finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he did not preach it again; because those who were to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* had already attained full realization, he no longer preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and instead preached the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
From "At that time, the sixteen bodhisattvas" onwards is the second section, which correctly clarifies the formation of karmic conditions (*karmapratyaya*).
Regarding the preceding causal origins, there are two types:
first, the remote; second, the proximate.
Now, two points are also opened:
first, clarifying the formation of karmic conditions in the past;
second, distinguishing the mutual encounters throughout successive lives.
The two sections each contain four [parts], totaling eight chapters of scripture.
Regarding the first section’s four parts:
the first clarifies that the Buddha’s entry into meditative concentration serves as the causal condition for the re-explanation.
Second, the formal exposition for the assembly;
third, clarifying how the assembly receives benefit;
fourth, distinguishing the Buddha’s praise.

Regarding the second passage, "Each Ascends the Dharma Seat": Just as when the sun hides its radiance, the bright moon takes up its brilliance, so too, because the Tathāgata withdraws his shadow, the Bodhisattvas extend their luster.
"Each and every one is delivered," and so forth; this third section clarifies that the assembly receives benefits.
Regarding "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 54, states: "'Showing' means showing them what is wholesome and what is unwholesome."
"Teaching" means instructing one to abandon evil and follow what is good.

"Benefit" refers to those whose minds have become discouraged before they have tasted the flavor of the Dharma; for their sake, one explains the supreme fruit of Nirvana to cause them to cultivate wholesome causes, so that their minds perceive benefit—this is "benefit."

"Regarding 'joy' (muditā): one praises and commends others according to their conduct to make them rejoice; for instance, if someone delights in giving, one praises that very act of giving. Thus, one adorns the teaching of the Dharma with these four matters."

Now, regarding the explanation of the four matters according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: first, it demonstrates that the three vehicles are skillful means and the one vehicle is the ultimate reality; therefore, this is called "demonstration" (*darśana*).
Second, it causes [beings] to abandon the three and enter the one; therefore, it is called "instruction" (*śāsana*).

Third, it explains that the fruits of the three vehicles are inferior while the fruit of the one vehicle is supreme, thereby inducing the cultivation of the cause of the one vehicle and causing the mind to perceive its benefits; this is called "benefit" (*lābha*).

Observing their faculties and conditions, he may teach by means of the door of Dharma-exposition to explain the One Vehicle, or by means of the door of parables, or by means of accounts of past causes and conditions; according to what they delight in, he teaches the Dharma in accordance with their capacities to cause them to give rise to joy, and thus it is called "joy."
From "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū" onwards is the fourth section, which clarifies the Buddha’s praise.

Because his preaching of the Dharma accords with principle and suits the capacities of the listeners, the Buddha now offers this seal of approval and praise so that the assembly of the time may believe and accept it.

Regarding the phrase, "You all should repeatedly draw near," this means that because they have a karmic affinity with the śrāmaṇeras, they are instructed to draw near, just as the Buddhas of the ten directions exhorted Sadāprarudita to draw near to Dharmodgata.
From "The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus" onwards is the second section, clarifying how they encountered one another life after life after forming a karmic connection.
This section also has four parts:
first, clarifying the benefits obtained by those who were transformed.
Second, distinguishing the benefits gained by those who are transformed;
third, correlating the ancient and the present;
fourth, clarifying the meeting with [the Buddha] in the future.
The first section consists of three sentences:
First, it clarifies that the śrāmaṇeras always delight in preaching the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Because the *Lotus Sūtra* elucidates the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), and because bodhisattvas constantly seek the fruit of Buddhahood, they always delight in preaching it.

Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* brings together the beginning and the end, fully encompassing all teachings; thus, if one speaks of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one encompasses all teachings.
The section beginning with "Each and every bodhisattva" clarifies the conditions for the benefits obtained in the present.
The third phrase, "In every lifetime where they are born," clarifies that benefits are obtained at a later time.
Question:
Since those who form a karmic connection here will always encounter one another thereafter, why is it that the impoverished son and his father lose each other and do not meet?
Answer: Some say that the statement here regarding meeting one another life after life refers to the long-term perspective of one or two kalpas, during which they constantly meet one another.
Regarding "the impoverished son not seeing [him]," this refers narrowly to not seeing him for one or two lifetimes.
Now, it is said that there are three grades of people who form a karmic connection with a śrāmaṇera:
first, the superior grade, as described here, which involves encountering many Buddhas and being born together with the teacher; such a person attains awakening in their past lives.

Second, there are those of middling capacity, as described in the passage below: "Those who currently abide on the stage of the śrāvaka did not realize the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the past; now, encountering Śākyamuni and hearing of the One Vehicle, they finally awaken"—these are like the impoverished son.

Third, those of inferior faculties, as stated in the subsequent passage: "Disciples of future generations who did not serve the Dharma Master in the present will only attain awakening after hearing [the teaching] in the future."
Because there are three faculties, the attainment of enlightenment differs according to the three periods of time; therefore, the present text does not contradict the parable of the impoverished son.
As for the phrase "not yet exhausted at present," it means: first, that past roots of goodness have not yet been exhausted;
second, that even though he has encountered many Buddhas, they still remain unexhausted.
"From 'All bhikṣus' below, secondly, it clarifies the benefits gained by the transformer.
The reason for clarifying the benefits gained by the transformer is to strike those of inferior faculties."

"I have realized that by hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, I have subsequently advanced to Buddhahood; yet you, having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, have instead regressed to become a śrāvaka—how truly pitiable this is!"
From "O bhikṣus, we" onwards is the third section, clarifying the connection between the past and the present.
This passage consists of three parts:
first, citing the aforementioned individuals of superior capacity.
“Among these beings, there are those who currently abide on the stage of the śrāvaka” refers to the second phrase, which clarifies those of middling faculties from the past.
“These people should gradually enter the Buddha-way by means of this Dharma” explains the aforementioned constant teaching toward unsurpassed bodhi.
A doubter asks:
"If you have always taught the unsurpassed bodhi, why do you now preach the Dharma of the śrāvakas?
Furthermore, since you even taught the Great Way when you were a śrāmaṇera in the past, why do you now preach the Hīnayāna?"
Therefore, the commentary states:
"The teaching of the Śrāvaka-dharma is intended to lead them gradually into the Buddha-way, for the Buddha-wisdom is so subtle that it cannot be entered all at once.
One should know that the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle is the gradual teaching of the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, in the past there were those of great capacity; therefore, it was called "Great. However, because they subsequently regressed from the Great and took up the Small, it is now spoken of as "Small.
The phrase "At that time, those transformed who were of inferior [capacity]" constitutes the third sentence, which correctly reconciles the ancient and the modern.
The section beginning with "After my parinirvāṇa" constitutes the fourth segment, which clarifies the meeting [of beings] in the future and reveals those of inferior capacity.

These are individuals who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, cultivate the path and become arhats; at the end of their lives, they are reborn in a Pure Land. There, Śākyamuni appears as a Buddha under a different name and preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them, only then enabling them to attain awakening.

The reason for speaking of this matter is to clarify that there are none who ultimately abide forever in the Two Vehicles; rather, they must hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and subsequently attain Buddhahood. This serves to encourage those of inferior faculties, urging them to believe and accept it in a timely manner.
Question:
What are the characteristics of the three faculties? Answer:

Those of superior capacity, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* once, encounter their teacher life after life and further meet forty trillion Buddhas, thereby early awakening to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Those of middling capacity regress from the Great [Vehicle] to take up the Small, meeting Śākyamuni at the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Those of inferior capacity also regress from the Great to take up the Small; they neither encounter Śākyamuni face-to-face nor hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, but will only encounter a Buddha and hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the future, at which point they finally attain realization.
Question:
For what reason is it said that there are further alternative names? Answer:
“Śākyamuni” is a name for a Buddha in a defiled land; since he is now transforming sentient beings in a pure land, he has yet another name.
The section beginning with “If, O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata... constitutes the second major section, clarifying that those who encounter him in the present are further taught the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is expanded into four parts:
first, the Dharma; second, the analogy; [third, the application; fourth, the conclusion].
3. The application;
4. The illustration followed by the application.
The Dharma-exposition consists of two parts:
First, the exposition of the Mahāyāna is clarified;
second, the exposition of the Hīnayāna is distinguished.
If one follows the sequence mentioned above, the exposition of the Hīnayāna is clarified first, followed by the exposition of the Mahāyāna.

Now, having sought back into the distant past, I find that I once received the Great Transformation; therefore, I now return to expound the Great Dharma. However, because I neglected and forgot it in the interim while practicing the Lesser Vehicle, I shall next clarify the Lesser [Vehicle].
The meaning in the subsequent parables is likewise the same.

Furthermore, there are two ways in which the Buddhas preach the Dharma: first, arising from the ultimate reality (paramārtha) to manifest expedient means (upāya); [and second, arising from expedient means to reveal the ultimate reality].
II. Subsuming the Provisional into the Real.

Thus far, we have primarily clarified the subsumption of the provisional into the real; now, we wish to distinguish how the provisional arises from the real. Within the exposition of the Great [Vehicle], there are two parts: [the first being the subsumption of the provisional into the real, and] the second being the arising of the provisional from the real.
First, knowing the capacity;
second, expounding the teaching.
Within "knowing the capacity," there are five phrases:
First, clarifying the time for preaching the Dharma:
entering Great Nirvana refers to the ripening of the faculties for hearing the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*;
now, the conditions for the One Vehicle have ripened, meaning that the time for [the Buddha's] Nirvana is approaching.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Belief and Understanding" says: "When he was about to pass away, he summoned his son. Regarding the phrase "the assembly was also pure":

they attained purity because their minds were made supple through the four teachings; because their minds were tamed by the teachings for humans, devas, and the two vehicles, they no longer possessed the afflictions of ordinary beings. Furthermore, through the secret transformation of entrusting them with wealth and the refinement of their limited minds, the afflictions of those in the two vehicles were gradually eliminated. Since they were now free from both the delusions of ordinary beings and sages, it is said that "the assembly was also pure."

Regarding "firmness of faith and understanding": whereas the preceding section distinguished the absence of obstacles, this section clarifies the presence of a receptive capacity; that is to say, one who possesses great faith and great understanding is able to hear this sutra.
Great faith is the faculty of dull capacity, while great understanding is the faculty of sharp capacity.
Furthermore, great faith comes first and great understanding follows.
When these two do not regress, they are termed "firm."

Regarding "thoroughly comprehending the dharma of emptiness": previously, one has already heard the Mahāyāna teachings on ultimate emptiness, such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, which awaken the great mind. If one has not heard the dharma of ultimate emptiness and non-attainment, then upon hearing it said that "one exists" or "three do not exist," one will fall into the two views [of existence and non-existence].

Regarding "entering deeply into meditative concentration" (dhyāna-samādhi), it does not necessarily mean entering deeply into the eight dhyānas. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "With a single mind directed toward the Buddha-way, there is no longer any movement or distraction arising from the attainments of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles. For this reason, it is called "concentration" (samādhi).
"Then he assembled all the bodhisattvas" and below is the second section, the actual exposition (*samyag-deśanā*).
The opening phrase serves as the introductory statement (*nidāna*), for it clarifies that the actual exposition of this sutra is about to be delivered.
Although there are many formal explanations, they do not go beyond the principle that there is no duality and only one vehicle.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Bhikṣus, you should know," this is the second section, which clarifies the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle.

The reason for teaching the Lesser Vehicle is that, since there is neither a second vehicle nor anything other than the single Buddha-vehicle, the former teaching of two vehicles was given because [the Buddha] knew that sentient beings were incapable of hearing the Great Vehicle and desired only the Lesser; therefore, he taught the Lesser for their sake.
The text consists of three sentences:
first, the knowledge of the capacity [of the audience], for which reason the correct teaching is elucidated;
[the second sentence,] "If this person hears it," distinguishes the benefits obtained.
In the *Zhijijing* (Treatise on Knowing the Occasion), it says: "The 'expedient means of the Tathāgata' is presented here to resolve doubts.
The doubter asks:
'If there are no two vehicles, for what reason did you previously teach that there are two nirvāṇas?'"
Therefore, the commentary states:
"The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom of skillful means and acts according to the capacities of beings; thus, he speaks of two [vehicles].

As for the phrase, "If such a person hears this, they immediately believe and accept it," since the teaching is given in accordance with their capacity, they immediately believe, accept, and thereby obtain benefit.
"Suppose, for example, five hundred yojanas... and so forth, is the second analogy.
It consists of nine sentences in total; with the ninth sentence—concerning the benefit gained by hearing the One Vehicle—omitted, it is divided into three chapters:
first, the initial analogy of the Great Vehicle.
Second, the intermediate teaching of the small parable; third, the concluding teaching of the great parable.

There are three reasons for opening these three sections: 1. To provide a gradual entry into the Dharma for sentient beings who have not yet awakened to the profound meaning. 2. To cause those who have already awakened to the profound meaning to further increase their understanding. 3. To cause those who have already increased their understanding to attain ultimate realization. Therefore, there are three meanings underlying this [opening of the three sections].
First, it is like the three matters that exist from beginning to end throughout the two periods [of the past and future lives]: the sixteen śrāmaṇeras were initially taught the Great [Vehicle].

Second, during the intermediate period, those who had regressed from the Mahāyāna were taught the Dharma of the Small [Vehicle]; this refers to the interval from when Śākyamuni first proceeded to the Deer Park until before Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Third, the abandonment of the minor to establish the major, which refers to the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Throughout the beginning and end of the two periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], there are only these three matters; therefore, three chapters are established.
Second, the Buddhas of the three periods possess three kinds of Dharma wheels:
First is the fundamental wheel of Dharma, which refers to the teaching of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Second is the derivative wheel of Dharma, which teaches the three vehicles within the context of the one.
Third is the wheel that gathers the derivatives back to the fundamental, which means subsuming the three vehicles into the one.
Three analogies are established to manifest the three wheels.

Thirdly, in the preceding "Parable Chapter," six analogies were presented because that chapter refuted the notion that the original vehicle for śrāvakas was small at first and large later; now, for the sake of those śrāvakas who have regressed from the Great [Vehicle] to realize the Small, it first clarifies the teaching of the Great, next clarifies the Small, and finally subsumes the Small back into the Great.
The initial passage consists of three sentences:
first, the analogy for the evil realms to be saved;
second, the analogy for the person who wishes to save them.
Third, the analogy of the guide leading [the way].
"Five hundred yojanas" refers to the evil paths to be crossed. Some say:
The "five hundred" is a metaphor for the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
Now, this is not so; for how could one avoid the three miserable paths? Furthermore, the name "three hundred" refers to those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
Moreover, since those of the two vehicles have already escaped the five realms of existence, they should already have crossed over the "five hundred."
Some say there are four kinds of birth and death:
first, the birth and death of flowing and coming; [and so forth].
2. Transformation-death (nirmāṇa-maraṇa);
3. Intermediate-death (antarābhava-maraṇa);
4. Segmentary-death (paricchinna-maraṇa).
Transcending three hundred [stages], one is exempted from the death and rebirth of segmented existence;
transcending four hundred, one is exempted from the death and rebirth between the seventh stage and the two lands;
transcending five hundred, one is exempted from the death and rebirth of transformational existence from the eighth stage upward.
Some say: "The three realms constitute three hundred; the two vehicles at the seventh stage constitute one hundred; and from the eighth stage upward, they again constitute one hundred.
Now, I maintain that these interpretations are all incorrect, as is fully explained in the *Mysterious* [Treatise].

Now, we specifically take the three realms as three hundred and the two vehicles as two hundred. There is both doctrinal meaning and scriptural authority for providing this interpretation. Regarding the meaning:

we are currently transforming those of the two vehicles, leading them toward the Buddha-way. Although they have already transcended the three realms in the past, they have not yet transcended the stages of the two vehicles; they still remain within the evil paths. How could one abide within the midst of the evil paths and yet consider it nirvana?
One should abandon them, and then one will certainly reach the path of Buddhahood.
Question:
If one transcends the three realms and the stages of the two vehicles, how can one then reach the path of Buddhahood?

Answer: There are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival by way of cause; second, arrival by way of fruit. What is meant by "arrival by way of cause"? It refers to the stage where one has already attained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and is practicing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This is called arrival by way of cause. What is meant by "arrival by way of fruit"? It refers to the stage where one has already attained the path of cultivation and is practicing the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). This is called arrival by way of fruit. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of others; second, arrival through one's own power. What is meant by "arrival through the power of others"? It refers to those who have not yet attained the noble path but, relying on the power of others, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of others. What is meant by "arrival through one's own power"? It refers to those who, relying on their own power, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through one's own power. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of faith; second, arrival through the power of wisdom. What is meant by "arrival through the power of faith"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of faith, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of faith. What is meant by "arrival through the power of wisdom"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of wisdom, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of wisdom. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of diligence; second, arrival through the power of meditative concentration. What is meant by "arrival through the power of diligence"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of diligence, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of diligence. What is meant by "arrival through the power of meditative concentration"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of meditative concentration, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of meditative concentration. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of hearing; second, arrival through the power of reflection. What is meant by "arrival through the power of hearing"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of hearing, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of hearing. What is meant by "arrival through the power of reflection"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of reflection, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of reflection. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of practice; second, arrival through the power of realization. What is meant by "arrival through the power of practice"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of practice, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of practice. What is meant by "arrival through the power of realization"? It refers to those who, having realized the noble path, are able to enter the path of no-more-learning. This is called arrival through the power of realization. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of roots; second, arrival through the power of faculties. What is meant by "arrival through the power of roots"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the roots of goodness, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of roots. What is meant by "arrival through the power of faculties"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the spiritual faculties, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of faculties. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the truths; second, arrival through the power of the elements. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the truths"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the Four Noble Truths, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the truths. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the elements"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the eighteen elements, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the elements. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the bases; second, arrival through the power of dependent origination. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the bases"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the twelve bases, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the bases. What is meant by "arrival through the power of dependent origination"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the twelve links of dependent origination, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of dependent origination. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the aggregates; second, arrival through the power of the sense-spheres. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the aggregates"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the five aggregates, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the aggregates. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the sense-spheres"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the twelve sense-spheres, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the sense-spheres. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of mindfulness; second, arrival through the power of clear comprehension. What is meant by "arrival through the power of mindfulness"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of mindfulness, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of mindfulness. What is meant by "arrival through the power of clear comprehension"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of clear comprehension, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of clear comprehension. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of tranquility; second, arrival through the power of insight. What is meant by "arrival through the power of tranquility"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of tranquility, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of tranquility. What is meant by "arrival through the power of insight"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of insight, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of insight. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the foundations of mindfulness; second, arrival through the power of the right efforts. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the foundations of mindfulness"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the four foundations of mindfulness, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the foundations of mindfulness. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the right efforts"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the four right efforts, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the right efforts. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the bases of psychic power; second, arrival through the power of the faculties. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the bases of psychic power"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the four bases of psychic power, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the bases of psychic power. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the faculties"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the five faculties, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the faculties. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the strengths; second, arrival through the power of the limbs of enlightenment. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the strengths"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the five strengths, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the strengths. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the limbs of enlightenment"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the seven limbs of enlightenment, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the limbs of enlightenment. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the path; second, arrival through the power of the fruits. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the path"? It refers to those who, relying on the power of the eightfold noble path, are able to enter the noble path. This is called arrival through the power of the path. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the fruits"? It refers to those who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, are able to enter the fruit of once-returning, and so forth, up to the fruit of arhatship. This is called arrival through the power of the fruits. Furthermore, there are two kinds of arrival: first, arrival through the power of the Dharma; second, arrival through the power of the person. What is meant by "arrival through the power of the Dharma"? It refers to those who
Second is "arrival at the fruit.

Regarding "arrival by way of the cause," as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "The *srotāpanna* arrives in eighty thousand kalpas, and so on, up to the *pratyekabuddha*, who arrives in ten thousand kalpas. This refers to arriving at the bodhicitta, which is the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) where one becomes a person of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

Upon reaching this stage, one is freed from the rank of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and from regressing to the level of the two vehicles; because one will certainly reach the path of Buddhahood, it is called "reaching.

Second, the three realms constitute birth-and-death by segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*), while those of the two vehicles dwell in birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). To cross these five locations, to be freed from the two kinds of birth-and-death, and to attain Great Nirvāṇa is what is meant by "reaching the fruit."
Question:
For what reason is it known that there are two kinds of arrival? Answer:

The subsequent verse states: "I shall now speak the truth for you: what you have attained is not extinction. For the sake of the Buddha’s omniscience, you should exert great diligence. This refers to the arrival at the cause.
Your realization of omniscience is precisely true cessation, meaning that the fruit has been attained.

Regarding the scriptural evidence, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its commentary on the "Chapter on Hearing and Retaining," states: "Having crossed four hundred yojanas, one knows that the city is not far away."
Nāgārjuna’s commentary states:

"Three hundred [verses] represent the triple world, and four hundred represent the two vehicles. However, while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* combines the two vehicles into one hundred, this sutra opens them into two hundred; though the methods of opening and combining differ, the underlying meaning is no different.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) did not yet discard the Two Vehicles, whereas this sūtra begins to discard them; this constitutes their difference.
Yet, as both lead to the evil realms, there is no distinction between the two teachings.

Furthermore, within the analogies of this very sutra, it is clearly explained that the three realms constitute three hundred and the two vehicles constitute two hundred; yet the masters of the meaning of various other sutras have failed to examine the intent of the text and have instead offered arbitrary divergent interpretations.
"Perilous and evil paths" refers to the meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
The three realms are difficult to cross even for those of the two vehicles; therefore, they are called "perilous.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are two causes for a bodhisattva’s regression:..."
"First, it is the craving for the three realms and the delight in the two vehicles.
Regarding "evil paths": the three realms are evil paths for those of the two vehicles, and the two vehicles are, in turn, evil paths for bodhisattvas.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Those who seek the two vehicles are called unwholesome. For this reason, these five locations are all termed evil paths (*durgati*).
Furthermore, within the three realms, craving is their root;
for the two vehicles, views are their root.
Attachment and views are both evil.
Furthermore, three hundred [of these] are the views of ordinary beings, and two hundred are the views of emptiness held by the followers of the Two Vehicles; all such views are evil.

Furthermore, ordinary beings and non-Buddhists claim that the three realms are nirvana; since this is both delusion and perversion, so too is the claim of the two vehicles that the death-rebirth of transformation (parināma-śīti-bhava) is nirvana. Because both groups assert that birth-and-death is nirvana, and both take what is impermanent to be permanent, they are termed "evil."
Regarding the phrase "vast and desolate, devoid of people": it is called "vast and desolate" because it is profoundly remote for five hundred [yojanas];
it is said to be "devoid of people" because it is a place where Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not dwell.

Regarding "places of fear," those who study the Mahāyāna deeply dread these five places; there is no peace within the three realms, which are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings and most truly terrifying.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Now I fear the fruits of the paths of the two vehicles, just as one who cherishes their life fears the loss of that body.
This is precisely what is illustrated by the analogy in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the enemy tree.
"If there are many people" refers, secondly, to those who have attained eternal deliverance;
these are the disciples transformed by the śrāmaṇera.
Previously it was said that there were no wise persons; now it is clarified that he wishes to deliver many people, hence the phrase "many people."
Regarding the phrase "desiring to pass beyond this path to reach the place of rare treasures," there are generally two intentions for a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind:
first, the desire to cross over the stages of ordinary beings and the two vehicles;
second, the desire to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
"From 'There was a guide' onwards is the third section, which clarifies the analogy of the guiding teacher; this refers to the sixteen śrāmaṇeras mentioned above as well as Śākyamuni.
Since the Way is non-dual, those who realize the Way are likewise one."
Furthermore, he alone is one who well knows the signs of the paths' openings and obstructions; thus, he is called "One" (*eka*).
Because he possesses the ability to guide and demonstrate what is deviant and what is correct, he is named the "Guide" (*śāstṛ*).

Regarding "wise and sagacious": when wisdom resides in the ears, it is called "wisdom" (cōnghuì); when wisdom resides in the eyes, it is "sagacity" (míngdá). This is a brief praise of these two matters.

Furthermore, "wisdom" is a metaphor for the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā), while "sagacity" is a metaphor for the three types of penetration (trividya). The knowledge of all modes illuminates the myriad dharmas horizontally, whereas the three penetrations examine the three periods of time vertically.

Regarding the phrase "skillfully knowing the characteristics of the obstructions and openings of perilous paths": it means knowing that when a great capacity for awakening arises, it is termed an "opening" because one is capable of being delivered; when such capacity does not arise, it is termed an "obstruction."
Furthermore, knowing that accord with principle constitutes a thorough path while deviation from principle constitutes an obstruction clarifies the internal wisdom of the Guide.
The phrase "leading the multitude across this difficulty" praises his external capacity for transformation.
Pointing to the aspiration for the Buddha-way as being far beyond the two types of birth-and-death is the desire to transcend these difficulties.
"The multitude of people he leads become weary and retreat midway" is the second part: the parable of preaching the Lesser Vehicle midway.
There are also three phrases:
first, the analogy for knowing that those with inferior capacities have aroused [the aspiration];
second, the analogy for preaching the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.
Third, the analogy of receiving the teaching and attaining benefit.
Regarding the arousal of the small-capacity [practitioner], there are two parts:
first, clarifying the arousal of the small-capacity [practitioner].
Next, the illumination of the Buddha’s wisdom is explained.
Regarding the arousal of the small-capacity [practitioner], there are three phrases:
first, the indication of the desire to regress;
Second, the explanation of the desire to fall away;
third, the conclusion regarding the desire to fall away. This is the first.

"Those who stop halfway" refers to those who have initially resolved their great mind (*mahācitta*) with the desire to transcend birth and death, seeking the Buddha-way from afar and wishing to leave behind the practices of the Lesser Vehicle; yet, before their great understanding has been perfected, they regress midway through this process.

If one uses the aforementioned events of the past as an analogy, then from the time of the previous transformation until before the present transformation, the period between these two pillars—during which the Great Mind was neglected and the Great Practice was lost—is likewise the interval before attaining the Buddha-way, which is termed the "midway."

Regarding the phrase "addressed the Guide," since they had already withdrawn from the Great [Vehicle], they possessed the capacities of the Small [Vehicle] with which to strike upon the Buddha; being thus illuminated by the Buddha's wisdom is what is meant by the sense of "addressing the Teacher."

Regarding the phrase, "We are utterly exhausted and terrified; we cannot advance further, for the road ahead is still long," the former part indicates the onset of weariness and retreat, while the latter part explains that weariness and retreat.
There are three reasons for retreating:
first, one retreats due to extreme exhaustion; this is a metaphor for when the contemplative understanding of the Mahāyāna is weak and lacks power, such that one cannot advance to the Buddha-way.
Second, they regress due to fear, which is analogous to the many afflictions and hardships within saṃsāra.

Third, they regress because the path is distant, being analogous to the Buddha-way which is only reached after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas; since even a single practice beyond the Lesser Vehicle cannot be cultivated, it is said that they are unable to advance further.
Regarding the phrase "now wishing to withdraw and return," this third clause concludes the section on withdrawal.
There are two aspects to withdrawal:
first, withdrawing to become an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, "retreating to become a follower of the Two Vehicles.
Now, because one wishes to retreat back into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is called "retreating.
Furthermore, because one may initiate the aspiration but immediately cease seeking Buddhahood, stopping without advancing is termed "retreating and returning."
Question: This is already falling away; why then do you say "desiring to fall away"? Answer:
This clarifies that the nature of the faculties is not fixed:
first, one may regress to become an ordinary person;
second, one may abide as a follower of the Two Vehicles.
Third, those who are capable of advancing are designated as bodhisattvas; because they are not yet fixed, they are described as "desiring" [enlightenment].
"The Guide possesses many skillful means" refers to the second point: illuminating the capacities of sentient beings.
There are also three statements:
first, praising the transformative power of the teacher who possesses the virtue of knowing the capacities of others;
second, clearly describing the faults of those being transformed.
Third, the explanation of the faults of those to be converted.

Regarding the phrase "many skillful means": previously, there was the capacity to lead [beings] toward the Great [Vehicle]; now, moreover, one explains the inclination toward the small and trivial; therefore, it is said to be "many."
Furthermore, to allow them to retreat, or to compel them to advance, or to cause them to remain forever in the Two Vehicles—none of these are skillful means.

Now, he does not cause them to regress to the state of ordinary beings, nor does he compel them to advance in pursuit of Buddhahood; rather, he provisionally teaches the Lesser Vehicle along the way so that they may ultimately awaken to the Great Way. Therefore, it is said that there are "many skillful means."
"Then he formed this thought," and so forth, is the second section, which describes the faults of those to be converted.
"How can they discard such great treasures," and so forth, is the third section, which explains the faults of those to be converted.

To abandon the bliss of the Buddha is called "discarding a great treasure," and to delight in the suffering of birth and death is called "desiring to retreat"; by citing these two matters, the meaning of being "pitiable" as mentioned above is explained.

With many skillful means, he praises the wisdom of the Teacher; from "Having formed this thought" onwards, the second section clarifies the establishment of the Lesser Teaching (Hīnayāna). It praises the Teacher’s compassion out of pity for those below [him].
There are three statements in total:
first, the formal establishment of the teaching;
second, the admonition.
Third, the exhortation:

Although the two vehicles differ in terms of their sharp or dull faculties, they are alike in severing the afflictions of the three realms beyond the realm of birth and death; therefore, it is said that they have transcended three hundred [kalpas].
Because that which is not ultimately real is spoken of as ultimate, it is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).
Since the meaning of severing delusions is the same and the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is no different, they are referred to as "one."
Because it prevents the calamities of birth and death, it is called a "city.
"He addresses the multitude, saying: 'Do not fear; do not retreat,'" is the second [section], the admonition.
"Do not fear" means that you need not harbor deep dread of old age, sickness, and death.
"Do not retreat" means do not take pleasure in the five desires of birth and death.
"The phrase 'you may now dwell within this great city' is the third exhortation.
It is called 'great' because the nirvana attained through the exhaustion of all afflictions is comparable to the bliss of gods and humans."
The two kinds of nirvāṇa are the places where one halts the carriage; they are called "places where one may rest.
Regarding the phrase "acting according to one's will," it means that once all fetters and burdens are exhausted, the mind attains mastery.

Regarding the phrase, "If one enters this city, one swiftly attains peace and security": it means that if one realizes this nirvana, one departs from the perilous suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Some say: when the afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted and one acts with sovereign mastery at will, this is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder).

"If one enters this city, one will swiftly attain peace and stability; the two afflictions of cause and effect, along with all perilous suffering, will completely vanish—this is *nirvāṇa without remainder*.
Regarding the statement, "If one can reach the place of jewels, one may also go there," some say:

the fruit of Buddhahood is likened to the place of jewels; if a śrāvaka can resolve to attain bodhicitta and seek the wisdom of a Buddha, they too may go there, as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If you can resolve to do so, I shall likewise rejoice."

If explained according to the underlying principle, this phrase reveals the intent of the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*): it teaches that the instruction for the two vehicles is fundamentally intended to lead them to Buddhahood. It is like providing a temporary resting place for weary feet so that they may continue on their journey. Previously, this intent was not made manifest; therefore, these words were provisionally established to clarify that although one may temporarily realize the Lesser Vehicle, one ultimately returns to the Great Way.

If one explains this according to the former teachings, it is as it is said that one attains the state of a śrāvaka after cultivating for sixty kalpas, and realizes the state of a pratyekabuddha after cultivating for a hundred kalpas; these two alike realize the nirvana without remainder, and thus the metaphor may be applied here.
Now, this is like a bodhisattva practicing for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas to advance toward Buddhahood; therefore, it is said: "If one can reach the place of treasure beforehand, one may also go."
"Then the exhausted multitude felt great joy in their hearts," and so forth; this is the third section, on receiving the teaching and attaining benefit.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, faith and acceptance;
Second, practice;
third, the realization of nirvana.
The teaching is called "joyful" because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "marveling at what has never occurred before": the two kinds of *nirvāṇa* are supramundane dharmas that do not exist in the world; thus, they are called "what has never occurred before.
The statement, "We have now escaped this evil path," refers to being free from the suffering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
"Swiftly attaining peace and security" means obtaining the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Up to this point, all [descriptions] refer to the initial hearing of the Buddha's teaching and the arising of faith and acceptance.
"Thereupon, the multitude entered the conjured city" refers, secondly, to the discernment of practice and the seeking of nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "having been born, one conceives the thought of having crossed over and the thought of being at peace": this refers to the third line, which signifies the realization of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
To emerge from the cycle of birth and death within the three realms is called "the thought of having crossed over"; to realize *nirvāṇa* without remainder is "the thought of being at peace."
Furthermore, attaining the state of "with remainder" is called the perception of having crossed over; entering the state of "without remainder" is called the perception of peace.

Moreover, attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is called the perception of having crossed over; attaining the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is called the perception of peace.
Because that which is not actually ultimate is claimed to be ultimate, it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
Question:

While those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) may give rise to the perception of having already crossed over, can ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those still in training (*śaikṣa*) also give rise to this perception?
Answer:

Ordinary beings and those still in training have not yet emerged from the triple world, and they also regard the nirvana of the two vehicles as the ultimate dharma; therefore, they too can give rise to this notion.
From "At that time, the guide" onwards is the third section, the subsequent explanation of the great parable. This section is divided into two parts:
first, knowing the capacity [of the disciples]; second, the actual teaching. Regarding the first: knowing the capacity.
Second, the teaching on cessation (*śamatha*).
To avoid falling back into the state of an ordinary person or dwelling in the limited nirvāṇa is called "cessation" (*śama*).
In contrast to the progress toward seeking the Buddha-way, it carries the meaning of a temporary resting of the feet; therefore, it is termed "resting" (*kṣaya*).

"Being free from further fatigue" means that by using the teachings of the Hīnayāna to harmonize and soften the mind, one eliminates coarse afflictions; thus, the mental faculty becomes somewhat strengthened and capable of hearing the Mahāyāna.
"Immediately extinguishing the conjured city" refers, secondly, to the teaching of the doctrine.
Abolishing the ultimate teachings of the three vehicles is termed "extinguishing.
Furthermore, unifying the three into one so that the three names no longer exist is also "extinguishing."
The phrase "He says to the multitude, 'Go, you all, come! encourages the śrāvakas to practice and seek Buddhahood.
The phrase "The place of treasure is near" explains the intent behind this encouragement; since the path ahead is already close, one ought to proceed.
"Three hundred have already crossed over, and now there are only two hundred remaining; therefore, it is said they are 'near' [to liberation].
As for the statement, 'The great city you saw was created by my transformation,' this refers to the teaching of the three vehicles as a differentiation within the single Buddha-vehicle."

The phrase "for the purpose of cessation" explains the intent behind the three [terms]; there is both cessation (*śamatha*) and tranquility (*vyupaśama*), corresponding to the two meanings mentioned previously.
The section beginning with "O bhikṣus" constitutes the third part: the application of the analogy.
Combining the three analogies results in three distinct sections.
In the first analogy above, there are three phrases:
first, the evil realms to be saved;
Second, those who seek deliverance;
third, the enlightened guide.
This [text] precisely corresponds to the third, while also encompassing the meanings of the other two.

"Knowing all births and deaths" corresponds to the aforementioned deliverance from evil guides; "should be removed and should be delivered" corresponds to the aforementioned skillful knowledge of the signs of passage and obstruction, as well as the seeking of those who are to be delivered.
From "If sentient beings" onwards, this combines with the second section above to explain a minor analogy regarding the Middle Way.
Therein are three parts:
first, the arousal of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*).
Second, the teaching;
third, the benefit.
Now these shall be combined.
The arousal of the superior capacity has two parts:
first, clarifying the arousal of the capacity;
second, illuminating the capacity.
"Now, this corresponds to:
'They do not wish to see the Buddha nor wish to draw near him,' which corresponds to the preceding passage from 'becoming weary and retreating midway' up to 'we are utterly exhausted.
Furthermore, 'they then think that the path of the Buddha is long and distant' corresponds to the preceding passage 'the road ahead is still far.'"
"Only after enduring long-term diligent toil can one achieve success"—this [thought] leads to closing [the mind] and further fear.
"The Buddha knows this mind to be timid and inferior"—this corresponds to the second point: the Buddha’s illumination of the faculties.
The section beginning with "By the power of skillful means" corresponds to the second part, the formal exposition of the teaching.
The phrase "preaching two nirvāṇas" corresponds to the aforementioned creation of a single city.
Question:
Previously it was stated that there is one city; why is it now said that there are two nirvāṇas? Answer:

Some say: "The previous [passage] speaks of 'one' because it clarifies that the afflictions of the three realms are abandoned equally; the present [passage] speaks of 'two' based on the distinction between the remainder and the remainderless. Others say:
Great Nirvāṇa is the first; now this intermediate-path nirvāṇa is called the second, and thus they are termed "two.
As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "There are two kinds of nirvāṇa:
first, that without remainder, which belongs to the Buddhas;"
Second, there are those who say that "the remainder" refers to the two vehicles.
Now, I maintain that both these interpretations are incorrect; this passage simply takes what is realized by those of the two vehicles as the two kinds of nirvāṇa.
As the verse says: "There is only the Single Buddha Vehicle; it is spoken as two because they are places of rest.
Question:
Why was it called "one" above, yet now referred to as "two"?
Answer: The followers of the Two Vehicles share both commonalities and differences.

From a higher perspective, they are said to be "one" because they equally transcend the three realms and equally realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); however, from the present perspective, they are further clarified as "two" because their faculties differ—some being sharp and others dull.

Furthermore, to clarify the meaning of "five hundred yojanas," the three realms are divided into three hundred and the nirvana of the two vehicles is further divided into two hundred; it is said to be "two" because one wishes to cause [beings] to cross beyond the stage of the two vehicles.

"If sentient beings abide in the two stages" combines with the third [section], where it subsequently returns to explain the great parable. The preceding text has two parts: first, knowing the capacity [of the audience]; second, the teaching itself. Regarding the first part, "knowing the capacity": [it states that] the Buddha knows that sentient beings have long been weary of suffering and desire to transcend it; they seek liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Knowing this, he teaches the Dharma to enable them to transcend all such suffering. Furthermore, he knows that these sentient beings have long practiced wholesome roots and possess the capacity for the Mahāyāna. Knowing this, he teaches the Mahāyāna Dharma to enable them to attain the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata. This is called "knowing the capacity. As for the second part, "the teaching itself," it refers to the subsequent explanation of the parable. Why is this? Because the Buddha’s intention is to teach the Mahāyāna. Therefore, he first speaks of the two vehicles to lead those of dull faculties, and subsequently returns to speak of the Great Vehicle to lead those of sharp faculties. This is called "the teaching itself. Thus, the entire discourse consists of these two parts. First, knowing the capacity; second, the teaching itself. Second, the exposition of the teaching.
This is now correlated with the text:
the initial passage corresponds to the subsequent "knowing the capacities," while simultaneously correlating with the meaning of the third preceding section on "attaining benefit."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "abiding in the second stage": having already ascended three hundred yojanas, two hundred remain; therefore, it is called the second stage.

This passage clearly takes the three realms as three hundred and the two stages as two hundred; because the masters of the old translations did not thoroughly examine this text, various divergent interpretations arose.
The passage beginning with "At that time, the Tathāgata" below corresponds to the second section, the actual exposition of the teaching.
The first correspondence is the extinguishing of the conjured city.
The phrase "The stage upon which you stand is near to the Buddha’s wisdom" corresponds to the earlier statement, "The place where you go and come—the treasure site—is near."
"One should observe and deliberate that the nirvāṇa thus attained is not ultimate reality," referring back to the great city I previously manifested.

However, there is a distinction between those of the Two Vehicles who possess a wisdom near to the Buddha's and those whose wisdom is far from it; they consider the nirvāṇa they have attained to be the ultimate and do not accept the Mahāyāna. Thus the Sūtra says: "Lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land, yet even those who have committed the five grave offenses of immediate retribution can still resolve their minds [upon enlightenment]. This means that those of the Two Vehicles are further from the Buddha’s wisdom than even ordinary worldlings are.
Regarding the statement "now, as for 'near'": because the Two Vehicles have severed coarse afflictions and thus surpass ordinary beings, they are said to be "near.
From the passage beginning "like that guide" onwards is the fourth section, which provides an analogy and its application.
Forty-nine and a half verses in gāthā form serve as a commentary on the prose.
This prose originally consists of two parts:
first, the account of establishing karmic connections in the past; [and second, the account of the present].
Second, he further expounds the Dharma for the present.
Now, these two points are restated in verse.
Furthermore, there are two parts concerning the events of the past:
First, the origin of forming the karmic connection;
second, the actual formation of the karmic connection.
Now, these two are again versified here.
There are two types of causal conditions:
first, remote causal conditions;
second, proximate causal conditions.
Now, I shall again provide verses on these two matters.
Regarding the first, there are four sections:
the first is the attainment of Buddhahood by Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
2. The sixteen princes entreat him to turn the wheel of the Dharma;
3. Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū manifests auspicious omens;
4. The Brahma kings of the ten directions entreat him to preach the Dharma.
Now I shall fully set forth these four in verse.
The first section has three parts;
the first clarifies that he had not yet attained Buddhahood.
Second, the exposition on the offerings of the devas;
third, the exposition on the attainment of enlightenment.
These are now fully set forth in verse.
The first line praises the first [verse];
the next two lines praise the second;
the following line praises the third.
"Those sixteen sons of that Buddha," and so forth, is the second section: Requesting the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
The prose version originally consists of three parts:
first, the sixteen princes go to the Buddha’s abode for the purpose of requesting the Dharma;
2. Because he had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he respectfully praised him;
3. He requested that the Dharma be taught.
Now, these are fully set forth in verse:
The first line praises the first [verse];
one phrase praises the second;
and the three phrases beginning with "and requested the turning of the wheel of Dharma" praise the third.
From "The World-Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter" onwards, the third [section] praises the manifestation of auspicious omens.
This section has three parts:
first, the earthquake;...
Second, the emission of light;
third, the results of these two portents.
Here, this single verse praises only the first.
Below the section "The various worlds of the eastern direction," the fourth verse describes the assembly of Brahmās from the ten directions.
This section has three parts;
first, it clarifies the Brahmā hosts of three directions.
2. Extending the example to the other six directions;
3. Clarifying the direction above.
This is now divided into two parts:
The first three lines eulogize one direction;
the subsequent two lines provide examples for the other nine directions.
In each of the aforementioned directions there were six [points], but here only five are eulogized, as the point regarding "counseling" is omitted for brevity.
Furthermore, the single phrase "The Brahmās saw these signs" encompasses the deliberations; thus, it comprises six lines of verse.
The section beginning with "The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom" eulogizes the second [section] above: the causes and conditions for establishing the connection and the proximate conditions.
There are four [sections] above:
first, accepting the invitation to preach the Small Dharma;
second, the sixteen princes requesting the preaching of the Great [Dharma].
Third, accepting the invitation and expounding the Great [Teaching];
fourth, concluding the discourse on the sutra and entering meditative absorption.
I shall now provide a verse summarizing these points.
The first part, receiving the invitation, is explained in three sections:
first, the formal acceptance of the invitation;
second, the clarification of the single assembly’s preaching of the Dharma.
3. Clarifying the preaching of the Dharma across multiple assemblies.
Now, these are fully versified.
The first half-verse summarizes the first [assembly].

The second verse consists of two and a half lines. Regarding the phrase "six hundred *koṭi-nayuta* *kṣaya*," the prose section clarifies "six hundred *koṭi-nayuta*. Here, the term *kṣaya* (used in this context) serves as a substitute for the *nayuta* found in the former.
The two lines following "At the second time of preaching the Dharma" praise the many assemblies to whom the Dharma was preached.
"At that time, the sixteen princes" praises the second [event]: their request to preach the Great Dharma.
There are three parts above:
first, the request for renunciation, consisting of half a verse;
second, the formal request itself, consisting of one and a half verses.
The third section, concerning the retinue of the king, is omitted from the verse.
"The Buddha knew the mind of the youth" refers to the third section: accepting the invitation and preaching the Great Dharma.
This section contains three parts:
First, the teaching;
second, the differences in realization;
third, clarifying the timing of the discourse.
These two lines and a half only eulogize the first [section].
"That Buddha, having finished preaching the sutra," eulogizes his entry into meditative concentration after the preaching was complete.
Above this, there are three [points]:
First, the entry into meditative absorption is explained by half a verse;
next, abiding in meditative absorption is explained by one line of verse;
third, the duration of abiding in meditative absorption is also explained by one line of verse.
"Regarding 'these śrāmaṇeras,' the second [section] is the verse that formally concludes the establishment of the connection.
This [section] has two parts:
first, clarifying the establishment of the connection within a single lifetime."
Second, explaining their meeting life after life.
I shall now present this in full verse.
The first chapter has four sections:
First, knowing that the Buddha’s meditation had not yet ended, he now recited half a verse;
second, for the purpose of teaching the doctrine, he recited one and a half verses;
third, to clarify how the assembly gained benefit, he recited one verse.
The fourth section, concerning the Buddha’s emergence from samādhi and his expression of praise, is omitted from the verse.
The line “After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa” praises the second point: meeting one another life after life.
The prose section consists of four parts:
first, a single verse praising the benefits gained by those to be converted;
second, a single verse clarifying that the converter has attained Buddhahood.
Third, clarifying the connection between the past and present, [the author] summarizes this in one verse.
He briefly omits a verse for the fourth section on the future meeting of signs.
From the line "I was among the sixteen" onwards, he summarizes the second major section: the preaching of the Dharma in the present.
The prose section has four parts:
first, the Dharma; second, the analogy; [third, the application; fourth, the conclusion].
Third, conjunction;
fourth, cohesion.
Now I shall provide the verses for these.
The first two lines of verse praise the first [section].
The preceding text has two parts: first, the exposition of the Great [Vehicle]; [the second follows].
Next, the "Small" [version] is explained.
Now, only the "Great" [version] is versified.
The passage beginning with "For example, a perilous and evil road" versifies the second section, the illustrative explanation (*dṛṣṭānta*).
There are three parts above:
first, the analogy for the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna;
second, the analogy for the intermediate teaching of the Hīnayāna.
Third, the subsequent return to the explanation of the great parable.
I shall now present it in full verse.
In the first parable above, there are three parts:
First, the evil realms to be crossed;
second, the persons seeking to cross them;
third, the guide who leads them across.
Now I shall set forth these verses in full.
Regarding the phrase "many venomous beasts": those who possess the afflictions of craving and false views can harm the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom; thus, they are called venomous beasts.
"Without water or grass" means that he lacks the untainted concentration and wisdom of the Mahāyāna to sustain himself.
"Countless tens of millions of beings" praises the second point: those whom he wishes to deliver.
"At that time there was a guide" praises the third [section], the leading forward.
"The multitude were all exhausted" and below praise the second [section], the intermediate teaching of the minor parable.
There are three aspects above:
first, knowing the capacity [of the audience];
second, expounding the teaching.
III. Benefits. Now, these shall be set forth in verse.
Regarding the superior knowledge of the capacities [of beings], there are two types:
First, one verse in praise of the arousal of the aspiration by those of lesser capacity;
next, one verse in praise of the illumination of their capacities.
From "Seeking at that time for skillful means" onwards, there is the second section, the verse on the actual teaching, which consists of three parts:
First, the exposition of the teaching;
second, the admonition;
third, the exhortation.
I shall now provide them in full verse.

Regarding the term "city and its suburbs" (*nagara-gopura*): "city" is a specific metaphor for the two types of *nirvāṇa*, while "suburbs"—referring to the walled towns outside the city—is a general metaphor for all the merits of the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

Regarding the phrase "adorned with various dwellings," dwellings and groves are all within the city walls; this serves as a separate metaphor for the various remaining merits of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). Since the contaminated five aggregates (*sāsrava-pañcaskandha*) are called the "dwellings of birth and death," the uncontaminated five aggregates (*anāsrava-pañcaskandha*), where the noble ones (*ārya*) reside, are likewise called "dwellings."
Regarding the phrase "surrounded by gardens and groves": the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* takes the dhāraṇīs as the garden, while the Hīnayāna also possesses them according to its respective capacity.

In the *Āgama-sūtras*, the four immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—are taken as the four gardens, and the various untainted practices (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*) are termed the groves.
Regarding the phrase "channels and bathing pools": the mutual infusion of the nine successive attainments is called the channels, and the eight liberations are called the bathing pools.
The *Āgama* scriptures designate the four dhyānas as four ponds:

first, the pond of with-applied-thought and sustained-thought; second, the pond of without-applied-thought and without-sustained-thought; third, the pond of pure mindfulness and awareness; and fourth, the pond of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "heavy gates and lofty towers": the three samādhis are called the "heavy gates," and the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising is termed the "lofty tower.

Furthermore, among the various dhyānas, there are the dhyāna of cultivation (*khuṇa-dhyāna*) and the dhyāna of refinement (*lana-dhyāna*); these represent the pinnacle of all dhyānas and are thus named the "lofty tower."

Regarding the phrase "both men and women fill [it]," meditative concentration and wisdom constitute the man and woman; alternatively, the mind of compassion constitutes the woman, while a virtuous and sincere mind constitutes the man. These are present to some degree among the śrāvakas.
"The moment this transformation was completed" (one half-line) praises the second section, the Gate of Admonition.
The subsequent half-line praises the third section, the Exhortation.
"Once all the people had entered the city" (one line) praises the third [result], the Attainment of Benefit.
"Once the Teacher knew their breath had ceased," this verse [verse 3] subsequently restates the great analogy.
It has two parts:
first, knowing the capacity [of the disciples], which is versified in the first line;
2. The teaching is presented in two lines and one verse.
From "I am also like this" onwards, the third section, the application of the analogy, is versified.
This section has three parts:
First, there is the parable of the Mahāyāna; second, midway, the parable of the Hīnayāna; third, at the end, returning once more to the parable of the Mahāyāna.
I shall now set these forth in verse.
The first half-verse constitutes the first section, the analogy for initially preaching the Mahāyāna:
"Seeing those who seek the Way. This corresponds to the second section, the analogy for preaching the Hīnayāna midway; the preceding text contains three parts:
first, knowing the capacities [of the disciples].
Second, the teaching;
third, the benefit.
Regarding the first practice, the first verse [states]:
Next, the second verse;
"Having known that one reaches nirvāṇa" refers to the third [verse], which subsequently restates the great parable.
The preceding section has two parts:
First, knowing the capacity [of the audience];
second, expounding the teaching.

One and a half lines of verse praise the first [section], which simultaneously praises the third [section] above regarding the benefits obtained; three and a half lines of verse praise the second [section].
The line "The Guide of all Buddhas" constitutes the fourth verse, which provides an analogy and its application.

On the middle day of the Huangzhong month in the year of Yongren Jiawu, monastics and laypeople, men and women alike, joined their efforts to carve these verses for universal distribution. It is our wish that this merit may be offered upward to repay the four debts of gratitude and bestowed downward upon the beings of the three realms of existence.
Recorded respectfully by the monk Sùqìng, who oversees all affairs,
as a note on the ninth fascicle of the *Fahua yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) composed by Hú Jízàng.
Chapter Eight: The Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples.
Within the explanation of past-life causes and conditions, there are two sections; the first, the actual preaching of the Dharma, is now concluded.

This is now the second section, wherein the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) follows; because they have attained awakening through understanding the Dharma and their practice accords with that of the Buddha, the Buddha grants them his prediction.
The text consists generally of two parts:
first, the bestowal of predictions upon the five hundred disciples constitutes one chapter.
Next, the bestowal of predictions upon those who are in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitutes one chapter.

The reason for opening these as two separate chapters is that while the preceding "Chapter on Predictions" (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta) provides the general title, the present section wishes to distinguish itself from that; thus, by categorizing them according to the individuals, the general and specific titles are established so that their names do not overlap.
The reason for categorizing persons into two groups is based on ten principles, arranged in five pairs:
first, there are five hundred disciples whose vows and practices are identical; they receive their predictions simultaneously in the present and will attain Buddhahood in succession in the future.

Furthermore, those who are still training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) also have identical vows and practices; they receive their predictions simultaneously in the present and will attain Buddhahood at one time in the future. For these reasons, the two groups are established.
Second, one may wish to encompass the meaning of "bestowing a prediction" (vyākaraṇa) exhaustively through these two points.
Generally speaking, the bestowal of predictions does not exceed two types:
first, attaining Buddhahood in successive succession; [and second, attaining Buddhahood simultaneously].
Second, attaining Buddhahood simultaneously.

Third, the former five hundred are the group of those with lofty reputations and manifest virtues, while the latter two thousand are the group of those who conceal their names and practice in secret; these are divided into two categories because their respective classes differ in terms of the manifest and the secret.
Fourth, this is intended to exhaustively reveal the meaning of the prophecies (vyākaraṇa) for both the exoteric and esoteric recipients.

Fifth, while the previous five hundred people were all in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), the subsequent two thousand were in the stages of both learning (śaikṣa) and no-more-learning; thus, they are divided into two categories because their respective classes differ.
Sixth, it is because one wishes to encompass the meaning of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) through these two points exhaustively.

Seventh, while the previous five hundred people all attained understanding, the later learners and non-learners did not; thus, they are divided into two chapters due to this difference in their categories.
Eighth, these two meanings are intended to encompass the meaning of the bestowal of predictions exhaustively.

Ninth, among the previous five hundred people, there are those whose origins are revealed and those whose origins are not; for example, Pūrṇa’s origin is revealed while the others’ are not, thus they constitute one category.

Among the later learners and non-learners, there are likewise those whose origins are revealed and those whose origins are not; for example, Ānanda and Rāhula’s origins are revealed while the others’ are not, thus they further constitute another category. For these reasons, they are divided into two chapters.
